Mettāvagga Mettāsutta (The Discourse on Loving-kindness)
(AN 8.1, PTS AN iv 150) Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus.
“Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:

"Bhikkhus, when the liberation of mind through loving-kindness has been practiced, developed, cultivated, made a vehicle, made a foundation, established, consolidated, and well undertaken, eight benefits are to be expected.
What are the eight?"
One sleeps happily, wakes up happily, and does not see evil dreams;
one is dear to human beings, dear to non-human beings, and is protected by deities; fire, poison, or weapons do not affect one;
and if one does not penetrate further, one goes to the Brahma-world.
“Bhikkhus, when the liberation of mind through loving-kindness has been practiced, developed, cultivated, made a vehicle, made a foundation, established, consolidated, and properly undertaken,
these eight benefits are to be expected. And he who, being mindful, develops immeasurable loving-kindness...”
The fetters are severed for one who sees the destruction of acquisitions.
Even if one were to harm a single living being with a mind free from malice—
The skillful one is so called because he practices loving-kindness;
being compassionate toward all living beings with his mind,
the noble one performs abundant merit.
Those royal seers who, having conquered the earth with its seven divisions,
went about performing sacrifices—
the horse sacrifice and the human sacrifice—
The Sammāpāsa, the Vājapeyya, and the Niraggaḷa sacrifices—
even these do not equal a sixteenth part of a well-developed mind of loving-kindness.
All those who possess the radiance of the moon do not equal even a sixteenth part of him who neither kills nor causes others to kill.
He does not conquer, nor does he cause others to conquer;
with a heart of loving-kindness toward all beings,
he has no enmity toward anyone.
First. Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.2 1.
Mettāvagga (The Chapter on Loving-kindness)
The Discourse on Wisdom (Paññāsutta): “Monks,

there are these eight causes and eight conditions that lead to the acquisition of wisdom fundamental to the holy life not yet acquired, and to its increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment once it has been acquired.”
What are the eight?

Here, monks, a monk dwells in dependence upon the Teacher or upon a certain venerable companion in the holy life, in whom he has established a keen sense of shame and dread of wrongdoing, as well as affection and reverence.

This, monks, is the first cause, the first condition, for the acquisition of the wisdom fundamental to the holy life not yet acquired, and for the increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of that which has been acquired.
Thus, dwelling in dependence upon that teacher, or upon a certain venerable fellow-celibate,
toward whom a keen sense of shame and fear of wrongdoing, as well as affection and reverence, are established, he approaches them from time to time and questions and interrogates them:
‘Venerable sir, what is this? What is the meaning of this?
Then those venerable ones reveal to him what has not been revealed, clarify what has not been clarified, and dispel his doubt regarding various doubtful points.

This, monks, is the second cause and the second condition that leads to the acquisition of the wisdom fundamental to the holy life when it has not yet been acquired, and to its increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment once it has been acquired.
Having heard that Dhamma, he accomplishes it through two kinds of seclusion: seclusion of body and seclusion of mind.

This, monks, is the third cause and the third condition that leads to the acquisition of the wisdom fundamental to the holy life not yet acquired, and to its increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment once it has been acquired.

He is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and having undertaken them, he trains himself in the rules of training.

This, monks, is the fourth cause, the fourth condition, for the acquisition of the wisdom fundamental to the holy life not yet acquired, and for the increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of that which has been acquired.

One is learned, a retainer of what has been heard, and a storehouse of what has been heard. Those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the perfectly complete and pure holy life—such teachings as these he [possesses].
The teachings are well-heard by them, retained, mastered through speech, examined by the mind, and well-penetrated by view.

This, monks, is the fifth cause, the fifth condition, for the attainment of the wisdom fundamental to the holy life that has not yet been attained, and for its increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment once it has been attained.

He dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and for the acquisition of wholesome states; he is steadfast, firm in effort, and does not relinquish his burden regarding wholesome states.

This, monks, is the sixth cause, the sixth condition that leads to the acquisition of the wisdom fundamental to the holy life not yet acquired, and to its increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment once it has been acquired.
Furthermore, when he has entered the Saṅgha, he is not one who engages in various kinds of talk, nor in frivolous talk.
Either he speaks Dhamma himself, or he encourages another [to do so], or he does not despise noble silence.

This, monks, is the seventh cause, the seventh condition that leads to the acquisition of wisdom fundamental to the holy life not yet acquired, and to its increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment once it has been acquired.
Furthermore, he dwells contemplating the arising and passing away of the five aggregates of clinging:
‘Such is form, such its origin, such its passing away;
such is feeling, such its origin, such its passing away;
such is perception ... and so on.
‘Such are volitional formations...
such is consciousness, such its origin, such its passing away.

Monks, this is the eighth cause, the eighth condition that leads to the acquisition of the wisdom fundamental to the holy life not yet acquired, and to its increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment once it has been acquired.
His fellow celibates regard him thus:

“This venerable one dwells in dependence upon the Teacher, or upon some other venerable senior companion in the holy life, toward whom he maintains a keen sense of shame and dread of wrongdoing, as well as affection and reverence.
Surely this venerable one knows what should be known and sees what should be seen.”
This quality, too, leads to endearment, to respect, to development, to concord, and to unity. Now,

this venerable one, dwelling in dependence upon the Teacher or some other senior fellow-celibate toward whom he maintains a keen sense of shame and fear of wrongdoing, as well as affection and reverence—
From time to time, they approach him and inquire and question him, saying:
"Venerable sir, what is this? What is the meaning of this?
Those venerable ones reveal to him what has not been revealed, clarify what has not been made clear, and dispel his doubt regarding various points that give rise to uncertainty.
‘Surely this venerable one knows what he knows and sees what he sees.
This quality also leads to endearment, respect, esteem, concord, and unity.
‘Having heard that Dhamma, this venerable one practices it with a twofold seclusion: seclusion of body and seclusion of mind.’
"Surely this venerable one knows what should be known and sees what should be seen.
This quality also leads to being dear, to being respected, to development, to concord, and to unity.

"Furthermore, this venerable one is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and having undertaken them, he trains himself in the rules of training."
‘Surely this venerable one knows what he knows and sees what he sees.
This quality also leads to being dear, to being respected, to development, to concord, and to unity.
Furthermore, ‘This venerable one is learned, a bearer of the teachings, one who has accumulated what he has heard. Those teachings which are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and...’
They proclaim the holy life that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, entirely complete and pure;
such teachings as these he has heard much of, retained in mind, mastered verbally, examined by the mind,
and well penetrated through right view.
‘Surely this venerable one knows what he knows and sees what he sees.
This quality also leads to being dear, to being respected, to development, to sameness, and to unity.

Furthermore, ‘this venerable one dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and for the acquisition of wholesome states; he is steadfast, firm in his exertion, and not one who casts off the burden regarding wholesome states.’
"Surely this venerable one knows what should be known and sees what should be seen.
This quality also leads to being dear, to being respected, to development, to concord, and to unity.
"Furthermore, when this venerable one has entered the Saṅgha, he does not engage in various kinds of talk, nor in frivolous chatter."
Either he speaks Dhamma himself, or he exhorts another, or he does not disregard noble silence.
Surely this venerable one knows what should be known and sees what should be seen.
This quality also leads to being dear, to being respected, to development, to concord, and to unity.
Furthermore, this venerable one dwells contemplating the arising and passing away in the five aggregates subject to clinging:
“Such is form, such its origin, such its passing away;
such is feeling … [and so on] …”
"Such is perception...
such are volitional formations...
such is consciousness, such is the arising of consciousness, such is the passing away of consciousness."
"Surely this venerable one knows what should be known and sees what should be seen.
This, too, is a quality that leads to endearment, to respect, to development, to concord, and to unity.

"Monks, these eight causes and eight conditions lead to the acquisition of the wisdom fundamental to the holy life not yet acquired, and to its increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment once it has been acquired."
The Second.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.3 1.
The Chapter on Loving-kindness (Mettāvagga)
The First Discourse on the Unpleasant (Paṭhama-appiya-sutta):
“Bhikkhus, possessed of eight qualities, a bhikkhu is unpleasant, disagreeable, not respected, and not esteemed by his fellow celibates.”
By which eight?
Here, monks, a monk praises those he dislikes, censures those he likes, desires gain, desires honor, is shameless, is unscrupulous, has evil desires, and holds wrong view.
Possessing these eight qualities, monks, a monk is disliked and displeasing to his fellow celibates, and is neither respected nor esteemed by them.
“Bhikkhus, possessing eight qualities, a bhikkhu is dear and agreeable to his fellow celibates, and is respected and esteemed by them.
What are these eight?

Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu does not praise those who are disliked, nor does he disparage those who are liked; he does not desire gain, nor does he desire honor; he is possessed of moral shame and moral dread; he has few desires and holds right view.”
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who possesses these eight qualities is dear and agreeable to his fellow celibates, and is respected and esteemed by them.
The third [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.4
1. The Chapter on Loving-kindness (Mettāvagga) The Second Discourse on the Unpleasant (Dutiya-appiyasutta) (AN 8.4, PTS AN iv 156)
“Bhikkhus, possessing eight qualities, a bhikkhu is displeasing and disagreeable to his fellow celibates, and is neither respected nor esteemed by them.
What eight?

Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is desirous of gain, desirous of honor, desirous of not being despised; he lacks knowledge of the proper time, lacks knowledge of moderation, is impure, is a talkative chatterer, and is one who reviles and insults his fellow celibates. Possessing these eight qualities, a bhikkhu is displeasing and disagreeable to his fellow celibates, and is neither respected nor esteemed by them.”
“Monks, a monk endowed with these eight qualities is disliked and displeasing to his fellow celibates, and he is neither respected nor esteemed by them.

Monks, a monk endowed with eight qualities is liked and pleasing to his fellow celibates, and he is respected and esteemed by them. With which eight? [The Buddha then enumerates the eight qualities.]”
“Here, monks, a monk does not desire gain, nor does he desire honor, nor does he desire not to be despised;
he knows the right time, he knows the proper measure, he is pure, he is not talkative, and he does not revile or disparage his fellow practitioners of the holy life.
Endowed with these eight qualities, monks, a monk is dear and agreeable to his fellow practitioners of the holy life, and he is respected and esteemed.”
The Fourth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.5 1.
Mettāvagga (The Chapter on Loving-kindness)
Paṭhamalokadhammasutta:

“Bhikkhus, these eight worldly conditions revolve around the world, and the world revolves around these eight worldly conditions. What eight? Gain and loss, fame and disrepute, praise and blame, pleasure and pain.”
What are the eight?
Gain and loss, fame and disrepute, blame and praise, pleasure and pain.
These, monks, are the eight worldly conditions that revolve around the world, and the world revolves around these eight worldly conditions.
Gain and loss, fame and disrepute,
blame and praise, pleasure and pain—
these things among human beings are impermanent.
They are impermanent and subject to change.
Having understood this, the mindful and wise one contemplates these things as subject to change.
Desirable things do not agitate his mind,
nor does he meet with aversion toward the undesirable.
Thus, through neither attraction nor repulsion, [his mind remains steady].
Blown out and gone to rest, they no longer exist;
having known the dustless, sorrowless state,
he understands with perfect wisdom, having reached the further shore of existence.
Fifth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.6 1.
Mettāvagga (The Chapter on Loving-kindness)
The Second Discourse on Worldly Conditions (Dutiyalokadhammasutta): “Bhikkhus,
these eight worldly conditions revolve around the world, and the world revolves around these eight worldly conditions.”
Which eight?
Gain and loss, fame and disrepute, blame and praise, pleasure and pain.
These, monks, are the eight worldly conditions that revolve around the world, and the world revolves around these eight worldly conditions.
“Bhikkhus, gain, loss, fame, infamy, blame, praise, pleasure, and pain arise for the uninstructed worldling.
Gain, loss, fame, infamy, blame, praise, pleasure, and pain also arise for the instructed noble disciple.
In this regard, bhikkhus, what is the distinction, what is the specific difference, what is the disparity between the instructed noble disciple and the uninstructed worldling?”
“Venerable sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, guided by the Blessed One, and have the Blessed One as their refuge.
It would be well, venerable sir, if the Blessed One himself would explain the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it.
“In that case, bhikkhus, listen and attend closely; I shall speak.”
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, gain arises for the uninstructed worldling.
Thus he does not reflect:
“This gain has arisen for me;
and it is indeed impermanent, suffering, and subject to change,” nor does he understand it as it really is.
Loss arises … fame arises … ill-fame arises … [and so on].
Censure arises… praise arises… pleasure arises…
Suffering arises.
He does not reflect thus:
‘This suffering has arisen in me;’
And yet he does not understand it as it really is: ‘This is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change.
For him, gain obsesses the mind; loss obsesses the mind; fame obsesses the mind;
disrepute obsesses the mind; and blame also obsesses the mind.
Praise remains, taking possession of the mind; pleasure remains, taking possession of the mind;
pain also remains, taking possession of the mind.
He becomes attached to gain that has arisen and repelled by lack of gain.
One is favorably disposed toward fame that has arisen and opposed to ill-repute;
one is favorably disposed toward praise that has arisen and opposed to blame;
one is favorably disposed toward pleasure that has arisen and opposed to pain.
Thus, being beset by attraction and aversion, one is not liberated from birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
"One is not liberated from suffering," I say.
But for the learned noble disciple, monks, gain arises.
Thus he reflects:
"This gain has arisen for me;
and it is indeed impermanent, suffering, and subject to change," and he understands this as it really is.
Loss arises … fame arises … ill-fame arises … [and so on] … disgrace arises.
Censure arises … praise arises … pleasure arises …
Suffering arises.
He reflects thus:
"This suffering has indeed arisen in me."
And he understands it as it really is: ‘This too is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change.
Thus, gain does not persist by obsessing his mind; loss does not persist by obsessing his mind;
fame does not persist by obsessing his mind; disrepute does not persist by obsessing his mind; and blame...
Praise does not persist by obsessing the mind; even pleasure does not persist by obsessing the mind;
even pain does not persist by obsessing the mind.
He does not become elated when gain arises, nor does he become dejected when there is no gain.
One does not cling to fame when it arises, nor does one resist ill-repute;
one does not cling to praise when it arises, nor does one resist blame;
one does not cling to pleasure when it arises, nor does one resist pain.
Thus, having abandoned both attraction and aversion, one is liberated from birth, aging, and death; from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
"One is liberated from suffering," I say.
This, monks, is the distinction, this is the specific intention, this is the difference between an instructed noble disciple and an uninstructed worldling.
Gain and loss, fame and disrepute,
blame and praise, pleasure and pain—
these conditions among human beings are impermanent.
They are impermanent and subject to change.
Having understood this, the mindful and wise one contemplates these things as being subject to change.
Desirable things do not disturb his mind,
nor does he meet with aversion toward the undesirable.
Because of neither attraction nor repulsion, [his mind remains steady].
Blown out and gone to rest, they no longer exist;
having known the dustless, sorrowless state,
he understands rightly, having reached the further shore of existence.
The Sixth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.7 1.
The Chapter on Loving-kindness (Mettāvagga)
The Discourse on Devadatta’s Downfall (Devadattavipattisutta).
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain, not long after Devadatta had departed.
There, regarding Devadatta, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“It is good, bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu from time to time to reflect upon his own failure.
It is good, bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu from time to time to reflect upon the failure of others.”
"It is good, bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu from time to time to reflect upon his own success.
It is good, bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu from time to time to reflect upon the success of others.
Overcome by eight things that are not true Dhamma, with a mind consumed by them, Devadatta is destined for the plane of misery, for hell, to remain there for an eon, beyond all remedy."
By which eight?
For, monks, Devadatta, being overcome and possessed by gain, is destined for the states of deprivation, for hell, remaining there for an eon, incurable.
By loss, monks... [and so on].
By fame, monks, ...
by ill repute, monks, ...
by honor, monks, ...
"Monks, Devadatta— overcome and with his mind consumed by lack of respect,
monks, by evil desires, monks,
and by evil friendship, monks— is destined for the states of deprivation, for hell, remaining there for an eon, beyond remedy."
"Overcome and possessed by these eight unrighteous qualities, monks, Devadatta is destined for the state of deprivation, for hell, remaining there for an eon, incurable.
It is good, monks, that a monk should dwell having repeatedly overcome gain when it arises;
[having repeatedly overcome] loss when it arises... [and so on]."
... arisen fame ...
arisen ill-repute ...
arisen honor ...
One should dwell having repeatedly overcome any disrespect that has arisen, any evil desire that has arisen, and any evil friendship that has arisen.
And for what purpose, monks, should a monk dwell having repeatedly overcome whatever gain has arisen,
whatever loss has arisen,
… [and] whatever fame has arisen?
... arisen ill repute ...
arisen honor ... arisen dishonor ...
“Could one dwell having repeatedly overcome arisen evil desires… arisen evil friends? For, monks,
those taints, vexations, and fevers that would arise in one who dwells without having overcome arisen gain do not exist for one who dwells having overcome arisen gain.”
For whatever loss has arisen for him, monks, ... [and so on] ... whatever fame has arisen, ... whatever ill-repute has arisen, ... [he does not give way to it].
... arisen honor ... arisen dishonor ...
arisen evil desire ...

“Monks, for one who dwells without having overcome arisen association with evil friends, taints that are vexation and fever might arise; but for one who dwells having overcome arisen association with evil friends, those taints that are vexation and fever do not exist.
It is for this purpose, monks, that a monk should dwell having repeatedly overcome arisen gain, and arisen loss … [and so on] …”
... arisen fame ...
arisen ill-repute ...
arisen honor ...
One should dwell having repeatedly overcome any disrespect that has arisen, any evil desire that has arisen, and any evil friendship that has arisen.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
“We will dwell having repeatedly overcome gain when it arises; we will dwell having repeatedly overcome loss when it arises... [and so on].
… arisen fame … arisen ill-repute … arisen honor …
‘We shall dwell having repeatedly overcome any disrespect that has arisen, any evil desire that has arisen, and any evil friendship that has arisen.’”
“In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
The seventh [sutta]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.8.

1. Mettāvagga Uttaravipattisutta (AN 8.8, PTS AN iv 162) “Monks, there are these five higher failures. What five? Failure in morality, failure in concentration, failure in wisdom, failure in liberation, and failure in the knowledge and vision of liberation. These, monks, are the five higher failures.”
On one occasion the Venerable Uttara was dwelling at Mahisavatthu, on Saṅkheyyaka Mountain, in the Banyan Grove.
There the Venerable Uttara addressed the bhikkhus:
“It is good, friends, for a bhikkhu from time to time to review his own failings.
“Excellent, friend! A bhikkhu should from time to time reflect upon the failure of others.
Excellent, friend! A bhikkhu should from time to time reflect upon his own success.
Excellent, friend! A bhikkhu should from time to time reflect upon the success of others.”
Now at that time, the Great King Vessavaṇa was traveling from the northern direction toward the southern direction on some business.
The Great King Vessavaṇa heard the Venerable Uttara teaching the Dhamma to the bhikkhus in this way at Vaṭajālikā on Mount Saṅkheyyaka in Mahisavatthu:
"It is good, friend, if a bhikkhu from time to time reflects upon his own failings."
“Excellent, friend! A bhikkhu should from time to time reflect upon the failure of others.
Excellent, friend! A bhikkhu should from time to time reflect upon his own success.
Excellent, friend! A bhikkhu should from time to time reflect upon the success of others.”
Then the Great King Vessavaṇa— just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm—
disappeared from the Vaṭajālikā cave on Mount Saṅkheyyaka in Mahisavatthu and reappeared among the Tāvatiṃsa devas.
Then Vessavaṇa the Great King approached Sakka, lord of the devas; having approached, he said this to Sakka, lord of the devas:
“Please know, dear sir, that this venerable Uttara, at Mahisavatthu on Mount Saṅkheyyaka, in the Vaṭajālikā grove, teaches the Dhamma to the bhikkhus thus:”
“It is good, friend, that a bhikkhu from time to time reflects upon his own failure.
It is good, friend, that a bhikkhu from time to time reflects upon the failure of others...
[and] reflects upon his own success...”
“He reflects upon the prosperity of others.
Then Sakka, lord of the devas, just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm,
vanished from among the Tāvatiṃsa devas and reappeared at Mahisavatthu.
On Mount Saṅkheyyaka, in a bower of creepers, he appeared before the Venerable Uttara.
Then Sakka, lord of the devas, approached the Venerable Uttara;
having approached and paid homage to the Venerable Uttara, he stood to one side. Standing to one side, Sakka, lord of the devas, said this to the Venerable Uttara:
“Is it true, venerable sir, that the Venerable Uttara teaches the Dhamma to the bhikkhus thus:
‘It is good, friends, if from time to time a bhikkhu reflects on his own failure;
it is good, friends, if from time to time a bhikkhu reflects on the failure of others...’?”
“Does he review his own success … and the success of others?”—
“Yes, Lord of the Devas.”
“But, venerable sir, was this the Venerable Uttara’s own inspired thought, or was it the word of the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One?
“In that case, Lord of the Devas, I shall give you a simile.
For by means of a simile some wise people here understand the meaning of what has been said.”
"Just as, Lord of the Devas, there might be a great heap of grain not far from a village or a town,
and a great crowd of people were to carry away that grain—
with carrying-poles, with baskets, with their laps, and with their cupped hands."
“Lord of the Devas, if someone were to approach that great multitude and ask:
‘From where do you bring this grain? how, Lord of the Devas, would that great multitude answer correctly if they were to answer rightly?
“Venerable sir, that great multitude would answer correctly by saying: ‘We bring it from that great heap of grain.’”
“In the same way, Lord of Devas, whatever is well-spoken is all the word of that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
It is from him, taking it as our basis, that both we and others speak.
“It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is marvelous, venerable sir!”
"How well spoken this was by the Venerable Uttara:
'Whatever is well spoken, all that is the word of the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
It is by taking that as our basis, again and again, that both I and others speak.'"
“On one occasion, venerable Uttara, the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain, not long after Devadatta had departed.
There, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus concerning Devadatta:
‘It is good, bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu from time to time to reflect upon his own failure.’”
It is good, bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu from time to time to reflect upon the failure of others...
[and so on] ...to reflect upon his own success and the success of others.
"Monks, Devadatta, overcome and possessed by eight things that are not true Dhamma, is destined for the states of deprivation, for hell, remaining there for an eon, beyond help.
By which eight?
Monks, Devadatta, overcome and possessed by gain... is destined for the states of deprivation, for hell, remaining there for an eon, beyond help."
By non-gain, monks … by fame,
monks … by ill-repute, monks …
“By honor, monks … by lack of honor,
monks … by evil desire, monks …”
"Overpowered by bad friendship, monks, and with his mind overwhelmed by it, Devadatta is destined for the states of deprivation, for hell, remaining there for an eon, incurable.

Overpowered and with his mind overwhelmed by these eight things that are not the true Dhamma, monks, Devadatta is destined for the states of deprivation, for hell, remaining there for an eon, incurable.
It is good, monks, if a monk should dwell having repeatedly overcome gain when it has arisen."
Arising loss …pe… arising fame … arising disrepute …
... arisen honor ... arisen dishonor ...
arisen evil desire ...
He should dwell having repeatedly overcome any arisen association with evil friends.
And for what purpose, monks, should a monk dwell having repeatedly overcome any arisen gain;
any arisen loss... [and so on]?"
... arisen fame ...
arisen ill-repute ...
arisen honor ...
Could one dwell having repeatedly overcome arisen lack of honor… arisen evil desires… arisen evil friendship?

For whatever taints, vexations, and fevers might arise in one who dwells without having overcome arisen gain, those taints, vexations, and fevers do not arise in one who dwells having overcome arisen gain. Whatever taints, vexations, and fevers might arise in one who dwells without having overcome arisen loss... [and so on] ...arisen fame... [and so on] ...arisen disrepute... [and so on] ...arisen praise... [and so on] ...arisen blame... [and so on] ...arisen pleasure... [and so on] ...arisen pain, those taints, vexations, and fevers do not arise in one who dwells having overcome them. Why is that?

Because, bhikkhus, for one who has abandoned craving, cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, obliterated it so that it is no more subject to future arising, there is no basis for the arising of taints, vexations, and fevers. Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus: "We will dwell having overcome arisen gain... arisen loss... arisen fame... arisen disrepute... arisen praise... arisen blame... arisen pleasure... arisen pain. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that you should train yourselves.
...arisen ill repute ...
arisen honor ... arisen dishonor ...

“Monks, for one who dwells without having overcome arisen evil desires… arisen evil friendship, taints that are distressing and feverish might arise; but for one who dwells having overcome arisen evil friendship, those taints that are distressing and feverish do not exist.
This, monks, is the purpose for which a monk, out of regard for his welfare, should dwell having repeatedly overcome arisen gain.”
Arising loss …pe… arising fame … arising disrepute …
... arisen honor ... arisen dishonor ...
arisen evil desire ...
One should dwell having repeatedly overcome any arisen intimacy with evil friends.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
"We will dwell having repeatedly overcome any arisen gain."
Arising loss...
arising fame...
arising disrepute...
...arisen honor... arisen dishonor...
arisen evil desire...
“Having repeatedly overcome any arisen intimacy with evil friends, we shall dwell [thus].
“In this way, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves.
To this extent, venerable Uttara, among humans there are four assemblies.
"Bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, male lay followers, and female lay followers.
This exposition of the Dhamma does not apply to anyone at all.
Venerable Uttara, please learn this exposition of the Dhamma."
"Venerable sir, let the Venerable Uttara master this discourse on the Dhamma.
Venerable sir, let the Venerable Uttara bear in mind this discourse on the Dhamma;
for this discourse on the Dhamma, venerable sir, is beneficial and pertains to the fundamentals of the holy life."
The Eighth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.9 1.
The Chapter on Loving-kindness (Mettāvagga)
“Monks, one who speaks rightly of Nanda would say: ‘He is a son of good family. (Nandasutta, AN 8.9, PTS AN iv 166)
“‘Strong,’ monks, is the right way to describe Nanda.
‘Charming,’ monks, is the right way to describe Nanda.
‘Intensely passionate,’ monks, is the right way to describe Nanda.”
"Monks, what else could it be but that Nanda guards the doors of his sense faculties, is moderate in eating, is devoted to wakefulness,
and is endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension— by means of which Nanda is able to lead the full and pure holy life?
In this regard, monks, this is how Nanda guards the doors of his sense faculties."
“Monks, if Nanda must look toward the eastern direction, he looks toward the eastern direction having applied his whole mind, thinking:
‘May no covetousness, grief, or evil unwholesome states flow into me as I look toward the eastern direction.
Thus, in that regard, he is clearly comprehending.”
“Monks, if Nanda must look toward the western direction...
[as before] ...if he must look toward the northern direction...
if he must look toward the southern direction...”
He must look upward;
he must look downward;
he must look toward the intermediate directions. Having applied his whole mind, Nanda looks toward the intermediate directions:
‘As I survey the quarters in this way, no evil, unwholesome states—such as covetousness and dejection—will flow in after me.
Thus, in that regard, he is clearly comprehending.
This, monks, is what constitutes Nanda’s guarding of the doors of the sense faculties.
In this regard, monks, this is Nanda’s moderation regarding food:
here, monks, Nanda consumes food with wise reflection:
“Neither for amusement, nor for intoxication, nor for physical beauty, nor for adornment, but only for the maintenance of this body.”
‘For the sake of sustenance, for the cessation of affliction, and for support of the holy life, thinking:
“I shall eliminate old feelings and not give rise to new feelings, and there will be for me maintenance, blamelessness, and a comfortable dwelling.
This, monks, is what constitutes moderation in food for Nanda.
In this regard, monks, this is Nanda’s application to wakefulness:
here, monks, during the day Nanda purifies his mind of obstructive states while walking and sitting;
during the first watch of the night, he purifies his mind of obstructive states while walking and sitting.

During the middle watch of the night, he lies down on his right side in the lion’s posture, with one foot placed upon the other, mindful and clearly comprehending, having fixed his mind on the perception of rising.
During the last watch of the night, having risen, he purifies his mind from obstructive states by means of walking and sitting.
This, monks, is Nanda’s practice of vigilance.
In this regard, monks, this is Nanda’s mindfulness and clear comprehension:
here, monks, Nanda’s feelings arise known, they persist known, and they pass away known; his perceptions... [as before]... arise known, they persist known, and they pass away known.
Thoughts, being understood, pass away... [as before] ...they go to their destruction.
This, monks, is what constitutes Nanda’s mindfulness and clear comprehension.
What else could it be, monks, other than that Nanda guards the doors of his sense faculties, is moderate in eating, and is devoted to wakefulness?
“Endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension, Nanda is able to lead the complete and pure holy life.
Thus was the ninth [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.10.
1. The Chapter on Loving-kindness:
The Kāraṇḍava Sutta (AN 8.10, PTS AN iv 168)
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Campā on the bank of the Gaggarā Lotus Pond.
Now at that time, monks were accusing a monk of an offense.
While being accused of an offense by the monks, that monk evaded the issue with irrelevant talk, diverted the conversation to extraneous matters, and displayed anger, hatred, and resentment.
Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Expel this person, bhikkhus! Expel this person, bhikkhus!”
“Monks, a person is one who should be removed.
What have you to do with that son of another who has been cleared?
Here, monks, for a certain person, his going forth and returning, his looking ahead and looking aside, are exactly as they were before.”

His looking about, his contracting [of limbs], his extending [of limbs], and his wearing of the outer robe, bowl, and robes were just like those of other excellent bhikkhus—so long as the bhikkhus did not perceive an offense in him.
But when the bhikkhus did perceive an offense in him, they knew him thus: [he is a transgressor].
‘This one is a defiler of ascetics, a chaff of ascetics, a mere duckweed among ascetics.
Having recognized him as such, they expel him from the community.
And for what reason?
"Do not corrupt other virtuous bhikkhus. Just as, monks,
when there is a good barley field, a barley-weed might grow— a mere chaff or a worthless weed of barley—
its root is exactly like that of the other good barley.
Its stalk is exactly like that of other excellent barley;
its leaf is exactly like that of other excellent barley—
until its head has emerged.
But when a head grows upon it, people recognize it as such, saying:
“This is a mere husk of barley, a chaff of barley, a weed of barley.
Having recognized it as such, they pull it up by the roots and cast it outside the barley field.
And why is that? Lest you should spoil the excellent barley!
In the same way, monks, here some person has such a gait and such a manner of returning from walking.
His looking ahead and looking aside, his bending and stretching, and his manner of carrying the outer robe, bowl, and inner robe were just like those of other excellent bhikkhus,
so that the bhikkhus did not perceive any offense in him.
But when the monks see his offense, they recognize him thus:
"This man is a defiler of ascetics, a chaff of ascetics, a mere reed of ascetics.
Having recognized him as such, they expel him from the community.
For what reason?
Lest you corrupt other excellent bhikkhus.
Just as, bhikkhus, when a great heap of grain is being winnowed, those grains there which...
Those grains that are firm and substantial form a heap on one side,
while the wind carries away to one side those grains that are weak and chaff-like.
Then the owners, taking a broom, sweep them away even more thoroughly.
And why is that? Lest he should spoil other excellent grain.
In the same way, monks, here some person has exactly such a manner of going forth and returning.
His looking ahead and looking aside, his bending and stretching, and his manner of wearing the outer robe, bowl, and inner robe were just like those of other excellent bhikkhus—
as long as the bhikkhus did not perceive any offense in him.
But when the monks see his offense, they know him thus:
"This man is a defiler of ascetics, a mere chaff of ascetics, a rotten reed among ascetics.
Having recognized him as such, they expel him from the community.
For what reason?
Lest you corrupt other excellent bhikkhus.
Just as if, bhikkhus, a man needing a well-pipe were to take a sharp axe and enter a forest.
Thus, whichever tree he might strike with the handle of his axe—those trees that are firm and possessed of heartwood, when struck by the handle of the axe, resound with a harsh sound;
but those trees that are rotten inside, sapless, and of a foul nature, when struck by the handle of the axe, resound with a hollow sound.

He cuts it at the root; having cut it at the root, he cuts it at the top; having cut it at the top, he thoroughly cleanses the interior; having thoroughly cleansed the interior, he fits it as a water-pipe for a well.
In the same way, monks, here some person’s manner of going forward and returning,
looking ahead and looking aside, drawing in and extending the limbs, and carrying the outer robe, bowl, and upper robe,
is exactly like that of other excellent bhikkhus.
As long as the monks do not perceive his offense, they remain unaware.
But when the monks do perceive his offense, they know him thus:
"This man is a defiler of ascetics, a mere chaff of ascetics, a mere reed of ascetics."
Knowing him to be such, they expel him from the community. Why is that?
So that he does not corrupt other excellent bhikkhus.
In living together, you should recognize him as one who has evil desires and is prone to anger,
as well as one who is hypocritical, stubborn, and spiteful.
Envious, stingy, and deceitful,
he speaks kindly among the people and talks like a true ascetic.
He acts in secret,
possesses evil views, and is disrespectful;
he is a crawler and a speaker of falsehood.
Having understood that as it truly is,
all of you, becoming united,
should utterly reject it.
Sweep away the kāraṇḍava reeds;
pull out the kasambu weeds;
then winnow away the chaff.
Having expelled those who are not ascetics yet pride themselves on being ascetics—
those of evil desires and evil conduct and resort—
Live with those who are pure among the pure,
being mindful; then, being harmonious and prudent, [you shall dwell in peace].
"You shall make an end of suffering.
Tenth. The First Chapter on Loving-kindness.
Its summary verse:
Loving-kindness and wisdom, two dear things,
two worlds, and two failures.
Devadatta and Uttara,
Nanda and Kāraṇḍava.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.11

2. Mahāvagga Verañjasutta (AN 8.11, PTS AN iv 172) Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Verañjā, in the fig tree grove of the Squirrels’ Feeding Place. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” they replied. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who dwells for the sake of self, not for the sake of others; the person who dwells for the sake of others, not for the sake of self; the person who dwells neither for the sake of self nor for the sake of others; and the person who dwells both for the sake of self and for the sake of others. And how, bhikkhus, does a person dwell for the sake of self, not for the sake of others? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person dwells pursuing the development of the basis for power that possesses concentration due to desire and volitional formations of desire; he does not pursue the development of the basis for power that possesses concentration due to energy... concentration due to mind... concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of investigation. This is called a person who dwells for the sake of self, not for the sake of others. And how, bhikkhus, does a person dwell for the sake of others, not for the sake of self? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person dwells pursuing the development of the basis for power that possesses concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of investigation; he does not pursue the development of the basis for power that possesses concentration due to desire... concentration due to energy... concentration due to mind. This is called a person who dwells for the sake of others, not for the sake of self. And how, bhikkhus, does a person dwell neither for the sake of self nor for the sake of others? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person does not dwell pursuing the development of the basis for power that possesses concentration due to desire and volitional formations of desire, nor does he dwell pursuing the development of the basis for power that possesses concentration due to energy... concentration due to mind... concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of investigation. This is called a person who dwells neither for the sake of self nor for the sake of others. And how, bhikkhus, does a person dwell both for the sake of self and for the sake of others? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person dwells pursuing the development of the basis for power that possesses concentration due to desire and volitional formations of desire; he also dwells pursuing the development of the basis for power that possesses concentration due to energy... concentration due to mind... concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of investigation. This is called a person who dwells both for the sake of self and for the sake of others. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is marvelous, venerable sir! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One:

‘There are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. “It is wonderful, Ānanda! It is marvelous, Ānanda! How well this has been stated by you: ‘It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is marvelous, venerable sir! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: "There are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. “Why is that, Ānanda? Because this Dhamma has been well-expounded by me—clear, open, evident, free from obscurity, accessible, leading onward, to be realized by the wise each for themselves. Therefore, Ānanda, it is fitting for you to state: 'It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is marvelous, venerable sir! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: "There are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, the Venerable Ānanda delighted in the Blessed One’s words. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Verañjā, in the fig tree grove of the Squirrels’ Feeding Place. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” they replied. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who dwells for the sake of self, not for the sake of others; the person who dwells for the sake of others, not for the sake of self; the person who dwells neither for the sake of self nor for the sake of others; and the person who dwells both for the sake of self and for the sake of others. And how, bhikkhus, does a person dwell for the sake of self, not for the sake of others? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person dwells pursuing the development of the basis for power that possesses concentration due to desire and volitional formations of desire; he does not pursue the development of the basis for power that possesses concentration due to energy... concentration due to mind... concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of investigation. This is called a person who dwells for the sake of self, not for the sake of others. And how, bhikkhus, does a person dwell for the sake of others, not for the sake of self? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person dwells pursuing the development of the basis for power that possesses concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of investigation; he does not pursue the development of the basis for power that possesses concentration due to desire... concentration due to energy... concentration due to mind. This is called a person who dwells for the sake of others, not for the sake of self. And how, bhikkhus, does a person dwell neither for the sake of self nor for the sake of others? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person does not dwell pursuing the development of the basis for power that possesses concentration due to desire and volitional formations of desire, nor does he dwell pursuing the development of the basis for power that possesses concentration due to energy... concentration due to mind... concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of investigation. This is called a person who dwells neither for the sake of self nor for the sake of others. And how, bhikkhus, does a person dwell both for the sake of self and for the sake of others? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person dwells pursuing the development of the basis for power that possesses concentration due to desire and volitional formations of desire; he also dwells pursuing the development of the basis for power that possesses concentration due to energy... concentration due to mind... concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of investigation. This is called a person who dwells both for the sake of self and for the sake of others. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is marvelous, venerable sir! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘There are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. “It is wonderful, Ānanda! It is marvelous, Ānanda! How well this has been stated by you: ‘It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is marvelous, venerable sir! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: "There are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. “Why is that, Ānanda? Because this Dhamma has been well-expounded by me—clear, open, evident, free from obscurity, accessible, leading onward, to be realized by the wise each for themselves. Therefore, Ānanda, it is fitting for you to state: 'It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is marvelous, venerable sir! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: "There are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, the Venerable Ānanda delighted in the Blessed One’s words.
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Verañjā, at the foot of the Naleru Pucimanda tree.
Then the brahmin of Verañjā approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
Having exchanged greetings and pleasantries with him, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the brahmin of Verañjā said this to the Blessed One:
“I have heard this, Master Gotama:
‘The ascetic Gotama does not pay homage to aged, elderly, senior brahmins who are advanced in years and have reached the end of their lifespan; nor does he rise for them or invite them to a seat.’”
"Indeed, Master Gotama, it is just so.
For Master Gotama does not pay homage to brahmins who are aged, elderly, advanced in years, come to the end of their life-span, nor does he rise up for them or invite them to a seat.
This, Master Gotama, is certainly not proper."

“Brahmin, I do not see anyone in the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, whom I should honor, rise for, or invite to a seat.
For if the Tathāgata were to honor, rise for, or invite anyone to a seat, his head would split apart.
“Master Gotama is devoid of flavor,” [said the brahmin].
“There is, brahmin, a way in which one speaking rightly could say of me:
‘The ascetic Gotama is devoid of flavor.

For those flavors of forms, flavors of sounds, flavors of odors, flavors of tastes, and flavors of tangibles that exist, brahmin, have been abandoned by the Tathāgata, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and are no longer subject to future arising.”
“This, brahmin, is the way in which one speaking rightly might say of me:
‘The ascetic Gotama is without flavor,’ yet it is not with reference to what you have said.
“The venerable Gotama is without enjoyment,” [he said].
“There is, brahmin, a way in which one speaking rightly might say of me:
‘The ascetic Gotama is one who enjoys nothing.

For those enjoyments of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tactile objects, brahmin, have been abandoned by the Tathāgata, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and rendered incapable of arising again in the future.”
“This, brahmin, is the way in which one speaking correctly might say of me:
‘The ascetic Gotama is one who abstains from enjoyment,’ but it is not with reference to what you have said.
“The venerable Gotama is a proponent of non-action.”
“There is, brahmin, a way in which one speaking rightly could say of me:
‘The ascetic Gotama is a proponent of non-action.
For I, brahmin, advocate non-action regarding bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct; I advocate non-action regarding various kinds of evil, unwholesome states.”
“This, brahmin, is the way in which one speaking rightly might say of me:
‘The ascetic Gotama is a proponent of non-action,’ but it is not with reference to what you have said.
“The venerable Gotama is a proponent of annihilationism.”
“There is, brahmin, a way in which one speaking rightly might say of me:
‘The ascetic Gotama is an annihilationist.
For I, brahmin, teach the annihilation of lust, hatred, and delusion; I teach the annihilation of various kinds of evil, unwholesome states.”
“This, brahmin, is the way in which one speaking correctly might say of me:
‘The ascetic Gotama is an annihilationist,’ but it is not with reference to what you have said.
“The venerable Gotama is one who feels disgust.”
“There is, brahmin, a way in which one speaking rightly could say of me:
‘The ascetic Gotama is loathsome.
For I, brahmin, am loathsome of bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct; I am loathsome of the attainment of various kinds of evil, unwholesome states.”
“This, brahmin, is the way in which one speaking rightly might say of me:
‘The ascetic Gotama is loathsome,’ but it is not with reference to what you have said.
“The venerable Gotama is an exterminator,” [the brahmin said].
“There is, brahmin, a method by which one speaking rightly could say of me:
‘The ascetic Gotama is a remover.
For I, brahmin, teach the Dhamma for the removal of lust, hatred, and delusion; I teach the Dhamma for the removal of manifold evil, unwholesome states.”
“This, brahmin, is the way in which one speaking rightly might say of me:
‘The ascetic Gotama is an extirpator,’ but it is not with reference to what you have said.
“The venerable Gotama is an ascetic.”
“There is, brahmin, a way in which one speaking rightly could say of me:
‘The ascetic Gotama is an ascetic.
For I declare, brahmin, that evil, unwholesome states are to be scorched—namely, misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind.”

“Brahmin, one for whom those evil, unwholesome qualities that lead to self-torment have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that they are no more subject to future arising—I call him an ‘ascetic’ (tapassin).

Brahmin, in the Tathāgata, those evil, unwholesome qualities that lead to self-torment have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that they are no more subject to future arising.
This, Brahmin, is the way in which one who speaks correctly of me might speak.”
‘The ascetic Gotama is an ascetic,’ yet it is not with reference to what you say that he is so called.
“He is childless, Master Gotama.
“There is indeed a way, brahmin, by which one speaking rightly of me might say: ‘The ascetic Gotama is an ascetic.’”
‘The ascetic Gotama is one who does not enter a womb.

Brahmin, for whom future lying in a womb—the production of renewed existence—is abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and incapable of arising again in the future, him I call ‘one who does not enter a womb.

Brahmin, for the Tathāgata, future lying in a womb—the production of renewed existence—is abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and incapable of arising again in the future.
“This, brahmin, is the way in which one speaking rightly could say of me:
‘The ascetic Gotama is one who avoids procreation,’ but it is not with reference to what you have said.
It is just as if, brahmin, there were a hen’s eggs—eight, ten, or twelve.”
“Suppose there were eggs properly laid by a hen, properly incubated, and properly brooded over.
If one of those chicks, by scratching with its claw-tips or pecking with its beak, were to break the shell first and emerge safely, how should it be called: the eldest or the youngest?”
“The eldest one should be addressed, Master Gotama; for he is their eldest, Master Gotama.

“In the very same way, brahmin, among the generation shrouded in ignorance, like an egg, enveloped [in darkness], I alone have burst asunder the shell of the egg of ignorance and awakened to supreme, perfect enlightenment in the world.
For I, brahmin, am the eldest and the best in the world.”
“Moreover, brahmin, my energy was aroused and unflagging, my mindfulness was established and unconfused, my body was tranquil and unstrained, and my mind was concentrated and one-pointed.

Then, brahmin, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, I entered and dwelt in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion.”

With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, I entered and dwelt in the second jhāna, which has internal tranquility and unification of mind, is without applied and sustained thought, and possesses the rapture and happiness born of concentration.
And with the fading away of rapture, I dwelt equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending, experiencing happiness with the body;
I entered and dwelt in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: "He dwells in happiness, mindful and equanimous."

With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, I entered and dwelt in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.

When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed it toward the knowledge of recollecting past lives.

I recollected my manifold past lives, that is: one birth, two births, three births... [four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand births; many aeons of world-dissolution, many aeons of world-evolution, many aeons of world-dissolution and evolution... I recollected my manifold past lives with their aspects and details.
Whether four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births,
a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, or many aeons of world-contraction,
many aeons of world-expansion, or many aeons of both world-contraction and expansion: "In such a place I was..."
‘I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experiences of pleasure and pain, and such a lifespan.
Passing away from there, I arose elsewhere; there too I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experiences of pleasure and pain, and such a lifespan.
Passing away from there, I was reborn here. Thus, with its aspects and particulars, he recollects his manifold past lives.
"I recollect my past lives.
This, brahmin, was the first true knowledge attained by me in the first watch of the night;
ignorance was dispelled and true knowledge arose; darkness was dispelled and light arose, as happens for one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute."
“Brahmin, this was my first breakthrough, like that of a chick from its eggshell.

When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed it toward the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings.
With the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, I saw beings passing away and being reborn.”
I understand beings as they pass away and reappear—inferior or superior, beautiful or ugly, fortunate or unfortunate—according to their kamma:
"These worthy beings, indeed, were possessed of misconduct in body, misconduct in speech, and misconduct in mind;
they were revilers of the noble ones, held wrong views, and undertook actions based on wrong views. With the breakup of the body..."
...after the breaking up of the body, have reappeared in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, perdition, even in hell.
But these worthy beings, endowed with good conduct of body, endowed with good conduct of speech, endowed with good conduct of mind,
not revilers of the noble ones, possessing right view, and undertaking actions based on right view— these, after the breaking up of the body, [reappear in a happy destination]...
‘Having died, they have been reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world. Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans,
I see beings passing away and being reborn— low and high, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—
and I understand how beings fare according to their kamma.
“This, brahmin, was the second true knowledge attained by me in the middle watch of the night;
ignorance was dispelled and true knowledge arose, darkness was dispelled and light arose, as happens for one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute.
This, brahmin, was my second breaking out, like that of a chick from its eggshell.”

When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed it toward the knowledge of the destruction of the taints.
I directly knew, as it really is: “This is suffering”; I directly knew, as it really is: “This is the origin of suffering”;
I directly knew, as it really is: “This is the cessation of suffering”; I directly knew, as it really is: “This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.”
I understood, as it really is, ‘this is the way leading to the cessation of the taints’;
I understood, as it really is, ‘these are the taints’; I understood, as it really is, ‘this is the origin of the taints’;
I understood, as it really is, ‘this is the cessation of the taints’; I understood, as it really is, ‘this is the way leading to the cessation of the taints.’
I directly knew it as it truly is.
As I knew and saw thus, my mind was liberated from the taint of sensual desire, my mind was liberated from the taint of existence, and my mind was liberated from the taint of ignorance.
When liberated, the knowledge arose: "It is liberated."
“I have realized: ‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
This, brahmin, was the third true knowledge attained by me in the final watch of the night;
ignorance was dispelled and true knowledge arose; darkness was dispelled and light arose, as happens for one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute.”
“This, brahmin, was my third breaking forth, like that of a chick from its eggshell.
When this was said, the brahmin of Verañjā said to the Blessed One:
“Master Gotama is the eldest; Master Gotama is the best.”
“Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama!

Just as, Master Gotama, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—just so has Master Gotama made the Dhamma clear in many ways.”
"In this very way, Master Gotama has elucidated the Dhamma by means of many methods.
I go for refuge to Master Gotama, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts."
First.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.12 2. Mahāvagga
The Lion Sutta (AN 8.12).
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Gabled Hall.
Now at that time, many well-known Licchavis, having sat down and assembled in the assembly hall,
were speaking in many ways in praise of the Buddha, in praise of the Dhamma,
and in praise of the Saṅgha.
Now at that time, Sīha the general, a disciple of the Nigaṇṭhas, was seated in that assembly.
Then it occurred to Sīha the general:
"Without a doubt, that Blessed One must be an Arahant, a perfectly enlightened Buddha; for these many..."
“Many well-known Licchavis, having gathered and assembled in the assembly hall, are praising the Buddha in many ways,
praising the Dhamma, and praising the Saṅgha.
What if I were to approach that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, in order to see him?”
Then Sīha the general approached the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta; having approached, he said this to the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta:
"Venerable sir, I wish to go and see the ascetic Gotama.
"But why, Sīha, being yourself a proponent of action, would you go to see the ascetic Gotama, who is a proponent of non-action?"
“For, Sīha, the ascetic Gotama is a proponent of non-action; he teaches the Dhamma of non-action, and by that he trains his disciples.
Then the general Sīha’s intention to go and see the Blessed One subsided.
A second time, many well-known Licchavis, having sat down and assembled in the assembly hall, spoke in many ways in praise of the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha.
A second time, it occurred to Sīha the general:
"Without doubt, that Blessed One must be an Arahant, a perfectly enlightened Buddha;
for these many well-known Licchavis have sat down and assembled in the assembly hall, and in many ways [they speak] of the Buddha."
“They speak in praise of the Dhamma... they speak in praise of the Saṅgha.
What if I were to approach that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, in order to see him?
Then Sīha the general approached the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta; having approached, he said this to the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta:
“I wish, venerable sir, to approach the ascetic Gotama to see him.
“But why, Sīha, being yourself a proponent of action (*kiriyavāda*), would you approach the ascetic Gotama, who is a proponent of non-action (*akiriyavāda*)?
For the ascetic Gotama, Sīha, is a proponent of non-action; he teaches a doctrine of non-action and trains his disciples by means of it.”
A second time, the general Sīha’s intention to go and see the Blessed One subsided.
A third time, many well-known Licchavis, having sat down and assembled in the assembly hall, were speaking in many ways in praise of the Buddha... [and] the Dhamma... [and] the Saṅgha.
A third time, it occurred to the general Sīha:
“Without a doubt, that Blessed One must be an arahant, a perfectly awakened Buddha;
for these many well-known Licchavis, seated together and assembled in the assembly hall, are praising the Buddha in many ways,
praising the Dhamma, and praising the Saṅgha.”
"What will these Nigaṇṭhas do to me, whether they have been consulted or not?
Suppose I were to go to see the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, without even consulting them.
Then Sīha the general set out from Vesālī toward the Blessed One during the very day, with about five hundred chariots, in order to see the Blessed One.
As far as the ground was passable for a vehicle, he went by vehicle; then, alighting from the vehicle, he proceeded on foot.

Then the general Sīha approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the general Sīha said this to the Blessed One:
"I have heard this, venerable sir:”
‘The ascetic Gotama is a proponent of non-action; he teaches the Dhamma for non-action, and by that he trains his disciples.
Venerable sir, as for those who say this: ‘The ascetic Gotama is a proponent of non-action;

he teaches the Dhamma for non-action, and by that he trains his disciples’—are they, venerable sir, speakers in accordance with what has been said by the Blessed One, and do they not misrepresent the Blessed One?
"Do they misrepresent him with what is untrue, yet explain the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma,
such that no legitimate point of criticism or reproach arises against him?
For we do not wish to misrepresent the Blessed One, venerable sir."
“Sīha, there is a way in which one speaking rightly might say of me:
‘The ascetic Gotama is a proponent of non-action; he teaches a doctrine of non-action, and by that he trains his disciples.
Sīha, there is a way in which one speaking rightly might say of me: [that I am a proponent of abstention]...”
‘The ascetic Gotama is a proponent of action; he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of action, and by that he trains his disciples.
There is, Sīha, a way in which one speaking rightly could say of me:
‘The ascetic Gotama is a proponent of annihilation; he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of annihilation, and by that he trains his disciples.’”
There is, Sīha, a way in which one speaking rightly might say of me:
‘The ascetic Gotama is loathsome; he teaches the Dhamma out of loathsomeness, and by that he trains his disciples.
There is, Sīha, a way in which one speaking rightly might say of me: [the rest of the passage].
‘The ascetic Gotama is a disciplinarian; he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of discipline, and by that he disciplines his disciples.
There is, Sīha, a way in which one who speaks correctly of me might say:
‘The ascetic Gotama is an ascetic; he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of asceticism, and by that he disciplines his disciples.’”
There is, Sīha, a way in which one speaking rightly might say of me:
‘The ascetic Gotama is one who does not enter a womb; he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of not entering a womb, and by that he trains his disciples.
There is, Sīha, a way in which one speaking rightly might say of me: [that I am one who has transcended birth].”
‘The ascetic Gotama is a comforter; he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of comfort, and by that he trains his disciples.
And what, Sīha, is the method by which one speaking rightly might say of me:
‘The ascetic Gotama is a proponent of non-action; he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of non-action, and by that he trains his disciples’?
For I, Sīha, advocate the non-doing of bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct;
I advocate the non-doing of various kinds of evil, unwholesome states.
This, Sīha, is the method by which one who speaks correctly of me might speak.
“The ascetic Gotama is a proponent of non-action; he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of non-action, and by that he trains his disciples.
And what, Sīha, is the method by which one speaking rightly might say of me:
“The ascetic Gotama is a proponent of action; he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of action, and by that he trains his disciples”?
For I, Sīha, speak of action—action consisting of good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind;
I speak of the performance of various kinds of wholesome states.
This, Sīha, is the method by which one speaking rightly might say of me: [“The ascetic Gotama speaks of action”].
“The ascetic Gotama is a proponent of action; he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of action, and by that he trains his disciples.
And what, Sīha, is the method by which one speaking rightly might say of me:
“The ascetic Gotama is a proponent of annihilation; he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of annihilation, and by that he trains his disciples”?
For I, Sīha, speak of the cutting off of lust, hatred, and delusion;
I speak of the cutting off of the many kinds of evil, unwholesome states.
This, Sīha, is the method by which one speaking rightly would speak of me: [that I am a cutter-off].
‘The ascetic Gotama is an annihilationist; he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of annihilation, and by that he trains his disciples.
And what, Sīha, is the method by which one speaking rightly might say of me:
‘The ascetic Gotama is loathsome; he teaches the Dhamma out of loathsomeness, and by that he trains his disciples’?
For I, Sīha, am disgusted by bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct;
I am disgusted by the attainment of various kinds of evil, unwholesome states.
This, Sīha, is the way in which one might rightly speak of me: [that I am a forest-dweller].
‘The ascetic Gotama is loathsome; he teaches the Dhamma out of loathsomeness, and by that he trains his disciples.
And what, Sīha, is the method by which one speaking rightly might say of me:
‘The ascetic Gotama is an eliminator; he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of elimination, and by that he trains his disciples’?
For I, Sīha, teach the Dhamma for the removal of lust, hatred, and delusion;
I teach the Dhamma for the removal of various kinds of evil, unwholesome states.
This, Sīha, is the method by which one speaking rightly would speak of me thus: [“The ascetic Gotama teaches the Dhamma for the removal of lust, hatred, and delusion”].
“The ascetic Gotama is a disciplinarian; he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of discipline, and by that he disciplines his disciples.
And what, Sīha, is the method by which one speaking rightly of me might say:
“The ascetic Gotama is an ascetic; he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of asceticism, and by that he disciplines his disciples”?
"Sīha, I call 'tormenting' those evil, unwholesome states consisting of bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct.

Sīha, one who has abandoned such tormenting, evil, unwholesome states—cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, obliterated them so that they are no longer subject to future arising—I call him 'an ascetic' (tapassin).
Sīha, for the Tathāgata, such tormenting, evil, unwholesome states have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that they are no longer subject to future arising."
This, Sīha, is the method by which one speaking rightly might say of me:
‘The ascetic Gotama is an ascetic; he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of asceticism, and by that he trains his disciples.

And what, Sīha, is the method by which one speaking rightly might say of me: [‘The ascetic Gotama is an ascetic; he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of asceticism, and by that he trains his disciples’]?
“‘The ascetic Gotama is one who does not enter a womb; he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of not entering a womb, and by that he trains his disciples’?

“Sīha, I call one ‘one who does not enter a womb’ in whose case the future lying in a womb—the production of renewed existence—has been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and is of a nature not to arise again in the future.

Sīha, for the Tathāgata, the future lying in a womb—the production of renewed existence—has been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and is of a nature not to arise again in the future.”
This, Sīha, is the method by which one speaking rightly might say of me:
‘The ascetic Gotama is one who has transcended the womb; he teaches the Dhamma for the transcendence of the womb, and he trains his disciples thereby.
And what, Sīha, is that method by which one speaking rightly might say of me: [‘The ascetic Gotama is one who has transcended the womb...’]?”
‘The ascetic Gotama is a comforter; he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of comfort, and by that he trains his disciples’?
Indeed, Sīha, I am a comforter through the supreme comfort; I teach the Dhamma for the sake of comfort, and by that I train my disciples.
This, Sīha, is the way in which one who speaks rightly of me might speak.”
“The ascetic Gotama is a consoler; he teaches the Dhamma for consolation, and by that he trains his disciples.
When this was said, General Sīha said to the Blessed One:
“Magnificent, Bhante! Magnificent, Bhante! … [as above] …”
“Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.
“Sīha, you should investigate thoroughly; thorough investigation is good for well-known people such as yourself.
“Venerable sir, I am even more satisfied and pleased with the Blessed One because the Blessed One said this to me.”
He said this: “Reflect thoroughly, Sīha; thorough reflection is good for well-known people such as yourself.
For, Bhante, if the followers of other sects were to gain me as a disciple, they would carry a banner all over Vesālī, proclaiming:
“Sīha, our general, has entered into discipleship under us!”
"And yet, the Blessed One has said this: 'Act with circumspection, Sīha. Circumspection is good for well-known people such as yourself.
Venerable sir, for a second time I go to the Blessed One for refuge, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts."
“For a long time, Sīha, your family has been like a well for the Nigaṇṭhas, such that you would think they should be given alms when they have approached.
“Venerable sir, I am even more satisfied and pleased with the Blessed One because he said this to me:
‘For a long time, Sīha, your family has been like a well for the Nigaṇṭhas, such that you would think they should be given alms when they have approached.’”
"I have heard this, venerable sir:
'The ascetic Gotama says thus:
"Gifts should be given only to me; gifts should be given only to my disciples. "
‘A gift given to me alone is of great fruit, not a gift given to others;
a gift given to my disciples alone is of great fruit,
not a gift given to the disciples of others,’ yet the Blessed One encourages me to give even to the Nigaṇṭhas.
"Moreover, venerable sir, we shall know the right time for this.
For a third time, venerable sir, I go to the Blessed One for refuge, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts."
Then the Blessed One gave a progressive discourse to Sīha the general, namely:
a talk on generosity, a talk on virtue, and a talk on heaven; he revealed the danger, degradation, and defilement of sensual pleasures, and the benefit of renunciation.

When the Blessed One knew that Sīha the general had a ready mind, a pliable mind, a mind free from hindrances, an uplifted mind, and a confident mind, then he revealed that teaching of the Buddhas which is uniquely excellent.
Suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

Just as a clean cloth, free from dark stains, would properly take up the dye, even so, while sitting right there on that very seat, the dustless, stainless Eye of Dhamma arose in Sīha the general: [that whatever is subject to origination is all subject to cessation].
“Whatever is subject to arising, all that is subject to cessation.

Then Sīha the general, having seen the Dhamma, attained the Dhamma, known the Dhamma, and plunged into the Dhamma; having crossed over doubt and being free from perplexity, having attained self-confidence and becoming independent of others in the Teacher’s instruction, addressed the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept my invitation for tomorrow’s meal, together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.”
The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.
Then Sīha the general, understanding the Blessed One’s consent, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to his right, departed.
Then Sīha the general addressed a certain man:
“Go, good man, and find some meat that is available.
Then, at the end of that night, the general Sīha had various kinds of fine food, both hard and soft, prepared in his own residence and had the Blessed One informed that it was time:
“It is time, venerable sir; the meal is ready.”

Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and went to the residence of Sīha the general. Having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat together with the community of monks.
Now at that time, many Nigaṇṭhas in Vesālī were crying out with uplifted arms from street to street and from crossroads to crossroads:
