"Today, Sīha the general has slaughtered a fat beast and prepared a meal for the ascetic Gotama!"
“The ascetic Gotama knowingly consumes meat prepared specifically for him, depending on that action.
Then a certain man approached General Sīha; having approached, he whispered into General Sīha’s ear:
“Please, venerable sir, you should know this.”
These many Nigaṇṭhas, from street to street and from crossroads to crossroad in Vesālī, cried out with uplifted arms:
“Today General Sīha has slaughtered a large animal and prepared a meal for the ascetic Gotama.
Knowing it to be meat specially prepared for him, the ascetic Gotama consumes it, being dependent upon that act.”
"Enough, noble sir! For a long time these venerable ones have been desirous of disrepute for the Buddha, desirous of disrepute for the Dhamma, and desirous of disrepute for the Saṅgha.
Yet these venerable ones do not succeed in slandering that Blessed One with what is untrue, empty, false, and unreal;
nor would we ever intentionally deprive a living being of life, even for the sake of our own lives."
Then Sīha the general, with his own hands, personally served and satisfied the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha with excellent hard food and soft food.
Then, when the Blessed One had finished eating and had withdrawn his hand from the bowl, Sīha the general sat down to one side.
As Sīha the general was sitting there, the Blessed One instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened him with a discourse on the Dhamma. Having done so, he rose from his seat and departed.
The Second.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.13 2. Mahāvagga
The Discourse on the Noble Steed (Assājānīyasutta):
“Bhikkhus, possessed of eight factors, a king’s noble thoroughbred steed is worthy of a king, an asset to a king, and is reckoned as a very limb of the king. What eight? [Text follows].”
What are the eight? Here,
monks, a king’s noble thoroughbred horse is well-born on both sides—
from the mother’s side and from the father’s side.
In whatever direction other noble thoroughbred horses are born, in that very direction he is born.
And whatever food they give him—
whether fresh or dried—
He consumes it with due care, without scattering it about.
He becomes disgusted at having to sit down or lie down upon excrement or urine.
He is gentle and pleasant to live with, and does not frighten other horses.
Furthermore, whatever deceptions, frauds, crookednesses, or tortuosity he may have, he reveals them to the charioteer as they truly are.
The charioteer strives to crush those [faults] of his.
Moreover, he is a swift driver.
He arouses the thought: “Let these horses carry me or not; I myself shall carry myself here.
And as he goes, he travels only by the straight path.
He is steadfast, maintaining his strength until the very end of life and death.
“Monks, possessed of these eight factors, a king’s noble thoroughbred horse is worthy of a king, an asset to a king, and is reckoned as a very limb of the king.

In the same way, monks, a monk possessed of eight qualities is worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of veneration, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. What are the eight?
[The text continues with the eight qualities.]”

In this case, monks, a monk is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and having undertaken them, he trains himself in the rules of training.
And whatever food they give him—whether coarse or refined—
He consumes that very food with care, without being distressed.
He is repelled by bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct;
he is repelled by the attainment of various kinds of evil, unwholesome states.
He is gentle and pleasant to dwell with, not one who causes alarm to other bhikkhus.
Whatever deceptions, frauds, crookednesses, or wriggling he may have, he discloses them as they truly are to the Teacher or to wise companions in the holy life.
The Teacher or wise companions in the holy life strive for his complete subduing of those traits.
Moreover, she is trained.
She arouses the thought: "Whether other bhikkhus train or not, I shall train myself in this.
Furthermore, when walking, she walks only along the straight path.
Therein, this is the straight path, namely:
right view … [and so on] … right concentration.
He dwells with energy aroused:
‘Let only skin, sinews, and bones remain, and let the flesh and blood dry up in the body;
yet as long as this goal has not been attained— which is to be achieved by manly strength, manly energy, and manly exertion—
there shall be no relaxing of my persistence.’
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with these eight qualities is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
The third.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.14
2. Mahāvagga: The Discourse on the Wild Colt of a Horse (Assakhaḷuṅkasutta) (AN 8.14, PTS AN iv 190)
“Monks, I will teach you about eight kinds of wild colts, eight faults of horses, eight kinds of wild men, and eight faults of men.
Listen to this and attend closely; I shall speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“And what, bhikkhus, are the eight kinds of wild colts and the eight faults of horses?
Here, bhikkhus, a certain wild colt, when told by his charioteer, ‘Go forward! and being pierced and urged on by him, instead retreats backward and makes the chariot turn back.
“Monks, such is one kind of wild colt among horses.
This, monks, is the first fault of a horse.
Furthermore, monks, here a certain wild colt among horses, when told by his driver, ‘Go forward! and being struck and urged on, leaps backward, strikes the pole, and breaks the triple-barred shaft.”
“Monks, such is one kind of wild colt among horses here.
This, monks, is the second fault of a horse.

Furthermore, monks, here some wild colt among horses, when told ‘Go forward! and being pierced and urged by the charioteer, having cast its foreleg over the pole of the chariot, tramples right over the charioteer himself.”
"Monks, such is one kind of wild colt among horses.
This, monks, is the third fault of a horse.
Furthermore, monks, here a certain wild colt among horses, when told 'Go! and being pierced and urged on by the charioteer, takes to the wrong path and makes the chariot go off course."
"Monks, such is one kind of wild colt found here.
This, monks, is the fourth fault of a horse.
Furthermore, monks, when a certain wild colt here is told, 'Go forward! and being struck and urged by the charioteer, it leaps up, raises its forebody, and lifts its front feet."
“Monks, such is one kind of wild colt here.
This, monks, is the fifth fault of a horse.
Furthermore, monks, here some wild colt, when told ‘Go! and being pierced and urged on...”
Without heeding the charioteer and disregarding the charioteer, it shatters the bit with its teeth and gallops off wherever it pleases.
Such, monks, is one kind of wild colt found here.
This, monks, is the sixth fault of a horse.
Furthermore, monks, here some wild colt, when told "Go forward! and being pricked and urged by the charioteer, neither moves forward nor moves backward, but stands right there like a fixed post.
Such, monks, is one kind of wild colt found here.
This, monks, is the seventh fault of a horse.
Furthermore, monks, here a certain wild colt, when told "Go forward!
and being struck and urged by the charioteer, draws up his forefeet and draws up his hind feet and sits down right there on all four feet.
"Monks, such is one kind of wild colt found here.
This, monks, is the eighth fault of a horse.
These, monks, are the eight kinds of wild colts and the eight faults of horses."
And what, monks, are the eight kinds of wild colts among men and the eight faults of a man?
Here, monks, when monks reprove a monk for an offense, that monk,
being reproved by the monks for an offense, evades them out of a lack of mindfulness, saying, "I do not remember."
“Just as that wild colt, monks, when told ‘Go forward! and being struck and urged on by the charioteer, instead retreats backward and makes the chariot turn back;
even so, monks, do I describe this kind of person.
Such, monks, is one type of human colt found here.”
This, monks, is the first fault of a person.
Furthermore, monks, when monks reprove a monk for an offense, that monk, being reproved by the monks for an offense, retorts against the reprover himself: [text continues]
“What is the use of what you say, you foolish and incompetent man?
Do you really think you are fit to speak?
Just as that wild colt, monks, when told “Go on! and being struck and urged by the charioteer, leaps backward, strikes the pole, and breaks the triple-barred shaft;
“Monks, I say that this person is just like that.
Monks, such is one kind of wild colt among men here.
This, monks, is the second fault of a person.”
Furthermore, monks, when monks reprove a monk for an offense, that monk, being reproved by the monks for an offense, counter-accuses the reprover:
“You have fallen into such-and-such an offense; you yourself should first make amends.”

“Just as that wild colt, monks, when told ‘Go forward! and being pierced and urged on by the charioteer, leaps over the chariot-pole and crushes the charioteer himself—that kind of person, monks, I call this individual.
Such, monks, is one kind of human colt found here.”
This, monks, is the third fault of a person. Furthermore, monks, when monks reprove a monk for an offense, that monk,
being reproved by the monks for an offense, evades the issue with irrelevant talk, diverts the conversation to external matters, and displays anger, hatred, and resentment.

“Just as that young colt, monks, when told ‘Go forward! and being struck and urged by the charioteer, takes to the wrong path and makes the chariot go off course—I say that this person is just like that, monks.
There is, monks, such a person here who is a colt among men.”
This, monks, is the fourth fault of a person.
Furthermore, monks, when monks reprove a monk for an offense,
that monk, being reproved by the monks for an offense in the midst of the Saṅgha, flails his arms about.
"Just as that young colt, monks, when told 'Go forward! and being struck and urged by the charioteer, leaps up and raises its forebody and front feet—just so, monks, do I describe this person.
Such, monks, is a certain kind of human colt found here."
This, monks, is the fifth fault of a person. Furthermore, monks, when monks reprove a monk for an offense, that monk—
being reproved by the monks for an offense— disregards the Saṅgha and disregards the accuser, and while still guilty of the offense, he departs wherever he wishes.
"Just as that wild colt, monks, when told 'Go forward! and being pierced and urged by the charioteer,
disregards the charioteer and disregards the goad-stick, and having broken through the bit with its teeth,
gallops off wherever it pleases— I say, monks, that this person is just like that."
"Monks, such is one kind of wild colt among men here.
This, monks, is the sixth fault of a person.
Furthermore, monks, monks reprove a monk for an offense."
Thus, when a bhikkhu is being charged by the bhikkhus with an offense, saying, "I have neither committed an offense nor have I not committed an offense," he harasses the Saṅgha by remaining silent.

Just as that wild colt, O bhikkhus, when told "Go on! and being pricked and urged by the charioteer, neither moves forward nor moves backward but stands right there like a fixed post—just so, I say, O bhikkhus, is this person.
"Monks, such is one kind of person who is like a wild colt among men.
This, monks, is the seventh fault of a person.
Furthermore, monks, there are cases where monks reprove a monk for an offense."
When that bhikkhu was being reproved for an offense by the bhikkhus, he said this:
“Why, venerable sirs, are you so excessively preoccupied with me, as if I were now going to renounce the training and return to the lower life?
Having renounced the training and returned to the lower life, he said this:
‘Are you now, venerable sirs, satisfied?

Just as that wild colt, monks, when told ‘Go on! and being struck and urged by the charioteer, draws up his forefeet and draws up his hind feet and sits down right there on all four feet—I say, monks, that this person is just like that.
“Monks, such is one kind of wild colt among men here.
This, monks, is the eighth fault of a man.
These, monks, are the eight kinds of wild colts among men and the eight faults of a man.”
The Fourth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.15 2. Mahāvagga
The Stain Discourse (Malasutta). “Monks,
there are these eight stains.”
What are the eight?
Monks, neglect of recitation is the stain of the mantras;
lack of exertion is the stain of households.
Laziness, monks, is the stain of beauty;
negligence, monks, is the stain of one who guards;
misconduct, monks, is the stain of a woman.
Avarice, monks, is a stain for one who gives;
evil, unwholesome states, monks, are stains both in this world and in the next;
but worse than those stains, monks, is ignorance—the supreme stain.
These, monks, are the eight stains:
"The stain of mantras is lack of recitation;
the stain of houses is lack of exertion."
Laziness is the stain of beauty;
negligence is the stain of one who guards [his wealth].
Misconduct is the stain of a woman.
Avarice is the stain for one who gives;
indeed, evil states are stains in this world and in the world beyond.
"Then filth is more filthy than filth;
ignorance is the supreme filth.
Thus ends the fifth [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.16 2. Mahāvagga Dūteyyasutta (The Messenger) “Bhikkhus, there are these eight kinds of messengers who are not to be sent on a mission by a noble disciple. What eight? (1) One who is a slave, a servant, one who has been bought with a price, and who is without means of subsistence;

(2) one who is a slave, a servant, one who has been bought with a price, but who has some means of subsistence; (3) one who is a slave, a servant, one who has not been bought with a price, and who is without means of subsistence; (4) one who is a slave, a servant, one who has not been bought with a price, but who has some means of subsistence; (5) one who is a slave, a servant, one who has not been bought with a price, and who is without means of subsistence, yet is a woman; (6) one who is a slave, a servant, one who has not been bought with a price, but who has some means of subsistence, yet is a woman; (7) one who is a slave, a servant, one who has not been bought with a price, and who is without means of subsistence, yet is a eunuch; (8) one who is a slave, a servant, one who has not been bought with a price, but who has some means of subsistence, yet is a eunuch. These, bhikkhus, are the eight kinds of messengers who are not to be sent on a mission by a noble disciple. There are, however, these eight kinds of messengers who are to be sent on a mission by a noble disciple. What eight? (1) One who is not a slave, a servant, one who has not been bought with a price, and who has means of subsistence; (2) one who is not a slave, a servant, one who has not been bought with a price, and who has some means of subsistence; (3) one who is not a slave, a servant, one who has not been bought with a price, and who is without means of subsistence; (4) one who is not a slave, a servant, one who has not been bought with a price, but who has some means of subsistence; (5) one who is not a slave, a servant, one who has not been bought with a price, and who is without means of subsistence, yet is a woman; (6) one who is not a slave, a servant, one who has not been bought with a price, but who has some means of subsistence, yet is a woman; (7) one who is not a slave, a servant, one who has not been bought with a price, and who is without means of subsistence, yet is a eunuch; (8) one who is not a slave, a servant, one who has not been bought with a price, but who has some means of subsistence, yet is a eunuch. These, bhikkhus, are the eight kinds of messengers who are to be sent on a mission by a noble disciple.”
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with eight qualities is worthy to go on a mission.
With which eight?

“Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is a listener, a speaker, one who has learned, one who retains, one who understands, one who makes understood, skilled in what is relevant and irrelevant, and not a maker of quarrels—
it is endowed with these eight qualities, bhikkhus, that a bhikkhu is worthy to go on a mission.
Sariputta, bhikkhus, being endowed with eight qualities, is worthy to go on a mission.”
"By which eight?
Here, monks, Sāriputta is a listener, a proclaimer, a receiver, a retainer, a knower, a communicator, skilled in what is relevant and irrelevant, and not a maker of quarrels.
Endowed with these eight qualities, monks, Sāriputta is worthy to go on a mission."
He who, having entered an assembly of fierce speech,
is not shaken and does not falter in his words—
Nor does he conceal the teaching;
he speaks without ambiguity,
and when questioned, he does not become angry.
“Such a bhikkhu indeed is worthy to go on a mission.
The sixth [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.17 2.

Mahāvagga Paṭhamabandhanasutta (The First Discourse on Bondage) “Bhikkhus, there are these eight bonds of the mind. What eight? Lust is a bond of the mind; hatred is a bond of the mind; delusion is a bond of the mind; anger is a bond of the mind; hostility is a bond of the mind; denigration is a bond of the mind; insolence is a bond of the mind; and envy is a bond of the mind. These, bhikkhus, are the eight bonds of the mind.”
“Monks, in eight ways does a woman bind a man. In what eight ways? [The Buddha said: (AN 8.17, PTS AN iv 196)
Monks, by weeping a woman binds a man;
by laughing, monks, a woman binds a man;
by speaking, monks, a woman binds a man.
By her appearance, monks, a woman binds a man;
by her forest garland, monks, a woman binds a man;
by her fragrance, monks, a woman binds a man.
“Monks, by means of taste a woman binds a man;
by means of touch, monks, a woman binds a man.
It is by these eight ways, monks, that a woman binds a man.”
“Those beings, monks, are well-bound who are bound by contact.
This is the seventh [sutta]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.18.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.19 2. Mahāvagga
The Pahārāda Sutta (AN 8.19).
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Verañjā at the foot of the Naleru Pucimanda tree.

Then Pahārāda, the lord of the asuras, approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he stood to one side. As Pahārāda, the lord of the asuras, was standing to one side, the Blessed One said this to him:
"But do the asuras take delight in the great ocean, Pahārāda?
"They do, Bhante; the asuras take delight in the great ocean."
“But, Pāhārāda, how many wonderful and marvelous qualities are there in the great ocean, seeing which the asuras take delight in the great ocean?
“There are eight wonderful and marvelous qualities in the great ocean, venerable sir, seeing which the asuras take delight in the great ocean.
Which eight?
“Venerable sir, the great ocean slopes away gradually, inclines gradually, and shelves away gradually, not falling off with a sheer precipice. That the great ocean, venerable sir,
slopes away gradually, inclines gradually, and shelves away gradually, not falling off with a sheer precipice— this, venerable sir,
is the first wonderful and marvelous quality of the great ocean, seeing which the asuras take delight in the great ocean.”
Furthermore, venerable sir, the great ocean is stable and does not overstep its shore.
That the great ocean is stable and does not overstep its shore— this, venerable sir,
is the second astounding and amazing quality of the great ocean, seeing which the asuras take delight in the great ocean.
Furthermore, venerable sir, the great ocean does not dwell with a dead corpse. Whatever dead corpse there is in the great ocean, it quickly carries to the shore and casts up onto the dry land.

That the great ocean does not dwell with a dead corpse, but whatever dead corpse there is in the great ocean, it quickly carries to the shore and casts up onto the dry land—this, venerable sir, is the third wonderful and marvelous quality of the great ocean, seeing which the asuras take delight in the great ocean.
Furthermore, venerable sir, whatever great rivers there are—

namely, the Ganges, the Yamunā, the Aciravatī, the Sarabhū, and the Mahī— upon reaching the great ocean, they abandon their former names and lineages and come to be designated simply as ‘the great ocean.

And it is because, venerable sir, whatever great rivers there are— namely, the Ganges, the Yamunā, the Aciravatī, the Sarabhū, and the Mahī— upon reaching the great ocean, they abandon their former names and lineages and come to be designated simply as ‘the great ocean’ [that this is so].
This, venerable sir, is the fourth amazing and wonderful quality of the great ocean, seeing which the asuras take delight in the great ocean.
Furthermore, venerable sir, whatever rivers flow into the great ocean from the world, and whatever showers fall from the sky, the great ocean shows neither depletion nor fullness because of them.

Furthermore, venerable sir, whatever rivers flow into the great ocean from the world, and whatever torrents fall into it from the sky, the great ocean shows neither decrease nor increase because of them.
This, venerable sir, is the fifth wonderful and marvelous quality of the great ocean, seeing which the asuras take delight in the great ocean.
Furthermore, venerable sir, the great ocean has a single taste, the taste of salt.
Furthermore, venerable sir, the great ocean has a single taste, the taste of salt;
this, venerable sir, is the sixth astounding and amazing quality of the great ocean, seeing which the asuras delight in the great ocean.

Furthermore, venerable sir, the great ocean possesses many treasures and manifold treasures. These are the treasures therein, namely: pearls, gems, beryl, conch shells, crystal, coral, silver, gold, red pearls, and cat’s-eye gems.

"Furthermore, Bhante, the great ocean possesses many treasures and manifold jewels; therein are these jewels, namely: pearls, gems, beryl, conch shells, crystals, coral, silver, gold, rubies, and cat's-eyes.
This, Bhante, is the seventh astounding and amazing quality of the great ocean, seeing which the asuras take delight in the great ocean.
Moreover, Bhante, the great ocean is the abode of mighty beings. Therein are these beings: the *timi*, the *timimigala*..."
The *timi*, the *timiṅgala*, and the *timirapiṅgala* are asuras, nāgas, and gandhabbas.

In the great ocean there are individual bodies (*attabhāva*) a hundred yojanas long, individual bodies two hundred yojanas long, individual bodies three hundred yojanas long, individual bodies four hundred yojanas long, and even individual bodies five hundred yojanas long.
Venerable sir, it is because the great ocean is the abode of great beings that these beings are found there: the *timi*, the *timiṅgala*, and the *timirapiṅgala*.
Asuras, nāgas, and gandhabbas; in the great ocean there are individual bodies a hundred yojanas long...
[and so on] ... three hundred yojanas... four hundred yojanas... even five hundred yojanas long.
This, venerable sir, is the eighth wonderful and marvelous quality of the great ocean, seeing which the asuras take delight in the great ocean.
“Venerable sir, these are the eight wonderful and marvelous qualities of the great ocean, seeing which the asuras take delight in the great ocean.
But, venerable sir, do the bhikkhus also take delight in this Dhamma and Discipline?
“They do, Pahārāda; the bhikkhus take delight in this Dhamma and Discipline.”
“But, Bhante, how many wonderful and marvelous qualities are there in this Dhamma and Discipline, which the bhikkhus, having seen again and again, take delight in this Dhamma and Discipline?
“Pahārāda, there are eight wonderful and marvelous qualities in this Dhamma and Discipline, which the bhikkhus, having seen again and again, take delight in this Dhamma and Discipline.
What are the eight?
"Just as, Pahārāda, the great ocean slopes gradually, inclines gradually, and shelves gradually, without falling away abruptly;
even so, Pahārāda, in this Dhamma and Discipline there is gradual training, gradual practice, and gradual progress, without penetration to final knowledge all at once.
And because, Pahārāda, in this Dhamma and Discipline there is gradual training, gradual practice, and gradual progress, without penetration to final knowledge all at once..."
This, Pahārāda, is the first wonderful and marvelous quality in this Dhamma and Discipline, seeing which the bhikkhus take delight in this Dhamma and Discipline.
Just as, Pahārāda, the great ocean is stable and does not overstep its shore,
even so, Pahārāda, whatever training rule has been laid down by me for my disciples, my disciples do not transgress it even for the sake of their lives.

Furthermore, Pāhārāda, even that training rule laid down by me for my disciples which they would not transgress even for the sake of their lives—this, Pāhārāda, is the second wonderful and marvelous quality in this Dhamma and Vinaya, seeing which the bhikkhus take delight in this Dhamma and Vinaya.
Just as, Pāhārāda, the great ocean does not dwell together with a dead corpse; whatever dead corpse there is in the great ocean, it quickly carries to the shore and casts up onto the dry land.
In the same way, Pāhārāda, that person who is immoral, of evil character, impure and of suspicious conduct, one whose actions are concealed,
who is not a recluse though claiming to be a recluse, who does not live the holy life though claiming to live the holy life— one who is inwardly rotten, leaking, and full of filth—
the Saṅgha does not dwell together with him; rather, having assembled quickly, they suspend him.
Even though he may be sitting right in the midst of the community of monks, he is nonetheless far from the Saṅgha, and the Saṅgha is far from him.
For, Pahārāda, that person who is immoral, of evil nature, impure and suspicious in his conduct, secretive in his actions, one who is not a recluse yet claims to be a recluse,
one who does not live the holy life yet claims to live the holy life, who is inwardly rotten, leaking, and corrupt—
The Saṅgha does not dwell together with him; having assembled quickly, it suspends him.
Even though he may be seated right in the midst of the community of monks, he is nonetheless far from the Saṅgha, and the Saṅgha is far from him.
This, Pahārāda, is the third wonderful and marvelous quality in this Dhamma and Discipline, seeing which the monks take delight in this Dhamma and Discipline.
"Just as, Pahārāda, whatever great rivers there are— namely, the Ganges, the Yamunā, the Aciravatī,
the Sarabhū, and the Mahī— upon reaching the great ocean, they abandon their former names and lineages and come to be designated simply as 'the great ocean';
even so, Pahārāda, these four castes— the khattiyas, the brāhmaṇas, the vessas, and the suddas— [when they enter the Dhamma and Vinaya] proclaimed by the Tathāgata..."
Having gone forth from the household life into homelessness in this Dhamma and Discipline, they abandon their former names and clans and come to be reckoned simply as “ascetics,
sons of the Sakyan. Furthermore, Pāhārāda,
these four castes— the khattiyas, brahmins, vessas, and suddas— [when they have gone forth] in what has been proclaimed by the Tathāgata...
Having gone forth from the home life into homelessness in this Dhamma and Vinaya, they abandon their former names and clans and come to be reckoned simply as “recluses, sons of the Sakyan”;
this, Pahārāda, is the fourth wonderful and marvelous quality in this Dhamma and Vinaya, seeing which the bhikkhus take delight in this Dhamma and Vinaya.
"Just as, Pahārāda, the rivers that flow into the great ocean and the showers of rain that fall from the sky do not cause the great ocean to appear either diminished or filled,
even so, Pahārāda, though many bhikkhus attain final nibbāna through the element of nibbāna without residue, the element of nibbāna does not thereby appear either diminished or filled."
Furthermore, Pāhārāda, even if many bhikkhus attain final nibbāna through the element of nibbāna without residue, neither a deficiency nor a fullness is perceived in that element of nibbāna.
This, Pāhārāda, is the fifth astounding and amazing quality in this Dhamma and Discipline, seeing which bhikkhus take delight in this Dhamma and Discipline.
Just as, Pāhārāda, the great ocean has but one taste, the taste of salt;
In the very same way, Pahārāda, this Dhamma and Discipline has a single flavor: the flavor of liberation.

That this Dhamma and Discipline has a single flavor—the flavor of liberation—is, Pahārāda, the sixth astounding and amazing quality in this Dhamma and Discipline, seeing which the bhikkhus take delight in this Dhamma and Discipline.

"Just as, Pahārāda, the great ocean contains many treasures and manifold treasures; that is to say, pearls, gems, beryl, conch shells, crystals, coral, silver, gold, rubies, and cat's-eyes—even so, Pahārāda, this Dhamma and Discipline contains many treasures and manifold treasures. These are the treasures, namely:
the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases for psychic power, and the five faculties."
The five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path.
Moreover, Pāhārāda, this Dhamma and Discipline possesses many jewels, manifold jewels; therein these are the jewels, namely:
the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right endeavors, the four bases for psychic power, the five faculties, and the five powers.
The seven factors of enlightenment and the noble eightfold path:
this, Pahrāda, is the seventh astounding and amazing quality in this Dhamma and Discipline, seeing which the bhikkhus take delight in this Dhamma and Discipline.
Just as, Pahrāda, the great ocean is the abode of great beings, and there these beings dwell—the *timi*, the *timigila*... [and so forth].
There are Asuras, Nāgas, and Gandhabbas of a smoky-brown hue;
in the great ocean there are individual bodies a hundred yojanas long, two hundred yojanas long, three hundred yojanas long, four hundred yojanas long, and even five hundred yojanas long.
In just this way, Pahārāda, this Dhamma and Vinaya is the abode of great beings; therein these beings are found—the stream-enterer... [and so forth].

One practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry, one who is a once-returner practicing for the realization of the fruit of once-returning, one who is a non-returner practicing for the realization of the fruit of non-returning, and an arahant practicing for arahantship.
In this regard, Pāhārāda, this Dhamma and Discipline is the abode of great beings; therein these beings are found: the stream-enterer... [and so forth].
One practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry, one who is a once-returner practicing for the realization of the fruit of once-returning,
one who is a non-returner practicing for the realization of the fruit of non-returning, and an arahant practicing for arahantship— this, Pāhārāda,
is the eighth astounding and amazing quality in this Dhamma and Discipline, seeing which the bhikkhus take delight in this Dhamma and Discipline.

“Pahārāda, these are the eight astounding and wonderful qualities in this Dhamma and Discipline, which the bhikkhus, having seen again and again, take delight in this Dhamma and Discipline. Thus it was said.
The ninth [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.20

2. Mahāvagga Uposathasutta (AN 8.20, PTS AN iv 204) On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” they replied. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, when it is the time for the Uposatha, if a bhikkhu has committed an offense and remembers it, he should go to a single bhikkhu, confess that offense, and then attend the Uposatha together with him. If he does not do so, he commits an offense of wrong-doing. When it is the time for the Uposatha, if a bhikkhu has committed an offense and remembers it, he should go to a group of two or three bhikkhus, confess that offense, and then attend the Uposatha together with them. If he does not do so, he commits an offense of wrong-doing. When it is the time for the Uposatha, if a bhikkhu has committed an offense and remembers it, he should go to a Saṅgha of four or more bhikkhus, confess that offense, and then attend the Uposatha together with them. If he does not do so, he commits an offense of wrong-doing. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in the Eastern Park, in the Mansion of Migāra’s Mother.
Now on that occasion, on the Uposatha day, the Blessed One was seated surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.

Then, when the night had advanced and the first watch had passed, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, extended his joined palms in reverential salutation toward the Blessed One, and said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, the night has advanced; the first watch has passed; the community of monks has been sitting for a long time.
May the Blessed One recite the Pātimokkha to the monks.
When this was said, the Blessed One remained silent.

A second time, when the night had advanced and the middle watch had passed, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, extended his joined palms toward the Blessed One, and said this to the Blessed One:
“The night has advanced, Bhante; the middle watch has passed; the Saṅgha of bhikkhus has been sitting for a long time.
May the Blessed One recite the Pātimokkha to the bhikkhus.”
A second time, the Blessed One remained silent.
A third time, when the night was far spent, during the last watch, at the rising of the dawn,
at the beginning of the night’s joy, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, and approached the Blessed One.
Having extended his joined palms in reverence, he said this to the Blessed One:
"The night has passed, venerable sir; the final watch has ended, the dawn has risen, the night is at its joyful close;
the community of monks has been seated for a long time."
“Venerable sir, let the Blessed One recite the Pātimokkha for the bhikkhus.
“The assembly is not pure, Ānanda.
Then it occurred to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna:
“With reference to what person, Ānanda, did the Blessed One say:
‘The assembly, Ānanda, is not pure’?
Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna encompassed the entire Saṅgha of bhikkhus with his mind and reflected upon their minds.
The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna saw that person— immoral, of evil nature, impure,
of suspicious conduct, secretive in his actions, a non-recluse claiming to be a recluse, not living the holy life while claiming to live it,
internally rotten, leaking, and putrid— sitting in the midst of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
Having seen him, he rose from his seat, approached that person, and having approached, said this to him:
"Arise, friend! You have been seen by the Blessed One.
You have no further association with the bhikkhus."
When this was said, that person remained silent.
A second time, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said to that person: “Arise, friend!
You have been seen by the Blessed One.”
“There is no association for you with the bhikkhus.
A second time, that person remained silent.
A third time, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said this to that person:
“Get up, friend! You have been seen by the Blessed One.
There is no longer any association for you with the bhikkhus.
For a third time, that person remained silent.

Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna took that person by the arm, led him out from the gateway, gave him the key to the bolt, and approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he said this to the Blessed One:
"That person, Bhante, has been led out by me.
The assembly is now pure."
“Venerable sir, let the Blessed One recite the Pātimokkha for the bhikkhus.
“It is wonderful, Moggallāna! It is marvelous, Moggallāna!
That that foolish man should even wait until he is seized by the arm!”
Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, from this day forward, you yourselves shall perform the Uposatha and recite the Pātimokkha.
Bhikkhus, from this day forth, I will no longer perform the Uposatha or recite the Pātimokkha.”
"It is impossible, monks, it cannot happen that a Tathāgata would recite the Pātimokkha before an impure assembly.

"In the same way, monks, there are these eight wonderful and marvelous qualities in this Dhamma and Discipline, which the monks, having seen them again and again, take delight in this Dhamma and Discipline.

"In the same way, monks, in this Dhamma and Vinaya there is gradual training, gradual practice, and gradual progress; there is no penetration of final knowledge all at once.

That, monks, in this Dhamma and Vinaya there is gradual training, gradual practice, and gradual progress, and no penetration of final knowledge all at once—this, monks, is the first wonderful and marvelous quality in this Dhamma and Vinaya, seeing which the monks take delight in this Dhamma and Vinaya... Just as, monks, the great ocean is the abode of great beings—such beings as these: the *timi*, the *timiṅgala*, the *timirapiṅgala*, the *asuras*, the *nāgas*, and the *gandhabbas*—who dwell in the great ocean with bodies a hundred leagues long... even with bodies five hundred leagues long; so too, monks, this Dhamma and Discipline is the abode of great beings. What beings? The stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*), the one practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphalasacchikiriyāya paṭipanna*), the once-returner (*sakadāgāmī*), the one practicing for the realization of the fruit of once-returning (*sakadāgāmiphalasacchikiriyāya paṭipanna*), the non-returner (*anāgāmī*), the one practicing for the realization of the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphalasacchikiriyāya paṭipanna*), the arahant, and the one practicing for the realization of the fruit of arahantship (*arahattaphalasacchikiriyāya paṭipanna*). This Dhamma and Discipline, monks, is the abode of such great beings. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We shall be those who dwell in the abode of the great beings. Thus, monks, should you train yourselves. Furthermore, monks, this Dhamma and Discipline is the abode of the noble ones (*ariya*), free from the defilements (*anāsava*), and it leads to disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, and Nibbāna. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We shall be those who dwell in the abode of the noble ones, free from the defilements, which leads to disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, and Nibbāna. Thus, monks, should you train yourselves. Furthermore, monks, this Dhamma and Discipline is well-proclaimed (*svākkhāta*), visible here and now (*sanditthika*), timeless (*akālika*), inviting one to come and see (*ehipassika*), leading onward (*opanayika*), and to be personally realized by the wise (*paccattaṃ veditabbo viññūhi*). Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We shall be those who dwell in that which is well-proclaimed, visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, and to be personally realized by the wise. Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.21 3. Gahapativagga First Discourse on Uggata “Bhikkhus, there are these eight qualities that make a householder dear and beloved, respected and revered by his kinsmen and relatives. What eight? Here, bhikkhus, a householder is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, possessed of good conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults; having undertaken the training rules, he trains in them. This is the first quality that makes a householder dear and beloved... by his kinsmen and relatives. Furthermore, bhikkhus, a householder is one who has provided for the support of his mother and father who are old, aged, advanced in years, come to the last stage of life. This is the second quality... Furthermore, bhikkhus, a householder is one who has provided for the support of his wife and children, his slaves, servants, and laborers, and who provides for their maintenance. This is the third quality... Furthermore, bhikkhus, a householder is one who is skillful and diligent in attending to his business, perceiving even the smallest details, and possessing foresight in his affairs. This is the fourth quality... Furthermore, bhikkhus, a householder is one who is liberal, open-handed, living as a giver, one who delights in charity, who is pure-handed in giving, ready to give, and rejoices in the distribution of gifts. This is the fifth quality... Furthermore, bhikkhus, a householder is one who possesses faith; he places faith in the Tathāgata’s enlightenment thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. This is the sixth quality... Furthermore, bhikkhus, a householder is one who possesses shame; he is ashamed of doing evil, ashamed of committing unwholesome deeds. This is the seventh quality... Furthermore, bhikkhus, a householder is one who possesses moral dread; he dreads doing evil, dreads committing unwholesome deeds. This is the eighth quality that makes a householder dear and beloved, respected and revered by his kinsmen and relatives. These, bhikkhus, are the eight qualities that make a householder dear and beloved, respected and revered by his kinsmen and relatives.”
(AN 8.21, PTS AN iv 208) At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Gabled Hall.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, you should remember the householder Ugga of Vesālī as one endowed with eight wonderful and marvelous qualities.
This is what the Blessed One said.
Having said this, the Sugata rose from his seat and entered his dwelling.
Then, in the morning, a certain bhikkhu dressed himself, took his bowl and robe, and went to the residence of the householder Ugga of Vesālī. Having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Then the householder Ugga of Vesālī approached that bhikkhu;
having approached and paid homage to him, he sat down to one side. As the householder Ugga of Vesālī was sitting there to one side—
That bhikkhu said this to him:
“Householder, you have been declared by the Blessed One to be endowed with eight wonderful and marvelous qualities.
What, householder, are those eight wonderful and marvelous qualities with which you have been declared by the Blessed One to be endowed?”
“Venerable sir, I do not know which eight astounding and amazing qualities the Blessed One declared he possessed.
However, venerable sir, those eight astounding and amazing qualities that I possess are as follows:”
“Listen to that and attend closely; I shall speak.
“Yes, householder,” that bhikkhu replied to Ugga the householder of Vesālī.
Ugga the householder of Vesālī said this:
“Venerable sir, when I first saw the Blessed One from afar,
my mind was immediately filled with confidence upon that very sight. This,
venerable sir, is the first wonderful and marvelous quality found in me.”
Thus, venerable sir, with a mind full of confidence, I attended upon the Blessed One.
To me, the Blessed One gave a graduated discourse, namely:
talk on generosity, talk on virtue, and talk on heaven; he revealed the danger, degradation, and defilement of sensual pleasures, and the benefit of renunciation.
When the Blessed One knew that my mind was ready, pliable, free from hindrances, uplifted, and confident, then he set forth the Dhamma teaching peculiar to Buddhas:
suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Just as a clean cloth, free from dark stains, would properly take the dye;
In this very way, while sitting on that very seat, the dust-free, stainless eye of Dhamma arose in me:
"Whatever is subject to origination, all that is subject to cessation.

Then, venerable sir, having seen the Dhamma, attained the Dhamma, known the Dhamma, and fathomed the Dhamma, with my doubts crossed over and my perplexity vanished, I attained self-confidence and became independent of others in the Teacher's dispensation.
Right there, I went for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, and I undertook the five training rules with celibacy as the fifth.
This, venerable sir, is the second wonderful and marvelous quality found in me.
Furthermore, venerable sir, I had four young wives.
Then, venerable sir, I approached those wives; having approached them, I said this to those wives:
“Sisters, I have undertaken the five training rules with celibacy as the fifth.
Whoever wishes may remain right here and enjoy wealth and perform meritorious deeds, or she may go to her own family circle.”
"Or did you have a man in mind, saying, 'To whom shall I give you?
When this was said, venerable sir, the eldest wife said this to me:
"Give me to such-and-such a man, noble son."
Then, venerable sir, having summoned that man, I took my wife with my left hand and, taking a water-pitcher with my right hand, I poured it over that man.
Yet, venerable sir, as I was giving away my young bride, I do not recall any change in my state of mind.
This, venerable sir, is the third wonderful and marvelous quality found in me.
Furthermore, Bhante, there exist wealth in my family;
and that is shared with those who are virtuous and of good character.
This, Bhante, is the fourth wonderful and marvelous quality found in me.
Furthermore, Bhante, whenever I attend upon a bhikkhu,
I attend upon him with respect, not without respect.
This, Bhante, is the fifth astounding and amazing quality found in me.
If, venerable sir, that venerable one teaches me the Dhamma,
I listen to it with due respect, not without respect.
If that venerable one does not teach me the Dhamma, I teach him the Dhamma.
“Venerable sir, this is the sixth astounding and wonderful quality found in me.
Furthermore, venerable sir, it is not surprising that deities approach me and announce:
‘Householder, the Dhamma has been well-proclaimed by the Blessed One.’”
When this was said, Bhante, I said to those deities:
“Whether you say so, O deities, or whether you do not say so, the Dhamma has indeed been well-proclaimed by the Blessed One.
Yet, Bhante, I do not recall on that account any inflation of mind.
‘Either deities approach me, or I converse with deities.
This, venerable sir, is the seventh wonderful and marvelous quality found in me.
Furthermore, venerable sir, regarding these five lower fetters taught by the Blessed One, I do not see anything among them that has not been abandoned within myself.
"Venerable sir, this is the eighth wonderful and marvelous quality found in me.
Venerable sir, these eight wonderful and marvelous qualities are found in me;
yet I do not know—"
“And with which eight astounding and wonderful qualities did I declare that I was endowed?
Then that bhikkhu, having received almsfood at the residence of the householder Ugga of Vesālī, rose from his seat and departed.
Later, after his meal, on returning from his almsround, he approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, that bhikkhu reported to the Blessed One the entirety of his conversation with the householder Ugga of Vesālī.
“Excellent, excellent, bhikkhu!

It is just as the householder Ugga of Vesālī would have answered correctly when he spoke. Bhikkhu, it was precisely because the householder Ugga of Vesālī possesses these eight wonderful and marvelous qualities that I declared him to be so.”
“Furthermore, bhikkhu, you should remember the householder Ugga of Vesālī as one endowed with these eight wonderful and marvelous qualities.
Thus was the first [sutta].
