3. Gahapativagga The Second Discourse on Ugga (AN 8.21–22, PTS AN iv 208)
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Vajjis at Hatthigāma.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, you should remember the householder Ugga of Hatthigāma as being endowed with eight astounding and amazing qualities.”
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Having said this, the Sugata rose from his seat and entered his dwelling.

Then, at the time of morning, a certain bhikkhu dressed himself, took his bowl and robe, and went to the residence of the householder Ugga at Hatthigāma; having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Then Ugga the householder of Hatthigāma approached that bhikkhu;
having approached and paid homage to him, he sat down to one side. As Ugga the householder of Hatthigāma was sitting there, that bhikkhu said this to him:
“Householder, you have been declared by the Blessed One to be endowed with eight wonderful and marvelous qualities.
What, householder, are those eight wonderful and marvelous qualities with which you have been declared by the Blessed One to be endowed?
“I do not know them, Bhante.”
“With which eight astounding and wonderful qualities was the Blessed One declared to be endowed?
“But, venerable sir, listen and pay close attention as I explain those eight astounding and wonderful qualities that exist in me.”
“Yes, householder,” that bhikkhu replied to Ugga the householder of Hatthigāma.
Ugga the householder of Hatthigāma said this:
“Venerable sir, when I was attending upon [the deities] in the Nāga Grove and saw the Blessed One for the first time from afar;”
"Venerable sir, at the very moment of seeing the Blessed One, my mind became serene and my intoxication with liquor was abandoned.
This, venerable sir, is the first wonderful and marvelous quality found in me.
With a serene mind, venerable sir, I attended upon the Blessed One."
The Blessed One gave me a graduated discourse, namely:
a talk on generosity, a talk on virtue, and a talk on heaven; he explained the danger, degradation, and defilement of sensual pleasures, and the benefit of renunciation.
When the Blessed One knew that my mind was ready, pliable, free from hindrances, uplifted, and confident, then he proclaimed that which is the special Dhamma teaching of the Buddhas.
Suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Just as a clean cloth, free from dark stains, would properly take up the dye,
even so, right there on that seat, the dustless, stainless eye of Dhamma arose in me:
‘Whatever is subject to arising, all that is subject to cessation.
Then, venerable sir, having seen the Dhamma, attained the Dhamma, known the Dhamma, and plunged into the Dhamma;
having crossed over doubt and being free from perplexity, having gained intrepidity and becoming independent of others in the Teacher’s dispensation, right there I [saw] the Buddha and the Dhamma.
I went for refuge to the Saṅgha and undertook the five training rules with celibacy as the fifth.
This, venerable sir, is the second wonderful and marvelous quality found in me.
Furthermore, venerable sir, I had four young wives.
Then, venerable sir, I approached those wives; having approached them, I said this to those wives:
"Sisters, I have undertaken the five training rules with celibacy as the fifth.
Whoever wishes may remain right here and enjoy wealth and perform meritorious deeds, or she may go to her own family circle."
"Or did you have a man in mind, saying, 'To whom shall I give you?
When this was said, venerable sir, my senior wife said this to me:
"Give me to such-and-such a man, noble son."
Then, venerable sir, having had that man summoned, I took my wife with my left hand and, taking a water-pitcher with my right hand, I poured it over that man.
Yet, venerable sir, as I was giving away my young bride, I do not recall any alteration in my mind.
This, venerable sir, is the third wonderful and marvelous quality found in me.
"Furthermore, venerable sir, there exist in my family wealth that is shared with those who are virtuous and of good character. This,
venerable sir, is the fourth wonderful and marvelous quality found in me."
Moreover, Bhante, whatever bhikkhu I attend upon,
I attend upon him with respect, not without respect.
If that venerable one teaches me the Dhamma...
I listen with respect, not without respect.
If that venerable one does not teach me the Dhamma, I teach him the Dhamma.
This, Bhante, is the fifth wonderful and marvelous quality found in me.
"It is not surprising, venerable sir, that when the Saṅgha has been invited, deities approach and announce:
'This householder, such-and-such a bhikkhu, is liberated both ways; this one is liberated by wisdom; this one is a body-witness; this one has attained to view;
this one is liberated by faith; this one is a Dhamma-follower; this one is a faith-follower.'"
‘Such-and-such a person is virtuous and of good character, while that one is immoral and of evil character.
Furthermore, Lord, while serving the Sangha, I do not recall ever giving rise to such a thought as:
‘I will give a little to this one, or a lot to that one.’”
"Then, venerable sir, I give with an even mind.
This, venerable sir, is the sixth astounding and wonderful quality found in me.
Furthermore, venerable sir, it is no marvel that deities approach me and announce: [that I am free from lust, hatred, and delusion]."
‘Householder, the Dhamma has been well-expounded by the Blessed One.
When this was said, venerable sir, I say to those deities:
‘Whether you deities say so or not, the Dhamma has indeed been well-expounded by the Blessed One.’”
"Yet, venerable sir, I do not recall on that account any inflation of mind such as:
'Those deities approach me, or I converse with those deities.
This, venerable sir, is the seventh astounding and wonderful quality found in me."
"But if, venerable sir, I were to pass away before the Blessed One, it would not be surprising if the Blessed One were to declare of me:
'There is no fetter by which the householder Ugga of Hatthigāma might return again to this world.
Venerable sir, this is the eighth wonderful and marvelous quality found in me."
“Venerable sir, these eight wonderful and marvelous qualities are found in me.
Yet I do not know:
‘By which eight wonderful and marvelous qualities am I endowed that the Blessed One has declared?’”
Then that bhikkhu, having received almsfood at the residence of the householder Ugga of Hatthigāma, rose from his seat and departed.
Later, after his meal, having returned from his almsround, he approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
As he was sitting there, he reported to the Blessed One everything that had been the conversation and discussion between him and the householder Ugga of Hatthigāma.
“Excellent, excellent, bhikkhu!

Just as the householder Ugga of Hatthigāma would answer correctly if he were to speak rightly, so too have I declared that the householder Ugga of Hatthigāma is endowed with these very same eight wonderful and marvelous qualities.
And you, bhikkhu, should remember the householder Ugga of Hatthigāma as being endowed with these eight wonderful and marvelous qualities.”
The Second.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.23.
3. The Chapter on Householders.
The First Hatthaka Sutta (AN 8.23).
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Āḷavī at the Aggāḷava Shrine.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, you should remember Hatthaka of Āḷavī as one endowed with seven wonderful and marvelous qualities.
With which seven?”
For, bhikkhus, Hatthaka of Āḷavī is endowed with faith;
Hatthaka of Āḷavī, bhikkhus, is virtuous;
Hatthaka of Āḷavī, bhikkhus, is possessed of a sense of shame.
Bhikkhus, Hatthaka of Āḷavī is conscientious;
bhikkhus, Hatthaka of Āḷavī is learned;
bhikkhus, Hatthaka of Āḷavī is generous.
“Bhikkhus, Hatthaka of Āḷavī is wise.
Bhikkhus, you should remember Hatthaka of Āḷavī as one endowed with these seven wonderful and marvelous qualities.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Having said this, the Sugata rose from his seat and entered his dwelling.
Then, in the morning, a certain bhikkhu dressed himself, took his bowl and robe, and went to the residence of Hatthaka Āḷavaka. Having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Then Hatthaka Āḷavaka approached that bhikkhu; having approached and paid homage to him, he sat down to one side. As Hatthaka Āḷavaka was sitting there, the bhikkhu said this to him:
“Friend, you have been declared by the Blessed One to be endowed with seven wonderful and marvelous qualities.
Which seven?
‘Bhikkhus, Hatthaka of Āḷavī is full of faith;’”
Virtuous … [and so on] … possessed of a sense of shame … possessed of a sense of dread of wrongdoing …
“Bhikkhus, Hatthaka of Āḷavī is learned, generous, and wise.”
“Friend, you have indeed been declared by the Blessed One to be endowed with these seven wonderful and marvelous qualities.
“Venerable sir, was there no householder dressed in white among them?
“There was no householder dressed in white here, friend.”
“It is well, Bhante, that no householder dressed in white was present here.
Then that bhikkhu, having received almsfood at the residence of Hatthaka of Āḷavī, rose from his seat and departed.
Later, after his meal, having returned from his almsround, that bhikkhu approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
Sitting there, that bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:
"Just now, Bhante, in the morning, having dressed and taken my bowl and robe, I went to the residence of Hatthaka Āḷavaka. Having arrived, I sat down on the prepared seat."
Then, venerable sir, Hatthaka of Āḷavī approached me; having approached and paid homage to me, he sat down to one side.
As he was sitting there, venerable sir, I said this to Hatthaka of Āḷavī:
“Friend, you have been declared by the Blessed One to be endowed with seven wonderful and marvelous qualities.”
By which seven?
Bhikkhus, Hatthaka of Āḷavī is endowed with faith;
he is virtuous... [and so on].
...possessing a sense of shame... possessing a sense of dread of wrongdoing...
being learned...
“...generous...
and wise, monks, is Hatthaka of Āḷavī.
It is for being endowed with these seven wonderful and marvelous qualities, friend, that you have been declared so by the Blessed One.”
When this was said, Bhante, Hatthaka said this to me:
“Venerable sir, was there no householder dressed in white here?
“There was no householder dressed in white here, friend.”
“It is well, Bhante, that no householder clad in white was present here.
“Excellent, excellent, bhikkhu!
That clansman is one of few desires.”
"Indeed, he does not wish for his own wholesome qualities to be known by others.
Therefore, bhikkhu, you should remember Hatthaka of Āḷavaka as being endowed with this eighth wonderful and marvelous quality, namely, fewness of desires.
This is the third.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.24 3.
Gahapativagga Dutiyahatthakasutta (The Second Discourse to Hatthaka)
(AN 8.24, PTS AN iv 218) On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Āḷavī at the Aggāḷava Shrine.
Then Hatthaka of Āḷavī, surrounded by about five hundred lay followers, approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As Hatthaka of Āḷavī was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
"This assembly of yours, Hatthaka, is indeed large."
“But how, Hatthaka, do you win over this great assembly?
“Venerable sir, it is by means of those four bases of sympathy taught by the Blessed One that I win over this great assembly.
Venerable sir, whatever I know...”
Thinking, "This person is to be won over by generosity," I win them over with generosity;
thinking,
"This person is to be won over by kind speech," I win them over with kind speech.
When I know:
"This person is to be gathered through beneficial conduct," I gather them through beneficial conduct; when I know: [I gather them through the same means].
‘This person is to be won over by equality,’ so I win him over with equality.
Furthermore, Bhante, there are indeed riches in my family;
people do not think one should listen to a pauper in such a manner.”
“Excellent, excellent, Hatthaka!
This is indeed the proper method for you, Hatthaka, to win over a large assembly.
For whatever persons, Hatthaka, have won over a large assembly in the past, they all did so by means of these very four bases of sympathy.”
“Hatthaka, whoever in the future will win over a large assembly will do so by means of these very four bases of sympathy.
And whoever, Hatthaka, at present wins over a large assembly, all of them do so by means of these very four bases of sympathy.”

Then Hatthaka of Āḷavī, having been instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened by the Blessed One with a discourse on the Dhamma, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to his right, departed.
Not long after Hatthaka of Āḷavī had left, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, you should remember Hatthaka of Āḷavī as one endowed with eight wonderful and marvelous qualities.”
By which eight?
Bhikkhus, Hatthaka of Āḷavī is endowed with faith;
he is endowed with virtue... [and so on].
...possessing a sense of shame ... possessing a sense of dread of wrongdoing ...
being learned ...
“Bhikkhus, Hatthaka of Āḷavī is generous; he is wise, bhikkhus, Hatthaka of Āḷavī;
he has few desires, bhikkhus, Hatthaka of Āḷavī.”
“Monks, you should remember Hatthaka of Āḷavī as one endowed with these eight wonderful and marvelous qualities.
The fourth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.25

3. Gahapativagga Mahānāmasutta (AN 8.25, PTS AN iv 220) Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then the householder Mahānāma approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how many things, when developed and cultivated, lead to the attainment of Nibbāna in this very life? “There are, Mahānāma, these four things which, when developed and cultivated, lead to the attainment of Nibbāna in this very life. What four? The faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, and the faculty of concentration. These four things, Mahānāma, when developed and cultivated, lead to the attainment of Nibbāna in this very life. “But, venerable sir, how is the faculty of faith developed and cultivated so that it leads to the attainment of Nibbāna in this very life? “Here, Mahānāma, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One. This, Mahānāma, is how the faculty of faith is developed and cultivated so that it leads to the attainment of Nibbāna in this very life. “And how, Mahānāma, is the faculty of energy developed and cultivated so that it leads to the attainment of Nibbāna in this very life? Here, Mahānāma, a noble disciple dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the acquisition of wholesome states; he is steadfast, firm in exertion, not remiss in developing wholesome states. This, Mahānāma, is how the faculty of energy is developed and cultivated so that it leads to the attainment of Nibbāna in this very life. “And how, Mahānāma, is the faculty of mindfulness developed and cultivated so that it leads to the attainment of Nibbāna in this very life? Here, Mahānāma, a noble disciple is mindful, possessing supreme mindfulness and alertness, remembering and recollecting what was done and said long ago. This, Mahānāma, is how the faculty of mindfulness is developed and cultivated so that it leads to the attainment of Nibbāna in this very life. “And how, Mahānāma, is the faculty of concentration developed and cultivated so that it leads to the attainment of Nibbāna in this very life? Here, Mahānāma, a noble disciple, withdrawn from sensual pleasures, withdrawn from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of withdrawal. With the subsiding of thought and examination, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without thought and examination, and has rapture and happiness born of concentration. With the fading away of rapture, he dwells equanimous and, mindful and clearly comprehending, experiences happiness with the body; he enters and dwells in the third jhāna of which the noble ones declare: ‘He is equanimous, mindful, and dwells happily. With the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous passing away of joy and dejection, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and includes the purification of mindfulness through equanimity.

This, Mahānāma, is how the faculty of concentration is developed and cultivated so that it leads to the attainment of Nibbāna in this very life. “It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is amazing, venerable sir! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘These four things, when developed and cultivated, lead to the attainment of Nibbāna in this very life. “Indeed, Mahānāma, it is because I have seen this danger in the five aggregates subject to clinging that I have declared: ‘These four things, when developed and cultivated, lead to the attainment of Nibbāna in this very life. What five? Whatever kind of form there is, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—this is called the form aggregate subject to clinging. Whatever kind of feeling there is... whatever kind of perception there is... whatever kind of formations there are... whatever kind of consciousness there is, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—this is called the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging. It is because I have seen this danger in these five aggregates subject to clinging that I have declared: ‘These four things, when developed and cultivated, lead to the attainment of Nibbāna in this very life. When this was said, the householder Mahānāma said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir! The Dhamma has been made clear in many ways by the Blessed One, as though he were turning upright what had been overturned, revealing what was hidden, showing the way to one who was lost, or holding up a lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms. I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May I receive the going forth under the Blessed One, may I receive the higher ordination! “Mahānāma, one who belongs to another sect cannot receive the going forth or the higher ordination here in this Dhamma and Discipline within less than a year. “Venerable sir, if one who belongs to another sect cannot receive the going forth or the higher ordination here in this Dhamma and Discipline within less than a year, then let me wait for a year. Then the householder Mahānāma, having pleased the Blessed One with his wise words, rose from his seat and departed. Not long after the householder Mahānāma had left, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, even if a person belonging to another sect comes and asks for the going forth and the higher ordination here in this Dhamma and Discipline, he should not be granted the going forth and the higher ordination within less than a year. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, there are some people belonging to other sects who harbor ill will toward the Tathāgata or toward the Tathāgata’s disciples. If they see someone receiving the going forth and the higher ordination here in this Dhamma and Discipline within less than a year, they might think: ‘We have gained an advantage over them; we are superior to them. Therefore, bhikkhus, even if a person belonging to another sect comes and asks for the going forth and the higher ordination here in this Dhamma and Discipline, he should not be granted the going forth and the higher ordination within less than a year. Then the householder Mahānāma returned to the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, I have waited for a year. May I receive the going forth under the Blessed One, may I receive the higher ordination! Then the Blessed One gave the householder Mahānāma the going forth and the higher ordination. And the Venerable Mahānāma, not long after his higher ordination, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, that unsurpassed consummation of the spiritual life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness, and having entered upon it, he dwelt therein. He directly knew: “Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being. And the Venerable Mahānāma became one of the arahants. And the Venerable Mahānāma was one of the disciples of the Blessed One who were foremost among those who possessed great wisdom. Thus it was said: “The householder Mahānāma was one of the disciples of the Blessed One who were foremost among those who possessed great wisdom. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated in heart, the Venerable Mahānāma delighted in the Blessed One’s words. Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” they replied. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is intent on the welfare of both himself and others; the person who is intent
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu in the Nigrodha Park.

Then Mahānāma the Sakyan approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, Mahānāma the Sakyan said this to the Blessed One:
“To what extent, Bhante, is one a lay follower?”
“Mahānāma, when one has gone for refuge to the Buddha, gone for refuge to the Dhamma, and gone for refuge to the Saṅgha—
to this extent, Mahānāma, one is a lay follower.
“But to what extent, Bhante, is a lay follower virtuous?”
“Mahānāma, when a lay follower abstains from the destruction of life, abstains from taking what is not given,
abstains from sexual misconduct, abstains from false speech, and abstains from fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence—
to this extent, Mahānāma, a lay follower is virtuous.”
“But to what extent, Bhante, is a lay follower practicing for his own benefit, but not for the benefit of others?
“Mahānāma, it is when a lay follower himself possesses faith, but does not encourage others in the possession of faith;
he himself possesses virtue, but does not encourage others in the possession of virtue.”
He himself is accomplished in generosity, but does not encourage others in the accomplishment of generosity;
he himself desires to see the bhikkhus, but does not encourage others to see the bhikkhus;
he himself desires to hear the true Dhamma, but does not encourage others to hear the true Dhamma.
He himself is one who retains the teachings he has heard, but does not encourage others to retain the teachings;
he himself examines the meaning of the teachings he has heard, but does not encourage others to examine their meaning;
having himself understood both the meaning and the teaching, he practices in accordance with the Dharma, but does not encourage others to practice in accordance with the Dharma.
“To this extent, Mahānāma, a lay follower has practiced for his own benefit, but not for the benefit of others.
“But to what extent, Bhante, has a lay follower practiced both for his own benefit and for the benefit of others?
“When, Mahānāma, a lay follower is himself accomplished in faith and encourages others to achieve accomplishment in faith;”
One is oneself accomplished in virtue and encourages others in the accomplishment of virtue;
one is oneself accomplished in generosity and encourages others in the accomplishment of generosity;
one is oneself desirous of seeing the bhikkhus and encourages others to see the bhikkhus.
One desires to hear the true Dhamma oneself and encourages others to listen to the true Dhamma;
one is naturally inclined to retain the teachings one has heard and encourages others to retain the Dhamma;
one examines the meaning of the teachings one has heard and encourages others to examine their meaning.
“Having understood the goal for himself and having understood the Dhamma, he practices in accordance with the Dhamma, and he encourages others to practice in accordance with the Dhamma.
To this extent, Mahānāma, a lay follower is practicing for his own welfare and for the welfare of others.
This was the fifth.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.26 3. Gahapativagga Jīvakasutta At one time, the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place. Then the physician Jīvaka Komārabhacca approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him: “Jīvaka, when a noble disciple possesses four qualities, it is fitting for him to go to a monastery, to visit the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, and to sit in the presence of the bhikkhus. What four? (1) Here, Jīvaka, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One.

(2) He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally realized by the wise. (3) He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. (4) He possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones—virtues that are untorn, unrent, unblotched, unmottled, liberating, praised by the wise, not adhered to, and conducive to concentration. When a noble disciple possesses these four qualities, Jīvaka, it is fitting for him to go to a monastery, to visit the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, and to sit in the presence of the bhikkhus. Then the physician Jīvaka Komārabhacca rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, and, raising his joined palms in reverential salutation toward the Blessed One, said this to him: “It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is amazing, venerable sir! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘When a noble disciple possesses these four qualities, Jīvaka, it is fitting for him to go to a monastery, to visit the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, and to sit in the presence of the bhikkhus. Venerable sir, I myself possess confirmed confidence in the Buddha... in the Dhamma... in the Saṅgha... I possess the virtues dear to the noble ones. Venerable sir, it is fitting for me to go to the monastery, to visit the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, and to sit in the presence of the bhikkhus. “Jīvaka, you are endowed with faith, but you have not seen the Four Noble Truths as they really are. What four? The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering. Jīvaka, you are endowed with faith, but you have not seen these Four Noble Truths as they really are. Then the physician Jīvaka Komārabhacca rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed. Not long after he had left, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, do you see how that physician Jīvaka Komārabhacca has gone away after paying homage to me and keeping me on his right? “Yes, venerable sir. “Bhikkhus, that physician Jīvaka Komārabhacca is endowed with faith, but he has not seen the Four Noble Truths as they really are. What four? The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering. Bhikkhus, that physician Jīvaka Komārabhacca is endowed with faith, but he has not seen these Four Noble Truths as they really are. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is wonderful, venerable sir! It is amazing, venerable sir! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘Jīvaka, you are endowed with faith, but you have not seen the Four Noble Truths as they really are…’” “Ānanda, it is because I know Jīvaka Komārabhacca intimately that I said this. For if I did not know Jīvaka Komārabhacca intimately, I would not have said this. But because I know Jīvaka Komārabhacca intimately, I said this. Ānanda, if a noble disciple possesses four qualities, it is fitting for him to go to a monastery, to visit the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, and to sit in the presence of the bhikkhus. What four? (As above. When a noble disciple possesses these four qualities, Ānanda, it is fitting for him to go to a monastery, to visit the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, and to sit in the presence of the bhikkhus. Then the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed. Not long after the Venerable Ānanda had left, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, do you see how the Venerable Ānanda has gone away after paying homage to me and keeping me on his right? “Yes, venerable sir. “Bhikkhus, the Venerable Ānanda is endowed with faith, but he has not seen the Four Noble Truths as they really are. What four? The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering. Bhikkhus, the Venerable Ānanda is endowed with faith, but he has not seen these Four Noble Truths as they really are. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is wonderful, venerable sir! It is amazing, venerable sir! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘If a noble disciple possesses four qualities, Ānanda, it is fitting for him to go to a monastery, to visit the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, and to sit in the presence of the bhikkhus. “Ānanda, it is because I know you intimately that I said this. For if I did not know you intimately, Ānanda, I would not have said this. But because I know you intimately, Ānanda, I said this. Ānanda, if a noble disciple possesses four qualities, it is fitting for him to go to a monastery, to visit the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, and to sit in the presence of the bhikkhus. What four? (As above. When a noble disciple possesses these four qualities, Ānanda, it is fitting for him to go to a monastery, to visit the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, and to sit in the presence of the bhikkhus. Then the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed. “Bhikkhus, do you see how the Venerable Ānanda has gone away after paying homage to me and keeping me on his right? “Yes, venerable sir. “Bhikkhus, the Venerable Ānanda is endowed with faith, but he has not seen the Four Noble Truths as they really are. What four? The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is wonderful, venerable sir!
(AN 8.26, PTS AN iv 222) On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in Jīvaka’s Mango Grove.

Then Jīvaka Komārabhacca approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, Jīvaka Komārabhacca said this to the Blessed One:
“In what way, venerable sir, is one a lay follower? “Jīvaka,
when one has gone for refuge to the Buddha, gone for refuge to the Dhamma, and gone for refuge to the Saṅgha—
in that way, Jīvaka, one is a lay follower.”
“But to what extent, venerable sir, is a lay follower virtuous?
“Jīvaka, when a lay follower abstains from the destruction of life … [and so on] … abstains from the occasion for negligence consisting in fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants;
to this extent, Jīvaka, a lay follower is virtuous.”
“But to what extent, venerable sir, is a lay follower practicing for his own benefit, but not for the benefit of others?
“Jīvaka, it is when a lay follower himself possesses faith, but does not encourage others in the possession of faith...
[and so on] ...he himself has understood the goal and understood the Dhamma, and practices in accordance with the Dhamma, but does not encourage others in the practice in accordance with the Dhamma.”
“To this extent, Jīvaka, a lay follower has practiced for his own benefit, but not for the benefit of others.
“But to what extent, Bhante, has a lay follower practiced both for his own benefit and for the benefit of others?
“Jīvaka, when a lay follower is himself accomplished in faith and encourages others to achieve accomplishment in faith;”
He himself is endowed with virtue and encourages others in the perfection of virtue;
he himself is endowed with generosity and encourages others in the perfection of generosity;
he himself desires to see the bhikkhus and encourages others to see the bhikkhus.
He himself desires to hear the true Dhamma, and he encourages others to listen to the true Dhamma;
he himself is inclined to retain the teachings he has heard, and he encourages others to retain the teachings;
he himself investigates the meaning of the teachings he has heard, and he encourages others to investigate their meaning.
“Having understood the goal for oneself and having understood the Dhamma, one practices in accordance with the Dhamma, and one encourages others to practice in accordance with the Dhamma.
To this extent, Jīvaka, a lay follower is practicing for their own welfare and for the welfare of others.
This was the sixth [discourse].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.27 3.

Gahapativagga Paṭhamabalasutta (The First Discourse on Strength) "Bhikkhus, there are these five strengths. What five? The strength of faith, the strength of energy, the strength of mindfulness, the strength of concentration, and the strength of wisdom. These, bhikkhus, are the five strengths."
“Bhikkhus, there are these eight powers. What are the eight? [The Buddha said: (AN 8.27, PTS AN iv 223)
“Monks, children have the power of weeping; women have the power of anger; thieves have the power of weapons;
kings have the power of sovereignty; fools have the power of self-pity; the wise have the power of consideration for others; those of great learning have the power of reflection;
and recluses and brahmins have the power of patience. These, monks, are the eight powers.”
Seventh. Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.28.
3. Gahapativagga (The Chapter on Householders)
The Second Discourse on Powers (Dutiyabalasutta).

Then the Venerable Sāriputta approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. As the Venerable Sāriputta was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Sāriputta, how many powers does a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed possess, by virtue of which he claims the destruction of the taints, saying:
‘My taints are destroyed’?
“Venerable sir, there are eight powers of a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, by virtue of which he claims the destruction of the taints, saying: ‘My taints are destroyed.’”
‘My taints are destroyed.
Which eight?
Here, venerable sir, for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, all conditioned phenomena have been well seen as they really are with correct wisdom as impermanent.

Furthermore, venerable sir, when all conditioned phenomena have been clearly seen as they really are with correct wisdom by a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed—as impermanent—this too is a power of the bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, by virtue of which power the bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed claims the destruction of the taints: [“I understand: ‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.’”]
‘My taints are destroyed.
Furthermore, venerable sir, for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, sensual pleasures have been well seen as they really are with correct wisdom as being like a pit of glowing coals.
Moreover, venerable sir, for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, sensual pleasures have been well seen as they really are with correct wisdom as being like a pit of glowing coals.

They are well seen. This too, venerable sir, is a power of a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, by virtue of which power a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed claims the destruction of the taints, saying:
"The taints are destroyed in me."

Furthermore, venerable sir, the mind of a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed slants, slopes, and inclines toward seclusion; it is withdrawn, delights in renunciation, and has completely become free from states that are the basis for the taints.
That the mind of a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed slants, slopes, and inclines toward seclusion;

that it is withdrawn, delights in renunciation, and has completely become free from states that are the basis for the taints—this too, venerable sir, [is a mark of one who has attained final knowledge].
“Venerable sir, there is a power possessed by a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, by virtue of which a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed claims the destruction of the taints, saying:
‘My taints are destroyed.
Furthermore, venerable sir, the four foundations of mindfulness have been developed and well-developed by a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed.”
Furthermore, venerable sir, when the four foundations of mindfulness have been developed and well-developed by a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed,
this too is a power of that bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, by virtue of which power the bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed claims the destruction of the taints: [as follows].
‘My taints are exhausted.

Furthermore, venerable sir, for a bhikkhu whose taints are exhausted, the four bases of psychic power have been developed and well-developed … the five faculties have been developed and well-developed …”
The seven factors of awakening have been developed, well-developed...
[and so on] ...the noble eightfold path has been developed, well-developed.
And, venerable sir, that the noble eightfold path has been developed, well-developed by a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed—this too is a quality of one whose taints are destroyed.
This too, venerable sir, is a power of a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, by virtue of which power a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed claims the destruction of the taints, saying:
"The taints are destroyed in me."
“Venerable sir, these are the eight powers of a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, possessed of which a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed claims the destruction of the taints, saying:
‘My taints are destroyed.
This is the eighth.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.29 3. Gahapativagga Akkhaṇasutta – The Discourse on Inopportune Moments “Bhikkhus, there are these eight inopportune moments for one who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness to attain the unsurpassed security from bondage, that is, arahantship. What eight? (1) Here, bhikkhus, a woman is reborn in a family of low birth—whether a candāla family, a veṇa family, a nesāda family, a rathakāra family, or a pukkusaka family—a family that is poor, destitute, and indigent, lacking food and clothing. She is ugly, unsightly, and ill-favored, with a body full of blemishes; she is blind, deaf, insane, or mentally deranged. This is the first inopportune moment for one who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness to attain the unsurpassed security from bondage, that is, arahantship.

(2) Again, a man is reborn in a family of low birth—whether a candāla family, a veṇa family, a nesāda family, a rathakāra family, or a pukkusaka family—a family that is poor, destitute, and indigent, lacking food and clothing. He is ugly, unsightly, and ill-favored, with a body full of blemishes; he is blind, deaf, insane, or mentally deranged. This is the second inopportune moment for one who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness to attain the unsurpassed security from bondage, that is, arahantship. (3) Again, a woman is reborn among the long-lived devas. This is the third inopportune moment for one who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness to attain the unsurpassed security from bondage, that is, arahantship. (4) Again, a man is reborn among the long-lived devas. This is the fourth inopportune moment for one who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness to attain the unsurpassed security from bondage, that is, arahantship. (5) Again, one is reborn in a border region where there is no access to the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata. This is the fifth inopportune moment for one who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness to attain the unsurpassed security from bondage, that is, arahantship. (6) Again, one is reborn in a central region, but at a time when a Tathāgata, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One has not appeared in the world, and the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata have not spread. This is the sixth inopportune moment for one who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness to attain the unsurpassed security from bondage, that is, arahantship. (7) Again, one is reborn in a central region, and at a time when a Tathāgata, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One has appeared in the world, and the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata have spread. Yet, one holds wrong view and has adopted a perverted perspective, thinking: ‘There is nothing given, nothing offered, nothing sacrificed; there is no fruit or result of good and bad deeds; there is no this world, no other world; there is no mother, no father; there are no beings spontaneously born; there are no ascetics and brahmins faring rightly and practicing rightly who, having realized this world and the other world for themselves by direct knowledge, make them known to others. This is the seventh inopportune moment for one who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness to attain the unsurpassed security from bondage, that is, arahantship. (8) Again, one is reborn in a central region, and at a time when a Tathāgata, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One has appeared in the world, and the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata have spread. One holds right view and has adopted an unperverted perspective, thinking: ‘There is what is given, what is offered, what is sacrificed; there is fruit and result of good and bad deeds; there is this world and the other world; there is mother and father; there are beings spontaneously born; there are ascetics and brahmins faring rightly and practicing rightly who, having realized this world and the other world for themselves by direct knowledge, make them known to others. However, one is dull-witted, slow to understand, and lacks wisdom. This is the eighth inopportune moment for one who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness to attain the unsurpassed security from bondage, that is, arahantship. These, bhikkhus, are the eight inopportune moments for one who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness to attain the unsurpassed security from bondage, that is, arahantship.”
“‘The world has its appointed task at the moment,
the world has its appointed task at the moment,’ monks, says the uninstructed worldling, yet he does not know what the moment is or what the non-moment is.
There are these eight non-moments, monks, which are not the right time for living the holy life.”
What are the eight? Here, monks,
a Tathāgata has arisen in the world, an Arhat, a perfectly enlightened one, perfect in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the worlds,
an unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.
The Dhamma is being taught— leading to peace, leading to Nibbāna, leading to enlightenment, proclaimed by the Sugata—
and yet this person has been reborn in hell.
This, monks, is the first inopportune moment, the unfavorable time for living the holy life.

Furthermore, monks, a Tathāgata has appeared in the world … [as before] … the Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One; and the Dhamma is being taught—conducive to peace, conducive to Nibbāna, leading to enlightenment, as proclaimed by the Sugata;
yet this person has been reborn in the animal realm … [as before] … Furthermore, monks … [as before].
And this person is reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts … [as before] … Furthermore, monks,
… [as before] … and this person is reborn in a certain class of long-lived deities … [as before].
Furthermore, monks, ...
this person is reborn in a remote border region among uncivilized barbarians where there is no access for bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, laymen, or laywomen...
Furthermore, monks, ... this person is reborn in the central regions, yet he holds wrong views and possesses a perverted perspective:
‘There is no giving, there is no sacrifice, there is no offering; there is no fruit or result of deeds well done or ill done;
there is no this world, there is no other world; there is no mother, there is no father;

there are no beings who arise spontaneously; there are in the world no recluses or brahmins who have attained rightly, who have practiced rightly, and who, having realized this world and the other world for themselves by direct knowledge, make them known to others.’
‘...and having realized the other world for themselves through direct knowledge, they make it known.
...Furthermore, monks,
...this person is reborn in the central provinces, yet he is dull-witted, stupid, and mute, incapable of discerning the meaning of what is well-spoken and what is ill-spoken.
This, monks, is the seventh inopportune and untimely occasion for living the holy life.
Furthermore, monks, a Tathāgata has not appeared in the world, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha... [pe] ...the Teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One;
and the Dhamma leading to peace, leading to Nibbāna, leading to awakening, proclaimed by the Sugata, is not being taught. And this—
A person is reborn in the central provinces, and he is wise, not dull-witted, not deaf-mute,
and capable of understanding the meaning of what is well-spoken and what is ill-spoken.
This, monks, is the eighth inopportune moment, the wrong time for living the holy life.
“Monks, these eight are inopportune moments, unsuitable times for living the holy life (*brahmacariya*).
There is, monks, only one opportune moment, one suitable time for living the holy life.
Which one? [The following:]”

In this case, monks, a Tathāgata has arisen in the world—an Arhat, a perfectly enlightened Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the worlds, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.
And the Dhamma is being taught—leading to tranquility, leading to Parinibbāna, leading to enlightenment, proclaimed by the Sugata.
And this person is reborn in the central provinces; he is wise, not dull-witted, not deaf-mute, and capable.
To understand the meaning of what is well-spoken and what is ill-spoken.
This, monks, is the one occasion and the one time for living the holy life.
Having obtained this human attainment...
Those who do not seize the opportune moment when the true Dharma is well-proclaimed,
they let that moment pass by.
For many are the unfavorable moments said to be obstacles to the path;
they occur only rarely in the world.
Tathāgatas arise;
this has now become manifest,
which is very difficult to find in the world.
The attainment of human birth and the teaching of the True Dharma—
these are sufficient grounds for striving therein.
By a person desiring their own welfare,
how should they recognize the true Dhamma?
Let not the opportune moment pass you by.
For those who have missed the opportune moment grieve when they are cast into hell;
if one fails in this very life, [one will surely fail in the next].
The certainty of the true Dhamma;
like a merchant who has missed his profit,
he will long regret it.
The person shrouded by ignorance,
having transgressed against the true Dhamma,
[enters] the saṃsāra of birth and death.
One will experience [the results] for a long time.
And those who, having attained human birth,
are well-established in the True Dharma that has been excellently proclaimed;
They have carried out the Teacher’s word;
they will carry it out, or they are carrying it out now.
They have found the opportune moment in the world.
The unsurpassed holy life;
those who have entered upon the path proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
Those restraints taught by the Visionary One,
the Kinsman of the Sun—
protected by them and ever mindful, [one should dwell].
Dwell untroubled,
having cut off all latent tendencies that follow the realm of Māra.
"Those indeed have reached the further shore in the world,
who have attained the destruction of the taints.
The ninth.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.30 3. Gahapativagga Anuruddhamahāvitakkasutta Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. There the Venerable Anuruddha addressed the bhikkhus: “Friends, friends! “Friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Anuruddha. The Venerable Anuruddha said this: “Friends, when a noble disciple possesses four things, he is one who has reached the goal, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained the true goal, destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through final knowledge. What four? Here, friends, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One.

He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. And he possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones—virtues that are untorn, unbroken, unspotted, unsplattered, liberating, praised by the wise, untarnished, leading to concentration. When a noble disciple possesses these four things, he is one who has reached the goal, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained the true goal, destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through final knowledge. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Venerable Anuruddha: “It is wonderful, friend Anuruddha, it is marvelous, friend Anuruddha! How the Blessed One has fully awakened to this Dhamma, and how the Venerable Anuruddha has fully penetrated it! For, friend Anuruddha, when a noble disciple possesses these four things, he is one who has reached the goal, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained the true goal, destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through final knowledge. “It is wonderful, friend Ānanda, it is marvelous, friend Ānanda! How the Blessed One has fully awakened to this Dhamma, and how the Venerable Ānanda has fully penetrated it! For, friend Ānanda, when a noble disciple possesses these four things, he is one who has reached the goal, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained the true goal, destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through final knowledge. Then the Blessed One, having understood the exchange between the Venerable Anuruddha and the Venerable Ānanda, addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, when a noble disciple possesses four things, he is one who has reached the goal, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained the true goal, destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through final knowledge. What four? Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha... [as above] ...and he possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones. When a noble disciple possesses these four things, he is one who has reached the goal, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained the true goal, destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through final knowledge. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “It is wonderful, Bhante, it is marvelous, Bhante! How the Blessed One has fully awakened to this Dhamma, and how the Venerable Anuruddha has fully penetrated it! For, Bhante, when a noble disciple possesses these four things, he is one who has reached the goal, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained the true goal, destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through final knowledge. “It is wonderful, Ānanda, it is marvelous, Ānanda! How the Tathāgata has fully awakened to this Dhamma, and how the Venerable Anuruddha has fully penetrated it! For, Ānanda, when a noble disciple possesses these four things, he is one who has reached the goal, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained the true goal, destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through final knowledge. “Bhante, as for the Venerable Anuruddha, he is one who has reached the goal, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained the true goal, destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through final knowledge. Why is that? Because the Venerable Anuruddha possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha... [as above] ...and he possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones. “Indeed, Ānanda, the Venerable Anuruddha is one who has reached the goal, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained the true goal, destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through final knowledge. Why is that? Because the Venerable Anuruddha possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha... [as above] ...and he possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “Bhante, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! How the Blessed One has fully awakened to this Dhamma, and how the Venerable Anuruddha has fully penetrated it! For, Bhante, when a noble disciple possesses these four things, he is one who has reached the goal, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained the true goal, destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through final knowledge. “It is wonderful, Ānanda, it is marvelous, Ānanda! How the Tathāgata has fully awakened to this Dhamma, and how the Venerable Anuruddha has fully penetrated it! For, Ānanda, when a noble disciple possesses these four things, he is one who has reached the goal, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained the true goal, destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through final knowledge. “Bhante, as for the Venerable Anuruddha, he is one who has reached the goal, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained the true goal, destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through final knowledge.

Why is that? Because the Venerable Anuruddha possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha... [as above] ...and he possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones. “Indeed, Ānanda, the Venerable Anuruddha is one who has reached the goal, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained the true goal, destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through final knowledge. Why is that? Because the Venerable Anuruddha possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha... [as above] ...and he possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones. What four? Here, Ānanda, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha... [as above] ...and he possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones. When a noble disciple possesses these four things, he is one who has reached the goal, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained the true goal, destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through final knowledge. Bhante, I am one who has reached the goal, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained the true goal, destroyed the fetters of existence, and am liberated through final knowledge. “Indeed, Ānanda, the Venerable Anuruddha is one who has reached the goal, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained the true goal, destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through final knowledge.
