(AN 8.30, PTS AN iv 228) At one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Bhaggas at Suṁsumāragira, in the Bhesakaḷā Grove, the Deer Park.
Now at that time, the Venerable Anuruddha was dwelling among the Cetis in the Eastern Bamboo Grove.
Then, while the Venerable Anuruddha was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in his mind:
"This Dhamma is for one of few desires, not for one of great desires;
this Dhamma is for one who is content, not for one who is discontented."
This Dhamma is for one who is secluded, not for one who delights in company;
this Dhamma is for one who has aroused energy, not for one who is indolent;
this Dhamma is for one whose mindfulness is established, not for one who is muddled in mindfulness.
“This Dhamma is for one who is concentrated, not for one who is unconcentrated;
this Dhamma is for one possessed of wisdom, not for one of poor wisdom.
Then the Blessed One, having known with his own mind the reflection that had arisen in the mind of the Venerable Anuruddha—as if [he were lifting up] a palm fruit in the palm of his hand—
Just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm, even so,
vanishing from the Bhesakaḷā Grove deer park at Susumāragira among the Bhaggas, he reappeared in the presence of the Venerable Anuruddha in the Pācīnavaṃsa Grove among the Cetis.
The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat.
The Venerable Anuruddha, having paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down to one side.
As the Venerable Anuruddha was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Excellent, excellent, Anuruddha!
It is well indeed, Anuruddha, that you have reflected upon this reflection of a Great Man:
‘This Dhamma is for one of few desires; this Dhamma is not for one of great desire.’”
This Dhamma is for one who is contented, not for one who is discontented;
this Dhamma is for one who is secluded, not for one who delights in company;
this Dhamma is for one who has aroused energy, not for one who is lazy.
‘This Dhamma is for one who is established in mindfulness, not for one who is muddled in mindfulness;
this Dhamma is for one who is concentrated, not for one who is unconcentrated;
this Dhamma is for one who possesses wisdom, not for one who lacks wisdom.’”
"In that case, Anuruddha, you should reflect on this eighth thought of a great person:
‘This Dhamma is for one who delights in the unproliferated, who takes delight in the unproliferated; this Dhamma is not for one who delights in proliferation, who takes delight in proliferation.
When you, Anuruddha, have reflected on these eight thoughts of a great person, then, Anuruddha..."
To whatever extent you desire, secluded from sensual pleasures and secluded from unwholesome states,
you will enter and dwell in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. When, Anuruddha,
you direct these eight thoughts of a great person, then, Anuruddha, you—

"As long as you wish, by the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, you will enter and dwell in the second jhāna, which is internal serenity and unification of mind, free from applied and sustained thought, born of concentration,
and filled with rapture and happiness. When, Anuruddha, you direct these eight thoughts of a great person, then, Anuruddha..."
To whatever extent you desire, through the fading away of rapture, you will dwell in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending, and experience happiness with the body;
thus, you will enter and dwell in the third jhāna, which the Noble Ones describe as: "One who dwells in happiness, mindful and equanimous."
Since you, Anuruddha, will direct these eight thoughts of a great person,
then, Anuruddha, as much as you desire, by the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief,
you will enter and dwell in the fourth jhāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.
Since you, Anuruddha, will reflect upon these eight thoughts of a great man and will become one who obtains at will,
without difficulty, and without trouble, these four jhānas that are higher mental states and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life,
then for you, Anuruddha, it will be just as it is for a householder or a householder’s son.
or a basket full of various colored cloths;
even so will that refuse-rag robe appear to you as you dwell contented, joyful, free from anxiety, living at ease, and entering upon Nibbāna.
Now, Anuruddha, when you direct these eight thoughts of a great person and these four...
You will obtain at will, without difficulty, and without hardship, the jhānas that belong to the higher mind and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life.
Then for you, Anuruddha, it will be just as if a householder or a householder’s son had rice from which the black grains have been winnowed, served with many soups and many curries.
In this very way, that alms-food will be eaten by you as one who dwells contented, joyful, free from anxiety, at ease, and who has entered upon nibbāna. And when, Anuruddha,
you have directed these eight thoughts of a great person and become one who obtains at will,
without difficulty, these four jhānas— states of higher mind that provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life— then [your food will be so].
It is not difficult to obtain, Anuruddha; therefore, for you who dwell contented, the dwelling at the foot of a tree will appear just like the gabled house of a householder or a householder’s son—
plastered inside and out, windless, with doors bolted and windows shut— and it will lead to delight,
to freedom from anxiety, to a comfortable dwelling, and to the descent into Nibbāna.
Since you, Anuruddha, will reflect upon these eight thoughts of a great person and will become one who gains at will—
without difficulty or trouble— these four jhānas that are higher mental states and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life,
then for you, Anuruddha, it will be just as it is for a householder or a householder’s son.
Or a couch spread with woolen blankets, covered with embroidered covers,
spread with a fine antelope hide, provided with a canopy above, and with red bolsters at both ends—
just so will that bed of grass appear to you as you dwell contented, for the sake of delight, freedom from distress, a comfortable dwelling, and for entering into Nibbāna.
Since you, Anuruddha, will reflect upon these eight thoughts of a great person and will become one who gains at will—
without difficulty and without hardship— these four jhānas that are higher mental states and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life,
then for you, Anuruddha, it will be just as it is for a householder or a householder’s son.
“Or various medicines, such as ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, and molasses—
even so will you consume the medicine of putrid urine while dwelling contented, without anxiety, in comfort,
and entering upon the realization of Nibbāna. Therefore, Anuruddha, you should spend the coming rains retreat right here in the Eastern Bamboo Grove among the Cetis.”
“Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Anuruddha replied to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, having exhorted the Venerable Anuruddha with this instruction,
just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm, vanished from among the Cetīs.
Having vanished from the Pācīnavaṃsa Grove, the Blessed One appeared in the Bhesakaḷā Grove, the Deer Park at Susumāragira in the country of the Bhaggas.
The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat.
Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Monks, I shall teach you the eight thoughts of a great person; listen to that...
And what, monks, are the eight thoughts of a great person?
This Dhamma, monks, is for one of few desires, not for one of great desire.”
“Bhikkhus, this Dhamma is for one who is contented, not for one who is discontented;
this Dhamma is for one who is secluded, not for one who delights in company;
this Dhamma is for one who has aroused energy, not for one who is lazy.”
“Bhikkhus, this Dhamma is for one who is established in mindfulness; it is not for one who is muddled in mindfulness.
Bhikkhus, this Dhamma is for one who is concentrated; it is not for one who is unconcentrated.
Bhikkhus, this Dhamma is for one who possesses wisdom; it is not for one who lacks wisdom.”

“Monks, this Dhamma is for one who delights in the non-proliferated (*nippapañca*), for one who takes delight in the non-proliferated; this Dhamma is not for one who delights in proliferation, for one who takes delight in proliferation.
‘Monks, this Dhamma is for one of few desires, not for one of great desires’—this, it was said, is so.
With reference to what was this said?”
In this case, monks, a monk being of few desires does not wish: "May they know me as one of few desires"; being content, he does not wish:
"May they know me as one who is content"; being secluded, he does not wish: "May they know me as one who is secluded";
being energetic, he does not wish: "May they know me as one who is energetic."
Being established in mindfulness, he does not wish: “May they know me as one who is established in mindfulness.
Being concentrated, he does not wish: “May they know me as one who is concentrated. Being possessed of wisdom, he does not wish: “May they know me as one who is possessed of wisdom.
Being one who delights in the non-proliferated, he does not wish: “May they know me as one who delights in the non-proliferated.”
‘Bhikkhus, this Dhamma is for one of few desires, not for one of great desires’—this is what was said, and it is in reference to this that it was said.
‘Bhikkhus, this Dhamma is for one who is contented, not for one who is discontented’—this too has been said; with reference to what was it said?
“Here, monks, a monk is content with any kind of robe, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
‘This is the Dhamma for one who is content, not for one who is discontent,’ this is what was said,
and it is on account of this that it was said.”
“Bhikkhus, this Dhamma is for one who is secluded; this Dhamma is not for one who delights in company. So it was said. With reference to what was this said?

Here, bhikkhus, while a bhikkhu is dwelling in seclusion, there come to visit him bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, male lay followers, female lay followers, kings, royal ministers, members of other sects, and disciples of other sects.

In this regard, with a mind inclined toward seclusion, leaning toward seclusion, tending toward seclusion, established in seclusion, and delighting in renunciation, a bhikkhu speaks only such talk as is connected with sending [others] away.
"Bhikkhus, this Dhamma is for one who is secluded; this Dhamma is not for one who delights in company"—it was with reference to this that it was said.
“‘This Dhamma, bhikkhus, is for one who has aroused energy; this Dhamma is not for one who is lazy’—thus it was said. And with reference to what was this said?

Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the acquisition of wholesome states; he is steadfast, firm in effort, and does not relinquish the burden regarding wholesome states.
‘This Dhamma, bhikkhus, is for one who has aroused energy; this Dhamma is not for one who is lazy.’”
Thus, that which was said—“This Dhamma, bhikkhus, is for one who is established in mindfulness; this Dhamma is not for one who is muddled in mindfulness”—this was said with reference to this.
But with reference to what was it said?
“Here, monks, a bhikkhu is mindful, endowed with supreme mindfulness and circumspection; he remembers and recollects what was done long ago and what was spoken long ago.
‘This Dhamma, monks, is for one who is established in mindfulness;
this Dhamma is not for one who is muddled in mindfulness’—this is said with reference to this.”
“‘This Dhamma is for one who is concentrated, monks;
this Dhamma is not for one who is unconcentrated’—thus it was said. With reference to what was this said?
Here, monks, a monk, quite secluded from sensual pleasures … [as above] … enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.”
“‘This Dhamma, bhikkhus, is for one who is concentrated;
this Dhamma is not for one who is unconcentrated’—this is what was said, and it was said with reference to this.
‘This Dhamma, bhikkhus, is for one who possesses wisdom; this Dhamma is not for one who lacks wisdom.’”
Thus indeed it was said. With reference to what was this said?
Here, monks, a monk is wise; he is endowed with the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble, penetrative, and leads to the complete destruction of suffering.
"Monks, this Dhamma is for one who is wise; this Dhamma is not for one who lacks wisdom. Thus it was said. And with reference to this was it said.
Thus, that which was said—this was said with reference to this:

“Monks, this Dhamma is for one who delights in the non-proliferated (*nippapañca*), for one who takes delight in the non-proliferated; this Dhamma is not for one who delights in proliferation, for one who takes delight in proliferation.
So it was said. With reference to what was this said?
“Here, monks, a bhikkhu’s mind leaps forward into the cessation of conceptual proliferation (*papañca*), becomes serene, settles, and is liberated in it.

‘This Dhamma, monks, is for one who delights in non-proliferation, for one who takes pleasure in non-proliferation; this Dhamma is not for one who delights in proliferation, for one who takes pleasure in proliferation.
It was with reference to this that it was said.”
Then the Venerable Anuruddha spent the subsequent rains retreat right there in the Pācinavaṃsa Grove among the Cetis.
Then, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, the Venerable Anuruddha, in no long time,
attained that supreme goal of the holy life for the sake of which young men of good family rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness.
Having realized it for himself through direct higher knowledge in this very life, he entered and dwelt therein.
He directly knew: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
And thus the Venerable Anuruddha became one of the Arahants.
Then, at that time, the Venerable Anuruddha, having attained arahantship, spoke these verses:
“Having understood my intention,
the Teacher, unsurpassed in the world, [spoke thus].”
With a mind-made body,
he approached by means of supernormal power;
just as my intention had been.
Beyond that he taught:
the Buddha, delighting in the unproliferated,
taught the unproliferated.
Having understood his Dhamma,
I dwelt delighting in the teaching;
the three knowledges were attained.
Thus was the teaching of the Buddha spoken.
Tenth. The third chapter, the Chapter on Householders, is concluded.
Its summary verse:
Two Uggas and two Hatthakas,
Mahānāma, and Jīvaka.
"Two powers are called 'opportune,' and ten, O Anuruddha," so it was said.
*Aṅguttara Nikāya* 8.31.

4. Dānavagga First Discourse on Giving (Paṭhamadānasutta) "Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of giving. What four? The gift given out of fear; the gift given for the sake of a reward; the gift given with the thought, 'In the past, my mother and father gave to me, so I should give to others'; and the gift given with a pure heart, thinking, 'Giving is good. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of giving."
“Bhikkhus, there are these eight gifts.
What are the eight?
One gives a gift out of resentment.”
One gives a gift out of fear;
one gives a gift thinking, “He gave to me”;
one gives a gift thinking, “He will give to me.”
One gives a gift thinking, "Giving is good";
one gives a gift thinking, "I cook, but these others do not cook; it is not right for me, while cooking, not to give a gift to those who do not cook";
one gives a gift thinking, "As I give this gift, a fine report of my reputation will spread abroad."
One gives a gift for the purpose of adorning the mind and equipping the mind.
These, monks, are the eight kinds of giving. Thus was the first [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.32 4. Dānavagga Second Discourse on Giving Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” they replied. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, there are these eight kinds of persons who are worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. What eight? (1) Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple has abandoned the five lower fetters; he is one who will reappear spontaneously [in the Pure Abodes] and will not return from that world. This is the first kind of person who is worthy of gifts... an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. (2) Again, a noble disciple has abandoned three fetters and has weakened lust, hatred, and delusion; he is a once-returner who, after returning to this world only one more time, will make an end of suffering. This is the second kind of person who is worthy of gifts... an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. (3) Again, a noble disciple has abandoned three fetters; he is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to perdition, bound for enlightenment, assured, heading toward the correct enlightenment. This is the third kind of person who is worthy of gifts... an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. (4) Again, one who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of non-returning—this is the fourth kind of person who is worthy of gifts... an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. (5) Again, one who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of once-returning—this is the fifth kind of person who is worthy of gifts... an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. (6) Again, one who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry—this is the sixth kind of person who is worthy of gifts... an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. (7) Again, a virtuous ordinary person—this is the seventh kind of person who is worthy of gifts... an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. (8) Again, a person of bad character who gives a gift to those who are virtuous—this is the eighth kind of person who is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. These, bhikkhus, are the eight kinds of persons who are worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, those bhikkhus delighted in the Blessed One’s words. [End of] the Second Discourse on Giving in the Chapter on Giving of the Book of Eights.
“Faith, moral shame, and wholesome generosity—
these qualities are followed by those who are true persons.”
For they call this the divine path;
by means of it, one goes to the world of the devas.
Second.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.33 4. Dānavagga Dānavatthusutta (The Discourse on the Bases for Giving) "Bhikkhus, there are these eight bases for giving. What eight? One gives a gift out of faith; one gives a gift out of a desire for [future] wealth; one gives a gift out of a desire for fame; one gives a gift because 'I gave before'; one gives a gift because 'they will give to me'; one gives a gift because 'they are giving to my relatives'; one gives a gift with the thought, 'By this gift, when I am in need, I will receive assistance'; one gives a gift with the thought, 'When I have gone forth, this will be my support for the training. These, bhikkhus, are the eight bases for giving."
“Monks, there are these eight grounds for giving. What eight?
One gives a gift out of lust; one gives a gift out of hatred; one gives a gift out of delusion; one gives a gift out of fear;
one gives a gift thinking, "This was given and performed by my father and grandfather; I ought not to let this ancient family lineage decline";
or one gives a gift thinking, "Having given this gift, with the breakup of the body, after death, I will reappear in a happy destination, in a heavenly world."
One gives a gift thinking, “As I give this gift, my mind becomes serene; gladness and joy arise.
One gives a gift for the purpose of adorning the mind and equipping the mind.
These, monks, are the eight grounds for giving.”
The Third.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.34 4.
The Chapter on Giving (Dānavagga)
The Discourse on the Field (Khettasutta): “Monks,
when seed is sown in a field endowed with eight factors, it does not yield great fruit, great enjoyment, or great profit.”
How is it endowed with eight factors?
Here, monks, a field is both high and low; it is full of stones and gravel; it is saline; it does not have deep water;
it is not possessed of good soil; it is not possessed of good drainage.
It is well-endowed with its seed-bed, but not well-endowed with boundaries.
In such a field, monks, a seed sown does not yield great fruit, nor great enjoyment, nor great excellence.
Even so, monks, a gift given to recluses and brahmins who possess these eight factors does not yield great fruit, nor great benefit, nor great splendor, nor great expansion.
How is it that [a gift] is not of great fruit among those endowed with eight factors?
Here, monks, recluses and brahmins possess wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration.

It is in this way, monks, that a gift given to recluses and brahmins who are endowed with these eight factors is not of great fruit, not of great benefit, not of great radiance, and not of great consequence.
“Monks, when seed is sown in a field endowed with eight factors, it becomes very fruitful, very productive, and very profitable.
Endowed with what eight factors?
Here, monks, a field is neither too high nor too low; it is free from stones and pebbles; and it is free from saline soil.”
It is well-prepared, it has deep furrows, it possesses ridges, it possesses channels, it possesses dikes,
and it possesses boundaries. Monks,
when a field is endowed with these eight factors, seed sown therein yields great fruit, provides great enjoyment, and brings great profit.
"In the same way, monks, a gift given to ascetics and brahmins who possess eight factors is of great fruit, of great benefit, of great splendor, and of great radiance.
In what way do they possess eight factors?
Here, monks, those ascetics and brahmins possess right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration."
"Monks, a gift given to ascetics and brahmins who are thus endowed with these eight factors is of great fruit, of great benefit, of great splendor, and of great result.
It is just as when, in a fertile field,
there is a sowing of excellent seed."
When one brings it to completion,
there comes the attainment of grain;
there comes the attainment of freedom from calamity.
There is growth in prosperity;
there is abundance in prosperity;
indeed, there is the fruit of prosperity.
Thus, when food is given to those who are endowed with perfected virtue,
it brings about perfection for the giver.
For what has been done by him is accomplished.
Therefore, a person here who desires accomplishment and seeks the goal of accomplishment, [should strive for it].
One should associate with those perfected in wisdom;
in this way, perfections succeed.
With one perfected in true knowledge and conduct...
Having attained the perfection of mind,
one performs the perfection of action and gains the perfection of welfare.
Having known the world as it truly is,
having attained perfection in view,
and having relied upon perfection in the path—
He goes forth with a perfected mind,
having shaken off all defilement and attained the perfection of Nibbāna.
“One is liberated from all suffering;
that is the perfection of all. Thus ends the fourth [verse].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.35 4.
The Chapter on Giving (Dānavagga) Sutta 35: Rebirth through Giving (Dānūpapatti-sutta)
“Bhikkhus, there are these eight rebirths through giving.
What eight?
In this case, monks, a certain person gives a gift to a recluse or a brahmin—food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, ointments, bedding, dwellings, and lamps.
What he gives, that he expects in return.
He sees wealthy kshatriyas, wealthy brahmins, or wealthy householders provided with and endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure, enjoying themselves.
It occurs to him:
"O, that after the breakup of the body, after death, I might arise in the company of wealthy kṣatriyas, or wealthy brahmins, or wealthy householders!
He fixes his mind on that, resolves upon that, and develops that mind.
His mind, being liberated in the inferior and not further developed, leads to rebirth there.
With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in the company of wealthy kṣatriyas, or wealthy brahmins, or wealthy householders.
And this, I say, is for one who is virtuous, not for one who is immoral.
“Monks, the mental aspiration of one who is virtuous succeeds because of its purity.
But here, monks, a certain person gives a gift—food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, ointments, bedding, dwellings, or lamps—to a recluse or a brahmin.
Yet, whatever he gives, he expects something in return.”
He has heard:
"The gods of the Four Great Kings are long-lived, beautiful, and abound in happiness.
It occurs to him:
‘Oh, that upon the breakup of the body, after death, I might arise in the company of the gods of the Four Great Kings!
He fixes his mind on this, resolves upon it, and develops that mind.
Since that mind is liberated in what is inferior and not developed further, it leads to rebirth there.
With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in the company of the gods of the Four Great Kings.
And that, I say, is for one who is virtuous, not for one who is immoral.
For the mental aspiration of one who is virtuous succeeds, monks, because of its purity.
"Furthermore, monks, here a certain person gives a gift to a recluse or a brahmin—food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, ointments, bedding, dwellings, and lamps.
He gives something while expecting something in return.
He has heard this:"
The gods of the Thirty-three … the Yāma gods … the Tusita gods …
"The Nimmānarati devas...
and the Paranimmitavasavatti devas are long-lived, beautiful, and abound in happiness.
It occurs to him thus:
‘Oh, that after the breakup of the body, after death, I might arise in the company of the Paranimmitavasavatti devas!
He fixes his mind on this, resolves upon it, and develops that state of mind.
Since that mind of his is liberated from the inferior and not developed further, it leads to rebirth there.
With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in companionship with the gods who wield power over the creations of others.
And this, I say, is for one who is virtuous, not for one who is immoral.
For the mental aspiration of one who is virtuous succeeds, monks, because of its purity.
"Furthermore, monks, here a certain person gives a gift to a recluse or a brahmin—food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, ointments, bedding, dwellings, and lamps.
What he gives, that he expects in return.
He has heard this:"
"The gods of Brahma’s retinue are long-lived, beautiful, and abound in happiness.
It occurs to him:
"Oh, that after the breakup of the body, after death, I might be reborn in the company of the gods of Brahma’s retinue!"
Thus he fixes that mind, resolves upon that mind, and develops that mind.
That mind of his, being liberated from the inferior and not developed further, leads to rebirth there.
With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn into the company of the deities of Brahma’s retinue.
And that, I say, belongs to one who is virtuous, not to one who is immoral;
to one who is free from lust, not to one who still has lust.
For, monks, the mental aspiration of one who is virtuous succeeds because of his freedom from lust.
“Monks, these are the eight rebirths resulting from giving.
The fifth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.36

4. Dānavagga: Puññakiriyavatthusutta (AN 8.36, PTS AN iv 241) “Monks, there are these three bases for the performance of merit. What three? Giving, virtuous conduct, and mental cultivation. These, monks, are the three bases for the performance of merit.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these three bases for meritorious action.
What are the three?
The basis for meritorious action consisting in giving, the basis for meritorious action consisting in virtue, and the basis for meritorious action consisting in mental development.”

In this case, monks, for a certain person, the basis of meritorious action consisting in giving has been performed to a small extent; the basis of meritorious action consisting in virtue has been performed to a small extent; and he does not achieve the basis of meritorious action consisting in development.
With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in the misfortune of human beings.

But here, monks, for a certain person, the basis for meritorious action consisting in giving has been performed to a moderate degree; the basis for meritorious action consisting in virtue has been performed to a moderate degree; yet he does not succeed in the basis for meritorious action consisting in development.
With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in the good fortune of human beings.

But here, monks, for a certain person, the basis of meritorious action consisting in giving has been practiced to an eminent degree; the basis of meritorious action consisting in virtue has been practiced to an eminent degree; yet he does not achieve the basis of meritorious action consisting in development.
With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in the company of the gods of the Four Great Kings.

In this regard, monks, the four great kings, having excelled in the basis of meritorious action consisting of giving and having excelled in the basis of meritorious action consisting of virtuous conduct, surpass the gods of the Four Great Kings in ten respects:
in divine lifespan, in divine beauty, in divine happiness, in divine fame, in divine sovereignty, and in divine forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tactile objects.

But here, monks, for a certain person, the basis for making merit consisting in giving has been practiced to an eminent degree, and the basis for making merit consisting in virtuous conduct has been practiced to an eminent degree, yet he does not achieve the basis for making merit consisting in mental development.
With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn into the company of the Tāvatiṃsa devas.

In this regard, monks, Sakka, lord of the devas, having made the basis for meritorious action consisting in giving superior and the basis for meritorious action consisting in virtue superior, surpasses the Tāvatiṃsa devas in ten respects:
by celestial life...
[and so on] ...by celestial tangibles.

But here, monks, for a certain person, the basis for meritorious action consisting in giving has been practiced to a high degree, and the basis for meritorious action consisting in virtuous conduct has been practiced to a high degree, yet he does not achieve the basis for meritorious action consisting in mental development.
With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in the company of the Yāma devas.

In this regard, monks, the young god Suyāma, having performed to a superior degree the basis for meritorious action consisting in giving and the basis for meritorious action consisting in virtue, surpasses the Yāma gods in ten respects:
in divine life-span … [and so on] … in divine tactile objects.

But here, monks, for a certain person, the basis for making merit consisting in giving has been practiced to an excessive degree, and the basis for making merit consisting in virtue has been practiced to an excessive degree, yet he does not achieve the basis for making merit consisting in development.
With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn into the company of the Tusita devas.

In this regard, monks, the young deva Santusita, having performed the basis of meritorious action consisting of giving to a superior degree, and having performed the basis of meritorious action consisting of virtuous conduct to a superior degree, surpasses the Tusita devas in ten respects:
in divine lifespan...
[and so on] ...in divine tactile sensations.

But here, monks, for a certain person, the basis for meritorious action consisting in giving has been practiced to a high degree, and the basis for meritorious action consisting in virtuous conduct has been practiced to a high degree, yet he does not achieve the basis for meritorious action consisting in mental development.
With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in the company of the gods who delight in their own creations.

In this regard, monks, the young deity Sunimmita, having performed to a greater degree the basis for meritorious action consisting in giving and the basis for meritorious action consisting in virtue, surpasses the Nimmānarati deities in ten respects:
by divine life-span ...
[and so on] ... by divine tactile objects.

"Furthermore, monks, in this case, for a certain person, the basis of meritorious action consisting in giving has been practiced to an eminent degree; the basis of meritorious action consisting in virtue has been practiced to an eminent degree; but the basis of meritorious action consisting in development has not been achieved.
With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in companionship with the Paranimmitavasavatti devas.
There, monks, that son of the gods who exercises power, having performed the basis of meritorious action consisting in giving to an exceeding degree..."
“Having made the basis for meritorious action consisting in virtue superior, one surpasses the gods who wield power over the creations of others in ten respects:
in divine life span, in divine beauty, in divine happiness, in divine fame, in divine sovereignty, and in divine forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tactile objects.
These, monks, are the three bases for meritorious action.”
The Sixth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.37.
Chapter 4: On Giving (Dānavagga).
Sappurisadānasutta: “Monks,
there are these eight gifts of a true person.”
What are the eight? One gives what is pure; one gives what is excellent; one gives at the right time; one gives what is permissible; one gives with discrimination; one gives frequently;
one gladdens the mind while giving; and having given, one is joyful. These, monks, are the eight gifts of a true person.
One who frequently gives gifts that are pure, excellent, timely, and permissible, consisting of food and drink—
Among those who practice the holy life with ease,
having renounced much material wealth, there is no remorse.
Thus are gifts given,
so the Vipassins praise;
thus having sacrificed, the wise one—
With a mind full of faith and liberated,
the wise person is reborn in a world of happiness free from affliction.
Seventh. Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.38. 4.
The Chapter on Giving (Dānavagga).
The Discourse on the True Person (Sappurisasutta): “Monks,
when a true person is born into a family, it is for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of many people.”
It leads to the welfare, benefit, and happiness of one’s mother and father; it leads to the welfare, benefit, and happiness of one’s wife and children;
it leads to the welfare, benefit, and happiness of one’s slaves, workers, and servants; it leads to the welfare, benefit, and happiness of one’s friends and companions;
it leads to the welfare, benefit, and happiness of one’s departed ancestors; and it leads to the welfare, benefit, and happiness of the king.
It is for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of the deities; it is for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of recluses and brahmins.
Just as, monks, a great rain-cloud, bringing all crops to fruition, is for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of many people;
even so, monks, a true person, when born into a family, is for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of many people.
It leads to the welfare, benefit, and happiness of one’s mother and father; it leads to the welfare, benefit, and happiness of one’s wife and children;
it leads to the welfare, benefit, and happiness of one’s slaves, laborers, and servants; it leads to the welfare, benefit, and happiness of one’s friends and companions;
it leads to the welfare, benefit, and happiness of one’s departed ancestors; it leads to the welfare, benefit, and happiness of the king.
"It brings benefit, welfare, and happiness to deities; it brings benefit, welfare, and happiness to recluses and brahmins.
Indeed, for the sake of many, the wise person dwells at home.
One who, unwearied by day and night, honors one's mother and father in accordance with the Dhamma—
Recalling their past deeds,
they have gone forth as homeless ones—
ascetics practicing the holy life.
One who is firmly established in faith,
having understood the Dhamma, is virtuous;
he is beneficial to the king and beneficial to the gods.
A benefactor to kinsmen and friends,
he is a benefactor to all who are well-established in the true Dhamma.
Having removed the stain of stinginess,
he frequents a world that is auspicious.
Thus ends the eighth [verse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.39 4. Dānavagga Abhisandasutta (The Outflow) “Bhikkhus, there are these eight outflows of merit, outflows of the wholesome, nutriments of happiness, celestial, ripening in happiness, conducive to heaven, leading to what is desirable, pleasing, and agreeable, that is, to Nibbāna.

What eight? (1) Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. (2) He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. (3) He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. (4) He possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones—untorn, unbroken, unspotted, unsplattered, liberating, praised by the wise, untarnished, leading to concentration. (5) He is free from ill will and has a mind of loving-kindness toward all living beings. (6) He is free from corrupt desire and dwells with a mind devoid of lust for the entire world. (7) He is free from anger and dwells with a mind devoid of resentment toward all living beings. (8) He is free from envy and does not covet the wealth and honors of others. These, bhikkhus, are the eight outflows of merit, outflows of the wholesome, nutriments of happiness, celestial, ripening in happiness, conducive to heaven, leading to what is desirable, pleasing, and agreeable, that is, to Nibbāna.”

“Monks, there are these eight outflows of merit, outflows of the wholesome, nutriments of happiness, leading to heaven, ripening in happiness, conducive to heaven; they lead to what is desirable, lovely, agreeable, beneficial, and pleasant. What are the eight? [The text continues with the eight specific meritorious deeds.]”
"Here, monks, a noble disciple has gone for refuge to the Buddha.

This, monks, is the first outflow of merit, an outflow of the wholesome, a nourishment of happiness—leading to heaven, ripening in happiness, conducive to heaven—which leads to what is desirable, pleasing, agreeable, beneficial, and happy.
Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple has gone for refuge to the Dhamma."
This, monks, is the second flood of merit... which leads to this.
Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple has gone for refuge to the Saṅgha.

This, monks, is the third flood of merit, a flood of the wholesome, a sustenance for happiness, leading to heaven, ripening in happiness, conducive to heaven; it leads to what is desirable, lovely, agreeable, beneficial, and pleasant.
“Monks, there are these five gifts, great gifts, foremost, long-standing, traditional, ancient,
unadulterated, never before adulterated, not being adulterated now, nor to be adulterated in the future, and not censured by wise recluses and brahmins.
What are the five?
In this case, monks, a noble disciple abandons the taking of life and abstains from taking life.
By abstaining from taking life, monks, a noble disciple gives fearlessness to immeasurable beings; he gives freedom from enmity;

he gives freedom from affliction. Having given fearlessness, freedom from enmity, and freedom from affliction to immeasurable beings, he partakes in immeasurable fearlessness, freedom from enmity, and freedom from affliction.

“Monks, this is the first gift, a great gift, primal, ancient, traditional, old, unadulterated, never before adulterated; it is not being adulterated, nor will it be adulterated; it is uncensured by wise recluses and brahmins.

This, monks, is the fourth outflow of merit, an outflow of the wholesome, a nourishment for happiness, leading to heaven, ripening in happiness, conducive to heaven; it leads to what is desired, liked, agreeable, beneficial, and pleasant.”
Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple, having abandoned taking what is not given, abstains from taking what is not given; ...
having abandoned sexual misconduct, abstains from sexual misconduct; ...
having abandoned false speech, abstains from false speech; ... [and so forth].

Having abandoned the use of fermented liquor, distilled spirits, and intoxicants that cause heedlessness, he abstains from fermented liquor, distilled spirits, and intoxicants that cause heedlessness.

By abstaining from fermented liquor, distilled spirits, and intoxicants that cause heedlessness, monks, the noble disciple bestows fearlessness upon immeasurable beings; he bestows freedom from enmity;

he bestows freedom from affliction. Having bestowed fearlessness, freedom from enmity, and freedom from affliction upon immeasurable beings, he partakes in immeasurable fearlessness, freedom from enmity, and freedom from affliction.

This, monks, is the fifth gift, a great gift, primal, ancient, traditional, old, unadulterated, never before adulterated; it is not being adulterated, nor will it be adulterated; it is uncensured by wise recluses and brahmins.

This, monks, is the eighth stream of merit, a stream of the wholesome, a nourishment for happiness, leading to heaven, ripening in happiness, conducive to heaven; it leads to what is desired, loved, liked, beneficial, and pleasant.

“Monks, these eight floods of merit, floods of the wholesome, are nourishers of happiness; they lead to heaven, have a happy result, and conduce to heaven; they lead to what is desirable, beloved, pleasing, beneficial, and happy.
Thus ends the ninth [sutta]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.40

“Bhikkhus, the destruction of life, when practiced, cultivated, and frequently indulged in, leads to rebirth in hell, leads to rebirth in the animal realm, and leads to rebirth in the sphere of hungry ghosts.
Even the lightest result of the destruction of life leads to a short lifespan for one who has become human.

Taking what is not given, bhikkhus, when practiced, cultivated, and frequently indulged in, leads to rebirth in hell, leads to rebirth in the animal realm, and leads to rebirth in the sphere of hungry ghosts.”
Whatever is the lightest ripening of taking what is not given leads, for one who has become a human, to the ruin of wealth.
Sexual misconduct, monks, when practiced, cultivated, and frequently pursued, leads to rebirth in hell, to rebirth in the animal realm, and to rebirth in the sphere of hungry ghosts.
Whatever is the lightest ripening of sexual misconduct leads, for one who has become a human, to enmity and hostility.
“Monks, false speech, when practiced, cultivated, and frequently indulged in, leads to rebirth in hell, to rebirth among animals, and to rebirth in the realm of hungry ghosts.
Even the lightest result of false speech is that it leads one, upon becoming a human, to being falsely accused.
Malicious speech, monks, when practiced, cultivated, and frequently indulged in, leads to rebirth in hell, to rebirth among animals, and to rebirth in the realm of hungry ghosts.”
The result of malicious speech that is least of all is conducive to being split from one's friends when one has become a human being.
Bhikkhus, harsh speech, when practiced, cultivated, and frequently indulged in, leads to rebirth in hell, to rebirth in the animal realm, and to rebirth in the sphere of hungry ghosts.
The result of harsh speech that is least of all is conducive to hearing unpleasant sounds when one has become a human being.
“Monks, idle chatter, when practiced, cultivated, and frequently indulged in, leads to rebirth in hell, to rebirth in the animal realm, and to rebirth in the sphere of hungry ghosts.
Even the lightest result of idle chatter is that, when one becomes a human, one’s speech will not be respected.

Drinking fermented and distilled liquors, monks, when practiced, cultivated, and frequently indulged in, leads to rebirth in hell, to rebirth in the animal realm, and to rebirth in the sphere of hungry ghosts.”
“The lightest possible result of drinking fermented or distilled liquors is that, for one who has become human, it leads to madness.
Tenth. The Fourth Chapter on Giving.
Its summary verse:
Two kinds of giving, the basis,
the field, and the rebirths resulting from giving;
Action, the two kinds of true persons,
the underlying tendency, and the result.
(Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.41)
5. Uposatha Chapter:
The Short Discourse on the Uposatha (Saṅkhittūposathasutta) (AN 8.41, PTS AN iv 248)
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Monks,” [he said].
“Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One spoke as follows:
“Monks, the Uposatha endowed with eight factors, when observed, is of great fruit, great benefit, great splendor, and great radiance.
And how, monks, is the Uposatha endowed with eight factors, when observed, of great fruit, great benefit, great splendor, and great radiance?
Here, monks, a noble disciple reflects thus:”

‘For as long as life lasts, the Arahants, having abandoned the taking of life, abstain from taking life; they lay aside the rod and the weapon, and being modest and compassionate, they dwell full of kindness and sympathy for all living beings.

Today, for this night and this day, I too, having abandoned the taking of life, abstain from taking life; I lay aside the rod and the weapon, and being modest and compassionate, I dwell full of kindness and sympathy for all living beings.
In this respect I emulate the Arahants, and my Uposatha will be observed.’
He is endowed with this first factor:

"For as long as life lasts, the Arahants, having abandoned taking what is not given, abstain from taking what is not given; they take only what is given, expect only what is given, and dwell with a heart pure and free from theft.

Today, for this night and this day, I too, having abandoned taking what is not given, abstain from taking what is not given; I take only what is given, expect only what is given, and dwell with a heart pure and free from theft."
‘By this factor I imitate the Arahants, and my Uposatha will have been observed.
Thus he possesses the second factor.
‘For as long as life lasts, the Arahants, having abandoned unchastity, live a life of celibacy, living apart, abstaining from sexual intercourse, the common way of the village.’
‘Today, for this night and this day, having abandoned unchastity, I am chaste, living apart, abstaining from sexual intercourse, the common practice of the village.
By this factor he emulates the Arahants, and his Uposatha will have been observed.
Thus he is endowed with this third factor.

‘For as long as life lasts, the Arahants, having abandoned false speech, abstain from false speech; they are speakers of truth, devoted to truth, trustworthy, reliable, and not deceivers of the world.
Today, for this night and this day, I too, having abandoned false speech, abstain from false speech; I am a speaker of truth, devoted to truth, trustworthy, reliable, and not a deceiver of the world.
In this respect I emulate the Arahants, and my Uposatha will be observed.’
He is endowed with this fourth factor:

"For as long as life lasts, the Arahants, having abandoned fermented liquor, distilled spirits, and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence, abstain from fermented liquor, distilled spirits, and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence.

Today, for this night and this day, I too, having abandoned fermented liquor, distilled spirits, and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence, abstain from fermented liquor, distilled spirits, and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence."
‘By this factor I imitate the Arahants, and my Uposatha will be observed.
He is thus endowed with this fifth factor:
‘For as long as life lasts, the Arahants eat only one meal a day, abstaining from eating at night and refraining from food outside the proper time.’
‘Today, for this night and this day, I shall eat only one meal, abstain from sexual activity, and refrain from eating at improper times.
In this respect I emulate the Arahants, and my Uposatha will have been observed.
Thus he is possessed of this sixth factor.
“For as long as life lasts, the Arahants, having abandoned the stage of dancing, singing, instrumental music,

watching performances, wearing garlands, using scents and unguents, and adorning themselves with cosmetics and ornaments, abstain from dancing, singing, instrumental music, watching performances, wearing garlands, using scents and unguents,

and adorning themselves with cosmetics and ornaments. Today, for this night and this day, I too [abstain] from dancing, singing, instrumental music, watching performances, wearing garlands, using scents and unguents, and adorning myself with cosmetics and ornaments.”

‘Having abandoned dancing, singing, instrumental music, and the viewing of spectacles, as well as the wearing of garlands, perfumes, and ointments, and the use of adornments and finery, I shall abstain from them.
By this factor, I shall emulate the Arahants, and my Uposatha shall be observed.
Thus he is endowed with this seventh factor.

‘For as long as life lasts, the Arahants, having abandoned high and luxurious beds and seats, abstain from high and luxurious beds and seats, and make use of a low resting place—either a small bed or a grass mat.

Today, for this night and this day, I too, having abandoned high and luxurious beds and seats, abstain from high and luxurious beds and seats, and make use of a low resting place—either a small bed or a grass mat.
In this way, I emulate the Arahants, and my Uposatha will be observed.’
He is endowed with this eighth factor.
Thus observed, monks, the uposatha endowed with these eight factors is of great fruit, of great benefit, of great splendor, and of great radiance. Thus ends the first [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.42 5. Uposatha Vagga Vitthatūposatha Sutta: The Detailed Discourse on the Uposatha “Monks, there are these eight factors for the observance of the Uposatha. What eight? (1) Here, monks, a noble disciple dwells with his mind well-restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha; he trains under the training rules of the Pātimokkha; he takes up the training rules of the Pātimokkha and trains accordingly.

This is the first factor for the observance of the Uposatha. (2) He dwells restrained by the restraint of the senses. In regard to the objects cognized by the eye, he does not grasp at their signs or secondary characteristics. Since, if he were to dwell with the faculty of the eye unguarded, evil and unwholesome states of covetousness and grief might arise, he practices for its guarding, for its restraint, and achieves its restraint. In regard to the objects cognized by the ear... the nose... the tongue... the body... the mind, he does not grasp at their signs or secondary characteristics. Since, if he were to dwell with the faculty of the mind unguarded, evil and unwholesome states of covetousness and grief might arise, he practices for its guarding, for its restraint, and achieves its restraint. This is the second factor for the observance of the Uposatha. (3) He is moderate in eating. Reflecting wisely, he takes his food neither for amusement nor for intoxication, nor for the sake of physical beauty and attractiveness, but only for the support and maintenance of this body, for its preservation, for ending discomfort, and for assisting the holy life, thinking: ‘Thus I shall terminate the old feeling and not give rise to a new feeling. This is the third factor for the observance of the Uposatha. (4) He is devoted to wakefulness. During the day, while walking back and forth and sitting, he purifies his mind of obstructive states. During the first watch of the night (from sunset until midnight), while walking back and forth and sitting, he purifies his mind of obstructive states. During the middle watch of the night (from midnight until dawn), he lies down on his right side in the lion’s posture, with one foot overlapping the other, mindful and clearly comprehending, after noting in his mind the time for rising. During the last watch of the night (from dawn until sunrise), while walking back and forth and sitting, he purifies his mind of obstructive states. This is the fourth factor for the observance of the Uposatha. (5) He possesses the virtue dear to the Noble Ones, unbroken, flawless, unblemished, unblotched, liberating, praised by the wise, ungrasped, leading to concentration. This is the fifth factor for the observance of the Uposatha. (6) He possesses a mind imbued with loving-kindness, extensive, sublime, immeasurable, without hostility, without ill will. This is the sixth factor for the observance of the Uposatha. (7) He possesses a mind imbued with compassion... (8) ...a mind imbued with sympathetic joy... (9) ...a mind imbued with equanimity, extensive, sublime, immeasurable, without hostility, without ill will. This is the ninth factor for the observance of the Uposatha. Monks, when a noble disciple dwells thus, possessing these eight factors for the observance of the Uposatha, he is said to be one who observes the Uposatha fully, completely, perfectly, and purely, like the moon on the fifteenth day.”
“Bhikkhus, the uposatha observed complete in eight factors is of great fruit, great benefit, great splendor, and great radiance. And how, bhikkhus,
is the uposatha observed complete in eight factors so that it is of great fruit, great benefit, great splendor, and great radiance?”
In this case, monks, a noble disciple reflects thus:

"As long as they live, the Arahants, having abandoned the taking of life, abstain from taking life; they lay aside the rod and the weapon, and being modest and compassionate, they dwell full of kindness and sympathy for all living beings.

Today, for this night and this day, I too, having abandoned the taking of life, abstain from taking life; I lay aside the rod and the weapon, and being modest and compassionate, I dwell full of kindness and sympathy for all living beings."
‘By this factor I imitate the Arahants, and my Uposatha will be observed.

Thus he is endowed with this first factor… [as before] … ‘For as long as life lasts, the Arahants, having abandoned high and luxurious beds and seats, abstain from high and luxurious beds and seats; they use low resting places, whether a small bed or a grass mat spread upon the ground.’”

‘Today, for this night and this day, having abandoned high and luxurious beds and seats, I shall abstain from high and luxurious beds and seats and make my bed low—either on a couch or on a spread of grass.
By this factor he emulates the Arahants, and his Uposatha will have been observed.
Thus he is endowed with this eighth factor.
“Monks, when the Uposatha is observed in this way, endowed with these eight factors, it is of great fruit, of great benefit, of great splendor, and of great radiance.
To what extent is it of great fruit, of great benefit, of great splendor, and of great radiance?
Suppose, monks, one were to exercise sovereign lordship and kingship over these sixteen great countries abounding in many kinds of precious gems, namely:”
The wealth of the Aṅgas, Magadhas, Kāsīs, Kosalas, Vajjis, Mallas, Cetis, Vaṅgas, Kurus, Pañcālas, Macchas,
Sūrasenas, Assakas, Avantīs, Gandhāras, and Kambojas is not worth a sixteenth part of the Uposatha endowed with its eight factors.
For what reason?
Because, monks, human sovereignty is wretched when compared with celestial bliss.
Monks, those fifty years of humans constitute a single day and night for the gods of the Four Great Kings.
Thirty nights of that [human] night make a month.
Twelve months of that month make a year.
Five hundred divine years of that year is the measure of the lifespan of the gods of the Four Great Kings.
"It is possible, monks, that here some woman or man, having observed the Uposatha complete in its eight factors,
at the breaking up of the body, after death, might be reborn in the company of the Cātumahārājika devas.
It was with reference to this, monks, that it was said:"
“Human sovereignty is miserable when compared with divine happiness.
Monks, those one hundred human years are a single day and night for the gods of the Thirty-three.
Thirty such nights make a month.”
Twelve months of that [lunar] reckoning make one year.
A thousand celestial years by that reckoning is the lifespan of the gods of the Thirty-three.
It is possible, monks, that here some woman or man, endowed with the eight factors—

“So it is, Vāseṭṭha; so it is, Vāseṭṭha.

5. The Chapter on the Uposatha.
The Anuruddha Sutta.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Park.
Now at that time, the Venerable Anuruddha had gone for his midday rest and was dwelling in seclusion.
Then a number of delightful-bodied deities approached the Venerable Anuruddha;
having approached and paid homage to the Venerable Anuruddha, they stood to one side. Standing there, those deities...
They said this to the Venerable Anuruddha:
“Venerable Anuruddha, we are deities named Manāpakāyikā who exercise sovereignty and wield power over three places.
Venerable Anuruddha, whatever kind of complexion we desire, we obtain that very complexion instantly.”
"Whatever kind of voice we desire, we obtain that very kind of voice immediately;
whatever kind of happiness we desire, we obtain that very kind of happiness immediately.
Venerable Anuruddha, we are deities named Manāpakāyikā, and we exercise sovereignty and wield power over these three things."
Then it occurred to the Venerable Anuruddha:
"Oh, if only all these deities were blue—blue in color, wearing blue garments, and adorned with blue ornaments!
Then those deities, knowing the Venerable Anuruddha's thought, all became blue—blue in color, wearing blue garments, and adorned with blue ornaments.
Then it occurred to the Venerable Anuruddha:
"O, if only all these deities were yellow...
[and so on] ...if only all were red..."
"May they all be entirely white—white in color, dressed in white garments, and adorned with white ornaments.
Then those deities, knowing the Venerable Anuruddha’s thought, became entirely white—white in color, dressed in white garments, and adorned with white ornaments.
Then those deities sang, one danced, and another played cymbals.
Just as the sound of a five-piece musical ensemble—well-trained, well-tuned, and skillfully performed by experts—is lovely, enchanting, desirable, pleasing, and intoxicating;
even so was the sound of the ornaments of those deities lovely, enchanting, desirable, pleasing, and intoxicating.
Then the Venerable Anuruddha withdrew his senses.
Then those deities, thinking, "Venerable Anuruddha does not consent," vanished right there.
Then, in the evening, the Venerable Anuruddha emerged from seclusion and approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Venerable...
Anuruddha said this to the Blessed One:

Venerable Anuruddha, whatever kind of complexion we desire, we obtain that very complexion instantly;
whatever kind of voice we desire, we obtain that very voice instantly.”
“Whatever kind of happiness we desire, that kind of happiness we obtain immediately.
Venerable Anuruddha, we are deities named Manāpakāyikā; in these three places we exercise sovereignty and wield power.
Then, venerable sir, this occurred to me:

Then, venerable sir, those deities, knowing my mind, all became blue—blue in color, wearing blue clothes, and adorned with blue ornaments.
Then, venerable sir, this occurred to me:

white in color, dressed in white garments, and adorned with white ornaments.’
