In this very way, the sound of those deities’ ornaments was charming, delightful, lovely, endearing, and intoxicating.
Then, venerable sir, I withdrew my senses.
Thereupon, venerable sir, those deities, thinking, “The worthy Anuruddha does not take pleasure in us,” vanished right there.
“Bhante, endowed with how many qualities does a woman, with the breakup of the body, after death, arise in the company of the Manāpakāyika devas?
“Anuruddha, endowed with eight qualities, a woman, with the breakup of the body, after death, arises in the company of the Manāpakāyika devas.
Which eight? [The Buddha then enumerates them.]”
In this case, Anuruddha, there is a woman whom her husband’s parents give to him out of desire for his welfare, seeking his benefit, being compassionate and moved by compassion;
she rises before him, retires after him, is attentive to what needs to be done, acts agreeably, and speaks kindly.
Those who are her husband’s elders—
She honors, respects, reveres, and worships those who are her mother, or her father, or ascetics and brahmins; and when they arrive, she welcomes them with a seat and water.

Regarding the household duties of her husband—whether involving wool or cotton—she is skillful and diligent therein, endowed with the discernment necessary for such tasks, capable of performing them and capable of organizing them.
As for those who are the master’s inner household members—whether they be slaves, messengers, or laborers—he recognizes what has been done by them as done, and what has not been done as not done;
he knows the strength and weakness of those who are ill, and he shares with them their portion of hard food and soft food.
Whatever wealth, grain, or gold his master brings in, he ensures it is accomplished through protection and security; and in that regard, he is no gambler, no thief, no drunkard, and no squanderer.
Furthermore, she is a female lay follower who has gone for refuge to the Buddha, gone for refuge to the Dhamma, and gone for refuge to the Saṅgha. She is virtuous,

abstaining from the destruction of life, abstaining from taking what is not given, abstaining from sexual misconduct, abstaining from false speech, and abstaining from fermented and distilled liquors that cause heedlessness.
Furthermore, she is generous.
She dwells at home with a mind free from the stain of stinginess, open-handed, pure of hand, delighting in relinquishment, devoted to prayer, and rejoicing in giving and sharing.
It is by possessing these eight qualities, Anuruddha, that a woman, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in the company of the Manāpakāyika devas.
He who always supports him,
constantly diligent and zealous—
that supporter grants all desires.
She does not despise her husband;
nor does the wife provoke her husband with angry words.
The wise person honors all their husbands and elders;
they are industrious and free from laziness.
She keeps her attendants restrained;
she acts agreeably to her husband and guards his wealth.
The woman who conducts herself in this way,
following the will and desires of her husband—
those gods are indeed called "the Delightful."
“Where she will be reborn.
The sixth [sutta]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.47
5. Uposatha Chapter:
The Second Discourse to Visākhā (AN 8.47, PTS AN iv 267)
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in the Eastern Park, in the Mansion of Migāra’s Mother.
Then Visākhā, Migāra’s Mother, approached the Blessed One;
having approached, she sat down to one side. As Visākhā, Migāra’s Mother, was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to her:
“Visākhā, endowed with eight qualities, a woman, upon the breakup of the body after death, is reborn in the company of the Manāpakāyika devas.
What are these eight?
Here, Visākhā, a woman gives her husband away to someone whose parents desire his welfare, seek his benefit, and are compassionate toward him.”
Out of compassion, she rises before him and retires after him; she is attentive to his needs, acts agreeably, and speaks kindly...
[as above] ...Furthermore, she is generous.

With a mind free from the stain of stinginess, she dwells at home as one who has renounced, with hands clean, delighting in relinquishment, devoted to soliciting others for gifts, and rejoicing in giving and sharing.
"Endowed with these eight qualities, Visākhā, a woman, upon the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in the company of the Manāpakāyika devas.
He who supports her at all times,
ever diligent and zealous..."
She does not despise her husband, who grants all her desires;
nor does Sotthi ever disregard her husband.
She does not provoke anger by speaking ill of others;
she honors all her husband’s elders, for she is wise.
Diligent and untiring,
she manages the household staff;
she conducts herself in a way that is pleasing to her husband.
She protects what has been gathered.
A woman who conducts herself in this way follows the will and influence of her husband.
"Those gods are called 'the Pleasant,' where she will be reborn.
Thus ends the seventh [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.48 5. Uposatha Vagga Nakulamātāsutta Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then Nakulamātā the lay follower approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how many qualities does a woman possess to be dear and pleasing to her husband, to be respected and esteemed by him, and to dwell in harmony with him? “A woman, Nakulamātā, who possesses eight qualities is dear and pleasing to her husband, is respected and esteemed by him, and dwells in harmony with him. What eight? Here, Nakulamātā, a woman is virtuous; she is well-conducted, restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, perfect in conduct and resort, and seeing fear in the slightest fault, she trains herself by undertaking the training rules. She is skilled and diligent in attending to her husband’s domestic duties, whether they concern wool or linen, such as spinning yarn or weaving cloth. She protects the wealth that has been acquired by her husband, whether it be gold or silver, grain or wealth, slaves or laborers, or goats and sheep.

She is hospitable toward kinsmen on both sides—toward her husband’s relatives and her own relatives—and she shows them due honor. She is hospitable toward ascetics and brahmins, and she shows them due honor. She manages the household economy prudently, ensuring that expenditures do not exceed income, nor that income exceeds expenditures. She is faithful, possessing unwavering confidence in the Tathāgata thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Fortunate One. She is virtuous, possessing unwavering confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. She is virtuous, possessing unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals. This Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. These, Nakulamātā, are the eight qualities a woman possesses to be dear and pleasing to her husband, to be respected and esteemed by him, and to dwell in harmony with him. When this was said, Nakulamātā the lay follower said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir! Just as one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, even so has the Dhamma been made clear by the Blessed One in many ways. I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May I receive the going forth under the Blessed One, may I receive the full admission! “Nakulamātā, when a woman has been married for a year, she might wish for the going forth and the full admission. But you, having been married for eight years, are now seeking the going forth and the full admission. Wait, Nakulamātā, until your husband gives his permission. Then Nakulamātā the lay follower, having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words, rose from her seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on her right, departed. She then approached her husband, paid homage to him, stood to one side, and said: “Master, please give me permission. I wish to go forth from the home life into homelessness under the Blessed One. When this was said, Nakula the householder said to Nakulamātā the lay follower: “If you, Nakulamātā, were to die while still a householder, would you be able to take your wealth and go? “No, master. I would not be able to take my wealth and go. “If you, Nakulamātā, were to die while still a householder, would you be able to take your children and go? “No, master. I would not be able to take my children and go. “But, Nakulamātā, you have been married for eight years, yet you speak like a child. Wait, Nakulamātā, until I give you my permission. Then Nakulamātā the lay follower approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, my husband has given me his permission. May I receive the going forth under the Blessed One, may I receive the full admission! Then the Blessed One gave Nakulamātā the lay follower the going forth and the full admission. Not long after she had received the full admission, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, Nakulamātā the bhikkhunī, by realizing it for herself with direct knowledge, in this very life entered and dwelt in that unsurpassed goal of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness, and she directly knew: “Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being. And Nakulamātā the bhikkhunī became one of the arahants. At that time, Nakula the householder approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, where is Nakulamātā the lay follower? “She has attained final Nibbāna, householder,” the Blessed One replied. “Venerable sir, when Nakulamātā the lay follower passed away, did she depart having taken her wealth with her? “No, householder. “Did she depart having taken her children with her? “No, householder. “But, venerable sir, she was married for eight years. Why did she depart like a child? “Householder, Nakulamātā the lay follower possessed these eight qualities. Therefore, when she passed away, she departed like a child. When this was said, Nakula the householder said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir! Just as one might set upright what had been overturned... even so has the Dhamma been made clear by the Blessed One in many ways. I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. From this day forth, may the Blessed One remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, Nakula the householder delighted in the Blessed One’s words. This is the meaning of what was said by the Blessed One, and so it was understood by the bhikkhus: “The bhikkhunī Nakulamātā has attained final Nibbāna. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir! those bhikkhus replied. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, a woman who possesses eight qualities is reborn in heaven. What eight? Here, bhikkhus, a woman is virtuous; she is well-conducted, restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, perfect in conduct and resort, and seeing fear in the slightest fault, she trains herself by undertaking the training rules.

She is skilled and diligent in attending to her husband’s domestic duties, whether they concern wool or linen, such as spinning yarn or weaving cloth. She protects the wealth that has been acquired by her husband, whether it be gold or silver, grain or wealth, slaves or laborers, or goats and sheep. She is hospitable toward kinsmen on both sides—toward her husband’s relatives and her own relatives—and she shows them due honor. She is hospitable toward ascetics and brahmins, and she shows them due honor. She manages the household economy prudently, ensuring that expenditures do not exceed income, nor that income exceeds expenditures. She is faithful, possessing unwavering confidence in the Tathāgata thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Fortunate One. She is virtuous, possessing unwavering confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma
(AN 8.48, PTS AN iv 268) On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Bhaggas at Suṃsumāragira, in the Bhesakaḷā Grove, the Deer Park.
Then Nakulamātā, the housewife, approached the Blessed One; having approached... [as before]... As Nakulamātā, the housewife, was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to her:
“Nakulamātā, endowed with eight qualities, a woman, upon the breakup of the body after death, is reborn in the company of the Manāpakāyika devas.
What are these eight?
Here, Nakulamātā, a woman is given by her parents to a husband who desires their welfare, seeks their benefit, and is compassionate.”
Out of compassion for him, she rises before him, retires after him, is obedient to his commands, acts agreeably, and speaks kindly.
Toward those whom her husband respects—
whether they be his mother or father, or ascetics and brahmins— she behaves likewise.
She honors, respects, esteems, and reveres them; and when they arrive, she welcomes them with a seat and water.

Regarding the internal household tasks of her husband—whether wool or cotton—she is skillful and diligent therein, endowed with the appropriate discernment to be capable of performing and organizing them.
As for the internal dependents of her husband—whether slaves, messengers, or laborers—

She knows what has been done for them as having been done, and what has not been done as not having been done; she knows the strength and weakness of those who are ill, and she distributes hard food and soft food to them with due consideration.

Whatever wealth her husband brings—whether money, grain, silver, or gold—she manages it with protection and security; and in this regard, she is not a spendthrift, nor a thief, nor a drunkard, nor a wastrel.
Furthermore, she is a lay follower who has gone for refuge to the Buddha, gone for refuge to the Dhamma, and gone for refuge to the Saṅgha.
Moreover, she is virtuous—abstaining from the destruction of life...
abstaining from the use of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence...
Moreover, she is generous; she dwells at home with a mind free from the stain of stinginess, open-handed, pure-palmed, delighting in relinquishment, devoted to charity, and fond of sharing.
"Indeed, Nakulamātā, a woman endowed with these eight qualities, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in the company of the Manāpakāyika devas.
He who supports her at all times,
ever diligent and zealous..."
She does not despise her husband, who grants all her desires;
nor does Sotthi ever disregard her husband.
She does not provoke anger with harsh speech;
the wise woman honors all her husband’s elders.
Diligent and untiring,
she keeps her attendants well-disciplined;
she conducts herself in a way that is pleasing to her husband.
She guards what has been gathered.
A woman who conducts herself thus,
following her husband’s will and influence;
"Those gods are called 'the Delightful,' where she will be reborn.
Thus ends the eighth [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.49 5. Uposatha Vagga First Discourse on This World “Bhikkhus, there are these eight worldly conditions that sweep over the world and the people of the world, and they have not overcome them. What eight? Gain and loss, fame and disrepute, praise and blame, pleasure and pain. These are the eight worldly conditions that sweep over the world and the people of the world, and they have not overcome them. When gain comes, bhikkhus, a noble disciple does not rejoice; when loss comes, he does not grieve. When fame comes, he does not rejoice; when disrepute comes, he does not grieve. When praise comes, he does not rejoice; when blame comes, he does not grieve. When pleasure comes, he does not rejoice; when pain comes, he does not grieve. Why is that? Because he understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We will understand as it really is: “This is suffering”; we will understand as it really is: “This is the origin of suffering”; we will understand as it really is: “This is the cessation of suffering”; we will understand as it really is: “This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having said this, the Sublime One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, soon after the Blessed One had left, the venerable Ānanda addressed the bhikkhus: “Friends, the Blessed One has risen from his seat and entered his dwelling after speaking only in brief, without explaining the detailed meaning. It is good for us to hear the detailed meaning of this. Let us go to the Blessed One and ask him about the meaning of this. As the Blessed One explains it to us, so we shall remember it. “Yes, friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the venerable Ānanda.

Then the venerable Ānanda and those bhikkhus went to the Blessed One. After paying homage to him, they sat down at one side and told the Blessed One all that had occurred. “Ānanda, it was with reference to this very meaning that I spoke in brief when I said: ‘Bhikkhus, there are these eight worldly conditions... And what, Ānanda, is the noble truth of suffering? Birth is suffering; aging is suffering; illness is suffering; death is suffering; association with the disliked is suffering; separation from the liked is suffering; not getting what one wants is suffering; in short, the five aggregates subject to clinging are suffering. This is called the noble truth of suffering. And what, Ānanda, is the noble truth of the origin of suffering? It is craving, which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, seeking delight here and there; that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. This is called the noble truth of the origin of suffering. And what, Ānanda, is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering? It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that same craving, the giving up and relinquishing of it, freedom from it, and non-reliance on it. This is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering. And what, Ānanda, is the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering? It is simply this Noble Eightfold Path; that is, right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This is called the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering. “This is how the detailed meaning of the Blessed One’s brief statement should be understood. Having said this, the venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, he departed. Then, soon after the venerable Ānanda had left, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, suppose a man were to throw a yoke with a single hole into the great ocean, and there were a blind turtle that would come to the surface once every hundred years. What do you think, bhikkhus, would that blind turtle, coming to the surface once every hundred years, thrust its neck through that yoke with a single hole? “It would be a rare occurrence, Bhante. “So too, bhikkhus, it is a rare occurrence for a human rebirth to be obtained. And it is a rare occurrence for the True Dhamma to appear in the world. And it is a rare occurrence for a Tathāgata, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One to arise in the world. And it is a rare occurrence for a well-spoken teaching and discipline to be taught in the world. And it is a rare occurrence for a person to be born into a family of faith. And it is a rare occurrence for a person to be born into a family of wealth. And it is a rare occurrence for a person to be born into a family of nobility. And it is a rare occurrence for a person to be born into a family of brahmins. And it is a rare occurrence for a person to be born into a family of householders. And it is a rare occurrence for a person to be born into a family of recluses. And it is a rare occurrence for a person to be born into a family of devas. And it is a rare occurrence for a person to be born into a family of humans. Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We will be grateful and thankful for the attainment of a human birth, and we will make it fruitful and meaningful. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having said this, the Sublime One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, soon after the Blessed One had left, the venerable Ānanda addressed the bhikkhus: “Friends, the Blessed One has risen from his seat and entered his dwelling after speaking only in brief, without explaining the detailed meaning. It is good for us to hear the detailed meaning of this. Let us go to the Blessed One and ask him about the meaning of this. As the Blessed One explains it to us, so we shall remember it. “Yes, friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the venerable Ānanda. Then the venerable Ānanda and those bhikkhus went to the Blessed One. After paying homage to him, they sat down at one side and told the Blessed One all that had occurred. “Ānanda, it was with reference to this very meaning that I spoke in brief when I said: ‘Bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus: “We will be grateful and thankful for the attainment of a human birth, and we will make it fruitful and meaningful. “And what, Ānanda, is gratitude and thankfulness? Here, Ānanda, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. This, Ānanda, is gratitude and thankfulness. And what, Ānanda, is making [the human birth] fruitful and meaningful? Here, Ānanda, a noble disciple dwells with a mind devoid of lust for the form element; he dwells with a mind devoid of lust for the feeling element; he dwells with a mind devoid of lust for the perception element; he dwells with a mind devoid of lust for the volitional formations element; he dwells with a mind devoid of lust for the consciousness element. This, Ānanda, is making [the human birth] fruitful and meaningful. “This is how the detailed meaning of the Blessed One’s brief statement should be understood. Having said this, the venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, he departed. Then, soon after the venerable Ānanda had left, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, suppose a man were to throw a yoke with a single hole into the great ocean, and there were a blind turtle that would come to the surface once every hundred years. What do you think, bhikkhus, would that blind turtle, coming to the surface once every hundred years, thrust its

(AN 8.49, PTS AN iv 269) On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in the Eastern Park, in the Mansion of Migāra’s Mother. Then Visākhā, Migāra’s Mother, approached the Blessed One … [as before] … On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in the Eastern Park, in the Mansion of Migāra’s Mother.
Then Visākhā, Migāra’s Mother, approached the Blessed One … [as before] …
As Visākhā, Migāra’s mother, was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to her:
“Visākhā, when a woman possesses four qualities, she is practicing for victory in this world; this world is undertaken by her.
Which four?
"Here, Visākhā, a woman is one whose work is well-organized, who has her attendants under control, who conducts herself agreeably to her husband, and who protects his earnings.
And how, Visākhā, is a woman one whose work is well-organized?

Here, Visākhā, a woman is skilled and diligent regarding those domestic tasks of her husband—whether wool or cotton—and she possesses the discernment necessary for them; she is capable of doing the work and capable of organizing it."
In this way, Visākhā, a woman is well-organized in her work.
And how, Visākhā, is a woman one who has a well-gathered retinue?
Here, Visākhā, a woman [treats] those who are her husband’s inner household members—whether they be slaves, messengers, or laborers—[with kindness].

She knows what has been done by them as having been done, and she knows what has not been done as not having been done; she knows the strength and weakness of those who are ill, and she distributes hard food and soft food to them with due consideration.
It is in this way, Visākhā, that a woman has her retinue well-supported.
And how, Visākhā, does a woman behave in a way that is pleasing to her husband?
Here, Visākhā, a woman does not transgress even for the sake of her own life against that which is considered disagreeable to her husband.
In this way, Visākhā, a woman conducts herself agreeably toward her husband.
And how, Visākhā, does a woman protect the wealth she has acquired?

"Here, Visākhā, a woman manages whatever wealth, grain, silver, or gold her husband brings home with care and protection; and in doing so, she is not a thief, nor a squanderer, nor a drunkard, nor a ruinous wastrel.
It is in this way, Visākhā, that a woman protects what has been gathered.
Endowed with these four qualities, Visākhā, a woman is practicing for victory in this world; this world is set in motion for her."
“Visākhā, when a woman possesses four qualities, she is practicing for victory in the world beyond; the world beyond has been undertaken by her.
What are the four?
Here, Visākhā, a woman is accomplished in faith, accomplished in virtue, accomplished in generosity, and accomplished in wisdom.”
And how, Visākhā, is a woman endowed with faith?
Here, Visākhā, a woman is faithful; she has faith in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata:

"Thus indeed is that Blessed One: an arahant, perfectly enlightened, perfect in knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One."
In this way, Visākhā, a woman is endowed with faith.
And how, Visākhā, is a woman endowed with virtue?
Here, Visākhā, a woman abstains from the destruction of life … [and so on] … she abstains from the use of fermented and distilled liquors that cause heedlessness.
In this way, Visākhā, a woman is endowed with virtue.
And how, Visākhā, is a woman endowed with generosity?
Here, Visākhā, a woman dwells at home with a mind free from the stain of stinginess; she is open-handed, pure-handed, delighting in relinquishment, devoted to charity, and fond of distributing gifts.
In this way, Visākhā, a woman is endowed with generosity.
And how, Visākhā, is a woman endowed with wisdom?
Here, Visākhā, a woman is wise... [and so on].
In this way, Visākhā, a woman is endowed with wisdom.
Possessing these four qualities, Visākhā, a woman is practicing for victory in the world beyond; the world beyond has been set in motion by her.
[She is] one whose work is well-organized.
She keeps her attendants restrained;
she acts agreeably to her husband and guards his wealth.
Endowed with faith and virtue,
generous and free from stinginess,
one constantly purifies the path.
And security for the life hereafter.
These eight qualities belong to that woman in whom they exist.
Her they call virtuous,
established in Dhamma, and truthful in speech;
she is endowed with sixteen qualities.
“Endowed with the eight factors,
such a virtuous female lay follower is reborn in the delightful world of the devas.”
The Ninth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.50 5.
Uposatha Vagga (Chapter on the Observance Day)
The Second Discourse on Victory in This World (Dutiyaidhalokikasutta):
“Bhikkhus, when a woman possesses four qualities, she is practicing for victory in this world; this world is undertaken by her.”
What are the four?
Here, monks, a woman is well-organized in her work, has her retinue well-gathered, conducts herself agreeably toward her husband, and protects his earnings.
And how, monks, is a woman well-organized in her work?
“Here, monks, a woman attends to those domestic duties for her husband...
In this way, monks, a woman is well-organized in her work.
And how, monks, is a woman one who has her dependents well-supported?”
“Here, bhikkhus, a woman [ensures that] those who are her husband’s inner circle of dependents...
In this way, bhikkhus, a woman has her dependents well-supported.
And how, bhikkhus, does a woman conduct herself in a manner pleasing to her husband?”
In this case, monks, a woman does not transgress even for the sake of her life against anything considered displeasing to her husband.
It is in this way, monks, that a woman conducts herself agreeably to her husband.
And how, monks, does a woman protect the household wealth?
“Here, bhikkhus, a woman preserves whatever her husband brings home… In this way, bhikkhus, a woman guards what has been acquired.
Possessing these four qualities, bhikkhus, a woman is practicing for victory in this world; this world is undertaken by her.”
“Bhikkhus, possessing four qualities, a woman is practicing for victory in the world beyond; the world beyond has been undertaken by her.
What are the four?
Here, bhikkhus, a woman is endowed with faith, endowed with virtue, endowed with generosity, and endowed with wisdom.”
And how, monks, is a woman endowed with faith? Here, monks, a woman is faithful...
[as before] ...In this way, monks, a woman is endowed with faith.
And how, monks, is a woman endowed with virtue? Here, monks,
a woman abstains from the destruction of life … [as above] … she abstains from the occasion for negligence consisting in fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants.
In this way, monks, a woman is accomplished in virtue.
And how, monks, is a woman accomplished in generosity?
Here, monks, a woman dwells at home with a mind free from the stain of stinginess... [as before] ...In this way, monks, a woman is accomplished in generosity.
In this way, monks, a woman is accomplished in generosity.
And how, monks, is a woman accomplished in wisdom?
Here, monks, a woman is wise … [as above] …
In this way, monks, a woman is endowed with wisdom.
Possessing these four qualities, monks, a woman is practicing for victory in the world beyond; the world beyond has been undertaken by her.
[She is] one whose work is well-organized.
She keeps her attendants restrained;
she acts agreeably to her husband and protects his earnings.
Endowed with faith and virtue,
generous and free from stinginess,
one constantly purifies the path.
And security for the future life.
These eight qualities belong to that woman in whom they are found.
Him too they call virtuous,
established in Dhamma, and a speaker of truth—
one endowed with sixteen qualities.
Endowed with the eight factors,
such a virtuous female lay follower is reborn in the delightful world of the devas.
The tenth.
The fifth chapter on the Uposatha.
Its summary verse:
In brief and in detail, O Visākhā,
Vāseṭṭha was the fifth for awakening;
then again, O Visākhā, it was Anuruddha.
"Two kinds of *nakula* pertaining to this world.
The first fifty-section concludes.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.51.

6. Gotamīvagga Gotamīsutta (AN 8.51, PTS AN iv 274) Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then the female lay follower Gotamī approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to him: “Venerable sir, how many things, when developed and cultivated, lead to the realization of the fruit of stream-entry? “There are these four things, Gotamī, which, when developed and cultivated, lead to the realization of the fruit of stream-entry. What four? (1) Here, Gotamī, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One. (2) He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. (3) He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. (4) He possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones—unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, freeing, praised by the wise, ungrasped, leading to concentration. These four things, Gotamī, when developed and cultivated, lead to the realization of the fruit of stream-entry. When this was said, the female lay follower Gotamī said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir!... From today let the Blessed One remember me as a female lay follower who has gone for refuge for life. When this was said, the Blessed One told her: “But, Gotamī, what is the name of your clan? “My clan, venerable sir, is the Gotamas. “That is why you are called ‘Gotamī,’ because you are of the Gotama clan. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, the female lay follower Gotamī delighted in the Blessed One’s words.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu in the Nigrodha Park.

Then Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, she stood to one side. Standing to one side, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī said this to the Blessed One:
“It would be good, Bhante, if women might obtain the going-forth from the home life into homelessness in the Dhamma and Discipline proclaimed by the Tathāgata.”
“Enough, Gotamī.
Let it not please you that women go forth from the home life into homelessness in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
A second time, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī said this to the Blessed One:
“It would be good, venerable sir, if women were permitted to go forth from the home life into homelessness in the Dhamma and discipline proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
“Enough, Gotamī.
Let it not please you that women should go forth from the home life into homelessness in the Dhamma and discipline proclaimed by the Tathāgata.”
A third time, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī said this to the Blessed One:
“It would be well, Bhante, if women might receive the going-forth from the home into homelessness in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
“Enough, Gotamī.”
“May it not please you that women go forth from the home life into homelessness in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.

Then Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, thinking, “The Blessed One does not permit women to go forth from the home life into homelessness in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata,” became sorrowful and dejected; with a tearful face and weeping, she [approached] the Blessed One.
Having paid homage and circumambulated him, he departed.
Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Kapilavatthu for as long as he pleased, set out on a wandering tour toward Vesālī.
Wandering by stages, he eventually arrived at Vesālī.
There the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Gabled Hall.
Then Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, having had her hair cut off and having donned saffron robes, set out for Vesālī together with many Sākiyan women.
Traveling by stages, she arrived at Vesālī, at the Great Wood, at the Gabled Hall.
Then Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, with swollen feet and limbs covered in dust, distressed, dejected, tearful, and weeping, stood outside the gateway.
The Venerable Ānanda saw Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī standing outside the gateway with swollen feet and limbs covered in dust, distressed, dejected, tearful, and weeping.
Having seen her, he said this to Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī:
“Why, Gotamī, are you standing outside the gateway with swollen feet, your limbs covered in dust, suffering and dejected, with tears on your face and weeping?
“Because, venerable Ānanda, the Blessed One does not permit the going forth from the home life into homelessness for women within the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.

“In that case, Gotamī, stay right here for a moment while I request the Blessed One [to grant] the going forth from the home life into homelessness for women within the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.”
Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, this Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī is standing outside the gateway with swollen feet and limbs covered in dust, suffering, dejected, tearful, and weeping, thinking:
‘The Blessed One does not permit the going forth from the home life into homelessness for women within the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.’”
“It would be good, Bhante, if women were allowed to go forth from the household life into homelessness in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
“Enough, Ānanda.
Let it not please you that women go forth from the household life into homelessness in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.”
A second time...
and a third time, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
"It would be well, Bhante, if women were to obtain the going-forth from the home life into homelessness in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata."
“Enough, Ānanda.
Let it not please you that women go forth from the home life into homelessness in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
Then, this thought occurred to the Venerable Ānanda:
“The Blessed One does not permit the going forth from the household life into homelessness for women within the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.

Suppose I were to request the Blessed One for the going forth from the household life into homelessness for women within the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata by means of another approach.
Then the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
“Is it possible, Bhante, for women, having gone forth from the household life into homelessness in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata,

to realize the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning, or the fruit of arahantship? “It is possible, Ānanda, for women, having gone forth from the household life into homelessness in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, to realize the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arahantship.”
“Venerable sir, if women are capable of going forth from the household life into homelessness in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata and realizing the fruit of stream-entry...

[and so on] ...even the fruit of arhatship, then, venerable sir, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī has been of great service to the Blessed One; she was his maternal aunt, his nurse, his foster-mother, and the giver of milk.
She suckled the Blessed One when his own mother had passed away.”
“It would be good, Bhante, if women were to receive the going-forth from the home life into homelessness in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
“If, Ānanda, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī accepts the eight weighty rules (garudhamma), let that be her full ordination: 1.

A bhikkhunī who has been ordained for a hundred years must perform acts of respect toward a bhikkhu ordained on that very day—namely, saluting him, rising up for him, joining one’s palms in reverential salutation, and performing duties of courtesy. ... [and so forth with the remaining seven rules] ...”
This rule also, having been honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped, is not to be transgressed for as long as life lasts:
A bhikkhunī must not enter the rains residence in a dwelling where no bhikkhus are present.
This rule also, having been honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped, is not to be transgressed for as long as life lasts.
Every half-month, a bhikkhunī must expect two things from the Saṅgha of bhikkhus:
the inquiry regarding the Uposatha day and the approaching for the exhortation.
This rule also is to be honored, revered, esteemed, and venerated throughout one’s life, and is not to be transgressed.
When a bhikkhunī has completed the rains residence, she should invite correction from both Saṅghas on three grounds:
what has been seen, what has been heard, or what is suspected.
This rule also is to be honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped, and it is not to be transgressed for as long as life lasts.
A bhikkhunī who has committed an offense against a Garudhamma must undergo the penance of *mānatta* for half a month before both Saṅghas.
This rule, too, is to be honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped, and it is not to be transgressed for as long as life lasts.
A *sikkhamānā* who has trained in the six rules for two years must seek full ordination (*upasampadā*) from both Saṅghas.
This rule also, having been honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped, is not to be transgressed for as long as life lasts.
By no means whatsoever may a bhikkhunī revile or abuse a bhikkhu.
This rule also, having been honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped, is not to be transgressed for as long as life lasts.
“From this day forward, Ānanda, the path of speech for bhikkhunīs toward bhikkhus is closed, while the path of speech for bhikkhus toward bhikkhunīs remains open.
This rule also must be honored, revered, esteemed, and venerated for as long as life lasts; it is not to be transgressed.
If, Ānanda, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī accepts these eight weighty rules, let that be her full ordination.”
Then the Venerable Ānanda, having learned these eight *garudhammas* in the presence of the Blessed One, approached Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī; having approached her, he said this to Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī:
"If you, Gotamī, would accept these eight *garudhammas*, that itself shall be your full ordination (*upasampadā*).
A nun who has been ordained for a hundred years must perform salutation, rising from her seat, joining of palms, and respectful service toward a monk ordained on that very day."
This rule also, having been honored, revered, esteemed, and venerated, is not to be transgressed for as long as life lasts...
From this day forward, the path of speech for bhikkhunīs toward bhikkhus is closed, while the path of speech for bhikkhus toward bhikkhunīs remains open.
This rule also, having been honored, revered, esteemed, and venerated, is not to be transgressed for as long as life lasts.
“If you, Gotamī, would accept these eight weighty rules (garudhamma), that itself shall be your full ordination.
“Venerable Ānanda, it is just as if a woman or a man— young, youthful, and fond of adornment—
having washed their head and received a garland of blue lotuses, or a garland of jasmine, or a garland of *adhimuttaka* flowers, were to receive them with both hands.”
“...I would place it upon my head, the highest limb;
even so, Bhante Ānanda, do I accept these eight weighty rules (garudhamma) for as long as life lasts, not to be transgressed.

Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, the eight weighty rules have been accepted by Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, which are not to be transgressed for as long as life lasts.

“If, Ānanda, women had not obtained the going-forth from the home life into homelessness in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, the holy life, Ānanda, would have endured for a long time;
the True Dhamma would have remained for a thousand years. But now, because women have gone forth, the holy life will not endure so long; the True Dhamma will remain for only five hundred years.”
But since, Ānanda, women have gone forth from the household life into homelessness in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, the holy life will no longer endure for long, Ānanda.
Now, Ānanda, the True Dhamma will remain for only five hundred years.
Just as, Ānanda, those families that have many women and few men are easily plundered by thieves and bandits; so too, Ānanda, because women have gone forth... [the holy life will not endure long].
In the same way, Ānanda, in whatever Dhamma and Discipline women obtain the going-forth from the home life into homelessness, that holy life does not endure for long.
Just as, Ānanda, when a disease called whiteheads falls upon a flourishing field of rice, that rice field does not endure for long;
even so, Ānanda, in whatever Dhamma and Discipline women obtain the going-forth from the home life into homelessness, that holy life does not endure for long.
"Just as, Ānanda, when a disease called *mañjiṭṭhikā* falls upon a fertile field of sugarcane, that sugarcane field does not last long;
even so, Ānanda, in whatever Dhamma and Discipline women obtain the going-forth from the home life into homelessness, that holy life does not last long.
Just as, Ānanda, a man might build a dam for a great reservoir beforehand, precisely so that the water might not overflow."
“In this very way, Ānanda, these eight weighty rules (garudhamma) have been laid down by me for the bhikkhunīs as lifelong principles that must not be transgressed.
The first.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.52

6. Gotamīvagga: Ovādasutta (AN 8.52, PTS AN iv 279) [The Blessed One said: “Gotamī, there are these five things that lead to the decline of a woman who has gone forth. What five? Here, Gotamī, a woman who has gone forth dwells without reverence and deference toward the Teacher; she dwells without reverence and deference toward the Dhamma; she dwells without reverence and deference toward the Saṅgha; she dwells without reverence and deference toward the training; and she dwells without reverence and deference toward her fellow nuns who are senior, of middle standing, or junior. These, Gotamī, are the five things that lead to the decline of a woman who has gone forth. “Gotamī, there are these five things that lead to the non-decline of a woman who has gone forth. What five? Here, Gotamī, a woman who has gone forth dwells with reverence and deference toward the Teacher; she dwells with reverence and deference toward the Dhamma; she dwells with reverence and deference toward the Saṅgha; she dwells with reverence and deference toward the training; and she dwells with reverence and deference toward her fellow nuns who are senior, of middle standing, or junior. These, Gotamī, are the five things that lead to the non-decline of a woman who has gone forth.”
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Gabled Hall.

Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
“Bhante, with how many qualities should a bhikkhu be endowed to be authorized as an instructor of bhikkhunīs?”
“Ānanda, a bhikkhu endowed with eight qualities should be appointed as an instructor of bhikkhunīs.
What are the eight?
Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu is virtuous … [as before] … having undertaken them, he trains in the rules of training.”
He is learned ... [as above] ... his view is well-penetrated.
Both Pātimokkhas have been properly handed down to him in detail, well-analyzed, well-mastered, and well-determined, both as to the rules and their detailed exposition.
He is a good speaker, possessed of a fine delivery, endowed with polished speech that is clear, articulate, and expressive of the meaning.
He is capable of instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening the community of bhikkhunīs with a discourse on the Dhamma;
he is for the most part dear and pleasing to the bhikkhunīs;
and he has never previously committed a grave offense (garudhamma) while having gone forth under the Blessed One and wearing the saffron robes.
“He may be twenty years of age or more than twenty years of age.
It is with these eight qualities, Ānanda, that a bhikkhu should be authorized as an instructor of bhikkhunīs.
The second [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.53 6. Gotamīvagga Saṅkhittasutta (The Short Discourse) “Bhikkhus, there are these eight persons found existing in the world. What eight? The person who is a stream-enterer; the person who is a once-returner; the person who is a non-returner; the person who is an arahant; the person who is practicing for realization of the fruit of stream-entry; the person who is practicing for realization of the fruit of once-returning; the person who is practicing for realization of the fruit of non-returning; and the person who is practicing for realization of the fruit of arahantship. These, bhikkhus, are the eight persons found existing in the world.”
(AN 8.53, PTS AN iv 280) On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Gabled Hall.

Then Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, she stood to one side. Standing to one side, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī said this to the Blessed One:

“It would be well, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute.

“Gotamī, those qualities of which you might know: ‘These qualities lead to passion, not to dispassion; they lead to bondage, not to the absence of bondage; they lead to accumulation, not to shedding; they lead to the building up, not to the laying down of the burden’—you should certainly abandon them.”
They lead to bondage, not to liberation;
they lead to accumulation, not to diminution;
they lead to great desire, not to fewness of wishes.
They lead to lack of contentment, not to contentment;
they lead to social entanglement, not to seclusion;
they lead to laziness, not to the arousal of energy.
“‘They lead to being difficult to support, not to being easy to support,’—
in this regard, Gotamī, you should categorically hold:
‘This is not the Dhamma, this is not the Vinaya, this is not the Teacher’s instruction.’”
And as for those qualities, Gotamī, that you might know:
"These qualities lead to dispassion, not to passion;
they lead to detachment, not to bondage."
They lead to diminution, not to accumulation;
they lead to fewness of wishes, not to great desire;
they lead to contentment, not to discontent.
‘They lead to seclusion, not to socializing;
they lead to the arousal of energy, not to laziness;
they lead to being easy to support, not to being difficult to support.’”
“Categorically, Gotamī, you should hold:
‘This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction. This is the third [section].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.54 6. Gotamīvagga Dīghajāṇusutta Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then the brahmin Dīghajāṇu approached the Blessed One and, having approached, exchanged greetings with him. When they had concluded their polite conversation and cordial greetings, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the brahmin Dīghajāṇu said to the Blessed One: “Master Gotama, I am one who holds the view that there is no harm in sensual pleasures; I do not see any danger in sensual pleasures. “Brahmin, you have spoken as one who has not seen the danger in sensual pleasures when you say, ‘I am one who holds the view that there is no harm in sensual pleasures; I do not see any danger in sensual pleasures. For what reason? Because, brahmin, those sensual pleasures are impermanent, suffering, subject to change, and unstable. Suppose, brahmin, there were a great heap of firewood, and a man would come along bringing a torch of dry grass. If he were to throw that torch of dry grass onto that great heap of firewood, what do you think, brahmin?

Would that great heap of firewood burn for a long time? “Yes, Master Gotama. Why is that? Because that great heap of firewood is abundant. “In the same way, brahmin, whatever sensual pleasures there may be—whether they belong to the past, the future, or the present; whether they are internal or external; whether they are gross or subtle; whether they are inferior or superior; whether they are far or near—all these sensual pleasures are impermanent, suffering, subject to change, and unstable. Suppose, brahmin, there were a great mountain of rock, solid from base to summit, and a man would come along bringing a single grain of mustard seed. If he were to place that single grain of mustard seed on top of that great mountain of rock, what do you think, brahmin? Would that single grain of mustard seed appear large compared to that great mountain of rock? “Yes, Master Gotama. Why is that? Because that great mountain of rock is vast. “In the same way, brahmin, whatever sensual pleasures there may be—whether they belong to the past, the future, or the present; whether they are internal or external; whether they are gross or subtle; whether they are inferior or superior; whether they are far or near—all these sensual pleasures are impermanent, suffering, subject to change, and unstable. Therefore, brahmin, it is because I have seen the danger in sensual pleasures that I have gone forth from the home life into homelessness. When this was said, the brahmin Dīghajāṇu said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama! Just as, Master Gotama, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—just so has Master Gotama explained the Dhamma in various ways. I go to Master Gotama for refuge, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has taken refuge from this day forward for as long as life shall last. “Brahmin, one does not become a follower by merely saying ‘I take refuge. Rather, one becomes a follower by practicing in accordance with the Dhamma. Therefore, brahmin, you should train yourself thus: ‘My mind will be inclined toward renunciation, not toward worldly involvement. It is in this way, brahmin, that you should train yourself. When this was said, the brahmin Dīghajāṇu said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama! Just as, Master Gotama, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—just so has Master Gotama explained the Dhamma in various ways. I go to Master Gotama for refuge, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has taken refuge from this day forward for as long as life shall last. “Brahmin, one does not become a follower by merely saying ‘I take refuge. Rather, one becomes a follower by practicing in accordance with the Dhamma. Therefore, brahmin, you should train yourself thus: ‘My mind will be inclined toward non-hatred, not toward hatred. It is in this way, brahmin, that you should train yourself. When this was said, the brahmin Dīghajāṇu said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama! Just as, Master Gotama, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—just so has Master Gotama explained the Dhamma in various ways. I go to Master Gotama for refuge, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has taken refuge from this day forward for as long as life shall last. “Brahmin, one does not become a follower by merely saying ‘I take refuge. Rather, one becomes a follower by practicing in accordance with the Dhamma. Therefore, brahmin, you should train yourself thus: ‘My mind will be inclined toward harmlessness, not toward harmfulness. It is in this way, brahmin, that you should train yourself. When this was said, the brahmin Dīghajāṇu said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama! Just as, Master Gotama, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—just so has Master Gotama explained the Dhamma in various ways. I go to Master Gotama for refuge, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has taken refuge from this day forward for as long as life shall last. “Brahmin, one does not become a follower by merely saying ‘I take refuge. Rather, one becomes a follower by practicing in accordance with the Dhamma. Therefore, brahmin, you should train yourself thus: ‘I will abandon wrong view and develop right view. It is in this way, brahmin, that you should train yourself. When this was said, the brahmin Dīghajāṇu said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama! Just as, Master Gotama, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—just so has Master Gotama explained the Dhamma in various ways.

I go to Master Gotama for refuge, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has taken refuge from this day forward for as long as life shall last. “Brahmin, one does not become a follower by merely saying ‘I take refuge. Rather, one becomes a follower by practicing in accordance with the Dhamma. Therefore, brahmin, you should train yourself thus: ‘I will abandon ill will and develop a mind of loving-kindness. It is in this way, brahmin, that you should train yourself. When this was said, the brahmin Dīghajāṇu said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama! Just as, Master Gotama, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—just so has Master Gotama explained the Dhamma in various ways. I go to Master Gotama for refuge, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has taken refuge from this day forward for as long as life shall last. “Brahmin, one does not become a follower by merely saying ‘I take refuge. Rather, one becomes a follower by practicing in accordance with the Dhamma. Therefore, brahmin, you should train yourself thus: ‘I will abandon harsh speech and develop gentle speech. It is in this way, brahmin, that you should train yourself. When this was said
(AN 8.54, PTS AN iv 281) On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Koliyans at a town of the Koliyans named Kakkarapatta.
Then Dīghajāṇu, the son of the Koliyans, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he [paid homage to] the Blessed One.
Having paid homage, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, Dīghajāṇu the Koliyan son said this to the Blessed One:

“Venerable sir, we are householders who enjoy sensual pleasures; we dwell in a bed crowded with children, we use Kāsī sandalwood, we wear garlands, scents, and unguents, and we accept gold and silver.”

“Venerable sir, may the Blessed One teach us such a Dhamma that would lead to our welfare in this present life and to our happiness in this present life, and to our welfare in the future life and to our happiness in the future life.

“Byagghapajja, there are these four qualities that lead to the welfare of a clansman in this present life and to his happiness in this present life. What are the four? [The Blessed One then proceeded to explain them.]”
Perfection of initiative, perfection of protection, good friendship, and balanced living.
And what, Byagghapajja, is perfection of initiative?
Here, Byagghapajja, a clansman earns his livelihood by whatever craft he practices—
Whether it be through farming, trade, cattle-rearing, archery, government service, or any other craft—
therein one is skillful and diligent, endowed with the investigative wisdom appropriate for that task, and capable of acting and capable of providing.
This, Byagghapajja, is called accomplishment in initiative.
And what, Byagghapajja, is the perfection of protection?
Here, Byagghapajja, a clansman possesses wealth acquired through initiative and energy, amassed by the strength of his arms, earned by the sweat of his brow, righteous, and righteously obtained.
He provides for its protection and preservation: [text continues].

‘How might these possessions of mine not be seized by kings, nor seized by thieves; how might they not be consumed by fire, nor carried away by water; and how might they not be taken by unpleasant heirs?
This, Byagghapajja, is called accomplishment in protection.
And what, Byagghapajja, is good friendship?
Here, Byagghapajja, a clansman lives in whatever village or town he may reside;

there, he stands together with, converses with, and engages in discussion with those who are householders or householders’ sons— young yet mature in character, or old and mature in character— who are endowed with faith, endowed with virtue, endowed with generosity, and endowed with wisdom.
He enters [upon this state]; he trains himself in the perfection of faith of those who are endowed with faith,
he trains himself in the perfection of virtue of those who are endowed with virtue, he trains himself in the perfection of generosity of those who are endowed with generosity,
and he trains himself in the perfection of wisdom of those who are endowed with wisdom.
This, Byagghapajja, is called having virtuous friends.
And what, Byagghapajja, is balanced living?
Here, Byagghapajja, a clansman, having understood the income of his wealth and having understood the expenditure of his wealth, [lives accordingly].
He maintains a livelihood that is balanced, neither excessive nor deficient, thinking: "In this way my income will suffice for my expenses, and my expenses will not exceed my income.
Just as, Byagghapajja, a weigher or a weigher’s apprentice, having held up a scale, knows: "By this much it has tilted down, or by this much it has tilted up."
In the same way, Byagghapajja, a clansman, having understood the income of his wealth and having understood the expenditure of his wealth,
maintains a balanced livelihood— neither excessive nor too frugal— thinking: "In this way my income will suffice for my expenditure, and my expenditure will not exceed my income."
If, Byagghapajja, this clansman has little income yet maintains a grand livelihood, there will be those who say of him: "This clansman eats his wealth like one eating figs.
But if, Byagghapajja, this clansman has great income yet maintains a meager livelihood, there will be those who say of him: "This clansman will die of starvation.
However, Byagghapajja, when a clansman understands both the income of his wealth and the depletion of his wealth...
Having understood this, he maintains a balanced livelihood, neither too extravagant nor too frugal, thinking:
"In this way my income will suffice for my expenses, and my expenses will not exceed my income.
This, Byagghapajja, is called a balanced livelihood.
“Byagghapajja, when wealth has thus arisen, there are four outlets for its dissipation:
a womanizer, a drunkard, a gambler, and one who has evil friends, evil companions, and evil associates.
Just as, Byagghapajja, a large reservoir might have four inlets and four outlets,” [so it is with wealth].
If a man were to close up its inflow channels and open up its outflow channels,
and the rain-god were not to send down rain in proper measure, then,
Byagghapajja, only the depletion of that great lake is to be expected, not its increase.
In the same way, Byagghapajja, for wealth thus acquired there are four outlets for its depletion:
a womanizer, a drunkard, a gambler, and one who has evil friends, evil companions, and evil associates.
Byagghapajja, for wealth thus acquired there are four sources of its increase: [the opposite of each of these].
He is not a womanizer, nor a drunkard, nor a gambler; he has virtuous friends, virtuous companions, and virtuous associates.
Just as, Byagghapajja, a great reservoir might have four inlets and four outlets, and a man were to open those inlets and close those outlets;
And if the rain-god were to send down rain properly,
then, Byagghapajja, one could expect only an increase for that great reservoir, not a decrease.
In the same way, Byagghapajja, there are four sources of income for wealth that has thus arisen:
He is not a womanizer, nor a drunkard, nor a gambler; he has virtuous friends, virtuous companions, and virtuous associates.
These, Byagghapajja, are the four qualities that lead to the welfare of a clansman in this present life and to his happiness in this present life.
There are, Byagghapajja, these four other qualities that lead to the welfare of a clansman in future lives and to his happiness in future lives.
Which four?
Perfection of faith, perfection of virtue, perfection of generosity, and perfection of wisdom.
And what, Byagghapajja, is the perfection of faith?
In this case, Byagghapajja, a clansman is endowed with faith; he has faith in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata:
"Thus indeed is that Blessed One … [as above] … the Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
This, Byagghapajja, is called the perfection of faith.
And what, Byagghapajja, is the perfection of virtue?
Here, Byagghapajja, a clansman abstains from taking life... [as above] ...he abstains from fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence.
This, Byagghapajja, is called the perfection of virtue.
And what, Byagghapajja, is the perfection of generosity?

Here, Byagghapajja, a clansman dwells at home with a mind free from the stain of stinginess, open-handed, pure in hand, delighting in relinquishment, devoted to charity, and taking pleasure in sharing.
This, Byagghapajja, is called the perfection of generosity.
And what, Byagghapajja, is the perfection of wisdom?
Here, Byagghapajja, a clansman is wise; he possesses the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble, penetrative, and leads to the complete destruction of suffering.
This, Byagghapajja, is called the perfection of wisdom.
"These four qualities, Byagghapajja, lead to the welfare and happiness of a clansman in the future life.
One who is industrious in their work,
diligent, and methodical;
He makes his livelihood even,
protects his accumulated store;
endowed with faith and perfected in virtue.
Generous and free from stinginess,
one constantly purifies the path for one’s own welfare in the life to come.
These eight qualities have been declared by the one named Truth for the faithful seeker of the household life.
It brings happiness in both places:
for the sake of welfare and benefit in this present life,
and for the sake of happiness in the future life.
"Thus it is for householders:
generosity increases their merit.
The fourth.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.55 6. Gotamīvagga Ujjayasutta “Bhikkhus, there are these eight grounds for the non-decline of a wheel-turning monarch. What eight? Here, bhikkhus, a wheel-turning monarch is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, accomplished in proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and having undertaken the training rules, he trains in them. This is the first ground for the non-decline of a wheel-turning monarch. Furthermore, bhikkhus, a wheel-turning monarch has abundant wealth and grain; he possesses great treasures and resources, and his treasury is full. This is the second ground for the non-decline of a wheel-turning monarch. Furthermore, bhikkhus, a wheel-turning monarch has a vast army consisting of four divisions: elephant troops, cavalry, chariot troops, and infantry. This is the third ground for the non-decline of a wheel-turning monarch. Furthermore, bhikkhus, a wheel-turning monarch is beloved and dear to the people, whether they be khattiyas, brahmins, vessas, or suddas. This is the fourth ground for the non-decline of a wheel-turning monarch. Furthermore, bhikkhus, a wheel-turning monarch is protected by heavenly beings; wherever he stands, sits, or lies down, the gods stand guard over him. This is the fifth ground for the non-decline of a wheel-turning monarch. Furthermore, bhikkhus, a wheel-turning monarch’s wheel-treasure rolls forward; wherever it rolls, there the king goes, followed by his fourfold army. This is the sixth ground for the non-decline of a wheel-turning monarch. Furthermore, bhikkhus, a wheel-turning monarch conquers the lands in the four directions, from the sea to the sea, and having conquered them, he does not oppress them with weapons or violence, but instead establishes them in security and peace.

This is the seventh ground for the non-decline of a wheel-turning monarch. Furthermore, bhikkhus, a wheel-turning monarch possesses the seven treasures and the four kinds of success. This is the eighth ground for the non-decline of a wheel-turning monarch. These, bhikkhus, are the eight grounds for the non-decline of a wheel-turning monarch. Just as these eight grounds for the non-decline of a wheel-turning monarch are found, so too, bhikkhus, there are eight grounds for the non-decline of a bhikkhu. What eight? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, accomplished in proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and having undertaken the training rules, he trains in them. This is the first ground for the non-decline of a bhikkhu. Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has heard much, has retained what he has heard, accumulated what he has heard; those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the perfectly complete and pure holy life—such teachings as these he has heard much of, retained, recited verbally, mentally examined, and penetrated well by view. This is the second ground for the non-decline of a bhikkhu. Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has developed the four foundations of mindfulness... [and so on with the remaining factors]. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having said this, the Sublime One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, soon after the Blessed One had departed, the venerable Ānanda addressed the bhikkhus: “Friends, the Teacher has spoken in brief and has explained the meaning in detail regarding the eight grounds for the non-decline of a bhikkhu. Then the venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus: “Friends, the Teacher has spoken in brief and has explained the meaning in detail regarding the eight grounds for the non-decline of a bhikkhu. Now, friends, let us go to the Blessed One and report this matter to him. As the Blessed One explains it to us, so we shall remember it. “Yes, friend,” the bhikkhus replied to the venerable Sāriputta. Then the venerable Sāriputta and the venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. The venerable Sāriputta then reported to the Blessed One everything that had occurred, saying: “Venerable sir, as the Blessed One has explained it to us, so we shall remember it. “Sāriputta, it is well, it is well! Sāriputta, it is exactly as you have understood it. These, Sāriputta, are the eight grounds for the non-decline of a bhikkhu. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, the bhikkhus delighted in the words of the Blessed One. Thus was the discourse on the eight grounds for non-decline spoken by the Blessed One while staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park, concerning the venerable Ānanda. It was heard by me thus. Therefore, it is called the Ānanda-saṃyutta. Thus was the section on the eight grounds for non-decline spoken by the Blessed One.
