(AN 8.55, PTS AN iv 285) Then the brahmin Ujjaya approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the brahmin Ujjaya said this to the Blessed One:
“Master Gotama, we wish to go abroad.

May Master Gotama teach us the Dhamma in such a way that those teachings might lead to our welfare in this present life, to our happiness in this present life, to our welfare in future lives, and to our happiness in future lives.
“Brahmin, there are these four qualities that lead to the welfare of a clansman in this present life and to his happiness in this present life.”
Which four?
Accomplishment in initiative, accomplishment in protection, good friendship, and balanced living.
And what, brahmin, is accomplishment in initiative?
In this case, brahmin, a clansman earns his livelihood by means of a certain occupation—
whether by agriculture, trade, cattle-herding, archery, government service, or some other craft—
in which he is skillful and diligent, endowed with the necessary ingenuity, and capable of acting and organizing.
This, brahmin, is called accomplishment in initiative.
And what, brahmin, is accomplishment in protection?
Here, brahmin, a clansman possesses wealth acquired through initiative and energy, amassed by the strength of his arms, earned by the sweat of his brow, righteous and righteously obtained.
He provides for their protection and security, thinking:
"How can it be that these riches of mine are not carried off by kings, nor carried off by thieves, nor consumed by fire, nor swept away by water, nor taken by unpleasant heirs?
This, brahmin, is called the perfection of protection.
And what, brahmin, is good friendship? Here, brahmin,
in whatever village or town a clansman dwells, there he associates with those who are householders or sons of householders—
whether young but mature in character, or old and mature in character— who are endowed with faith.
They are endowed with virtue, endowed with generosity, and endowed with wisdom; he stands together with them, converses with them, and engages in discussion with them.
He trains himself in accordance with the perfection of faith of those who are endowed with faith;

he trains himself in accordance with the perfection of virtue of those who are endowed with virtue; he trains himself in accordance with the perfection of generosity of those who are endowed with generosity.
He trains himself, training in the perfection of wisdom possessed by those who are endowed with wisdom.
This, brahmin, is called having virtuous friends.
And what, brahmin, is balanced livelihood?
Here, brahmin, a clansman, having understood the income of his wealth and having understood the expenditure of his wealth,
leads a balanced life— neither too extravagant nor too frugal— thinking: "In this way my income will suffice for my expenditure, and my expenditure will not exceed my income."
"Just as, brahmin, a weigher or a weigher’s apprentice, having held up a scale, knows: ‘It is tilted this much’ or ‘It is raised that much’;

even so, brahmin, a clansman, having understood the income of his wealth and having understood the expenditure of his wealth, maintains a balanced livelihood—neither extravagant nor too frugal—thinking: ‘In this way, my income will suffice for my expenditure.’"
‘And my income will not run out before my life-span does.
If, brahmin, this clansman has little income yet leads a luxurious life, there will be those who say of him: ‘This clansman eats his wealth like one eating figs from the udumbara tree.
But if, brahmin, this clansman has a great income yet leads a frugal life, there will be those who say of him: ‘This clansman will die an unnatural death.’”
And when, brahmin, this clansman, having understood the income of his wealth and having understood the expenditure of his wealth,
maintains a balanced livelihood— neither too extravagant nor too frugal— thinking: "In this way my income will suffice for my expenditure, and my expenditure will not exceed my income."
This, brahmin, is called living in moderation.
When wealth has been acquired in this way, brahmin, there are four ways of squandering it:
being a gambler with women, a gambler with liquor, a gambler with dice, and having evil friends, evil companions, and evil associates.
"Just as, brahmin, there might be a great reservoir with four inlets and four outlets.
Suppose a man were to close those inlets and open those outlets, and the rain-god were not to send down rain in proper measure. In this way, brahmin, for that great reservoir..."
Only decline is to be expected, not growth;
even so, brahmin, for wealth thus acquired there are four ways of loss:
being addicted to women, being addicted to liquor, being addicted to gambling, and having evil friends, evil companions, and evil associates.
“Thus, brahmin, for wealth that has arisen in this way, there are four sources of income:
one who is not a womanizer, not a drunkard, not a gambler, but one who has good friends, good companions, and good associates.
Just as, brahmin, a large reservoir might have four inlets and four outlets.”
If a man were to open its inflow channels and close its outflow channels,
and the rain-god were to send down rain in proper measure, then, brahmin, it can only be expected that this great reservoir would increase, not diminish.
In the same way, brahmin, for wealth thus acquired, there are four avenues of income: one who is not a libertine with women...
[and so on] ...one who does not associate with what is lovely.
These, brahmin, are the four qualities that lead to the welfare and happiness of a clansman in this very life.
"Brahmin, there are these four qualities that lead to the welfare of a clansman in the future life and to his happiness in the future life.
What are the four?
Perfection of faith, perfection of virtue, perfection of generosity, and perfection of wisdom."
And what, brahmin, is the perfection of faith?
Here, brahmin, a clansman is endowed with faith; he has faith in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata:
"Thus indeed is that Blessed One: ... [as above] ... the Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One."
This, brahmin, is called perfection in faith.
And what, brahmin, is perfection in virtue?

Here, brahmin, a clansman abstains from taking life ... [and so on] ... he abstains from the use of fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence. This, brahmin, is called perfection in virtue.
This, brahmin, is called the perfection of virtue.
And what, brahmin, is the perfection of generosity?
Here, brahmin, a clansman dwells at home with a mind free from the stain of stinginess, open-handed, pure in hand, delighting in relinquishment, devoted to charity, and fond of distributing gifts.
This, brahmin, is called perfection in generosity.
And what, brahmin, is perfection in wisdom?

Here, brahmin, a clansman is wise; he possesses the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble and penetrative, leading to the complete destruction of suffering. This is called perfection in wisdom.
“This, brahmin, is called the perfection of wisdom.
‘These four qualities, brahmin, lead to the welfare of a clansman in future lives and to his happiness in future lives.
One who exerts himself in the fields of action...”
Diligent and observant of the rules,
he maintains his livelihood with moderation and protects his accumulated store.
Endowed with faith, perfected in virtue,
generous and free from stinginess,
one constantly purifies the path.
And security for the life to come.
Thus these eight qualities belong to the faithful seeker of the household life.
Proclaimed under the name of Truth,
it brings happiness in both worlds;
for the sake of welfare and benefit in this very life, it leads to peace in the future world.
And for the sake of happiness in the future life;
thus, for householders,
generosity causes merit to increase.
Fifth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.56. Chapter 6:
The Section on Gotamī.
The Discourse on Fear (Bhayasutta): "Monks,
'fear' is a designation for sensual pleasures."
“‘Suffering,’ monks, is a designation for sensual pleasures.
‘Disease,’ monks, is a designation for sensual pleasures.
‘A boil,’ monks, is a designation for sensual pleasures.”
“‘Arrows,’ monks, is a designation for sensual pleasures.
‘Entanglements,’ monks, is a designation for sensual pleasures.
‘Mud,’ monks, is a designation for sensual pleasures.”
“‘The womb,’ monks, is a designation for sensual pleasures.
And why, monks, is ‘fear’ a designation for sensual pleasures?

Because one who is inflamed by lust for sensual pleasures, bound by desire and passion, is not freed from fears pertaining to this present life, nor is he freed from fears pertaining to future lives. Therefore, ‘fear’ is a designation for sensual pleasures.”
And why, monks, is it said: ‘It is suffering’ … [as before] … ‘It is a disease’ … ‘It is a tumor’?
‘A dart’ … ‘a bond’ … ‘a mire’ …
‘The womb’ is a designation for sensual pleasures.

And because one who is stained by lust for sensual pleasures, monks, being bound by desire and lust, is not freed from the wombs pertaining to this present life, nor is he freed from the wombs pertaining to future lives; therefore, ‘the womb’ is a designation for sensual pleasures.
It is fear, it is suffering, and it is disease.
The boil, the arrow, and the snare;
the mire and the womb— both of these are called sensual pleasures.
Wherein the ordinary person,
a being submerged by the appearance of pleasure,
goes again to the womb.
And since a bhikkhu is ardent,
he does not lack clear comprehension.
He [crosses] this quagmire, this difficult path.
Having transcended such a state,
he gazes upon the flickering multitude beset by birth and old age.
The Sixth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.57.
Chapter 6: The Gotamī Division.
The First Discourse on Those Worthy of Offerings (Paṭhama-āhuneyyasutta):
“Bhikkhus, possessing eight qualities, a bhikkhu is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.”
By which eight?
Here, monks, a monk is virtuous ... [as before] ... he trains himself in the rules of training he has undertaken;
he is learned ... [as before] ... his view is well-penetrated.
He has virtuous friends, virtuous companions, and virtuous associates;
he holds right view and is endowed with right vision;
he is one who gains at will, without difficulty, and without trouble, the four jhānas that belong to the higher mind and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life.
He recollects his manifold past abodes, that is to say, one birth, two births... [and so on] ... thus he recollects his manifold past abodes with their modes and details;
with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human... [he sees beings passing away and being reborn] according to their kamma;
through the destruction of the taints... having realized for himself, he enters and dwells in that state.
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with these eight qualities is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
The seventh. *Aṅguttara Nikāya* 8.58

6. Gotamī Chapter The Second Discourse on Those Worthy of Offerings (Dutiya-āhuneyyasutta) “Monks, there are these four persons worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. What four? The person who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry; the person who has realized the fruit of stream-entry; the person who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of once-returning; and the person who has realized the fruit of once-returning. These, monks, are the four persons worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. [Similarly, the discourse continues with the remaining pairs: “The person who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of non-returning... the person who has realized the fruit of non-returning... the person who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of arahantship... the person who has realized the fruit of arahantship. These, monks, are the four persons worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. What four? The person who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry... the person who has realized the fruit of stream-entry... the person who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of once-returning... the person who has realized the fruit of once-returning... the person who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of non-returning... the person who has realized the fruit of non-returning... the person who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of arahantship... the person who has realized the fruit of arahantship. These, monks, are the four persons worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then the female lay follower Gotamī approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to him: “Venerable sir, how many kinds of persons are worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world? “There are, Gotamī, these four persons worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. What four? The person who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry... the person who has realized the fruit of stream-entry... the person who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of once-returning... the person who has realized the fruit of once-returning... the person who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of non-returning... the person who has realized the fruit of non-returning... the person who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of arahantship... the person who has realized the fruit of arahantship.

These, Gotamī, are the four persons worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. When this was said, the female lay follower Gotamī said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir! Just as one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, even so has the Dhamma been made clear by the Blessed One in many ways. I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May I receive the going forth under the Blessed One, may I receive the higher ordination! “You have been a stream-enterer, Gotamī, for a long time; you have long since abandoned the states of misery. Thus spoke the Blessed One. “Bhikkhus, possessing eight qualities, a bhikkhu is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
What eight?
Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is virtuous... [as above] ...he trains himself by undertaking the training precepts.”
He is learned … [as above] … he has well penetrated the view;
he dwells with energy aroused, steadfast, firm in his exertion, not casting off the burden regarding wholesome qualities;
he is a forest-dweller, frequenting remote lodgings.
He is one who endures both lack of delight and delight; having repeatedly overcome arisen lack of delight, he dwells [therein];
he is one who endures fear and terror; having repeatedly overcome arisen fear and terror, he dwells [therein];
he is one who obtains at will, without difficulty, and without hardship, the four jhānas that belong to the higher mind and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life.
“With the destruction of the taints, he enters and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having realized it for himself in this very life.

It is by possessing these eight qualities, monks, that a bhikkhu is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
This is the eighth [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.59 6. Gotamīvagga Paṭhamapuggalasutta (The First Discourse on Persons) “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Which four? The person who is intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others; the person who is intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare; the person who is intent neither on his own welfare nor on the welfare of others; and the person who is intent both on his own welfare and on the welfare of others. And how, monks, is one a person intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others? Here, monks, someone dwells having undertaken the precepts of virtue, yet he does not encourage others to undertake the precepts of virtue; he does not praise the undertaking of the precepts of virtue; he does not rejoice in those who have undertaken the precepts of virtue. This is called a person intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others. And how, monks, is one a person intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare? Here, monks, someone does not dwell having undertaken the precepts of virtue, yet he encourages others to undertake the precepts of virtue; he praises the undertaking of the precepts of virtue; he rejoices in those who have undertaken the precepts of virtue. This is called a person intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare. And how, monks, is one a person intent neither on his own welfare nor on the welfare of others? Here, monks, someone does not dwell having undertaken the precepts of virtue, and he does not encourage others to undertake the precepts of virtue; he does not praise the undertaking of the precepts of virtue; he does not rejoice in those who have undertaken the precepts of virtue. This is called a person intent neither on his own welfare nor on the welfare of others. And how, monks, is one a person intent both on his own welfare and on the welfare of others? Here, monks, someone dwells having undertaken the precepts of virtue, and he encourages others to undertake the precepts of virtue; he praises the undertaking of the precepts of virtue; he rejoices in those who have undertaken the precepts of virtue. This is called a person intent both on his own welfare and on the welfare of others. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”

“Bhikkhus, these eight persons are worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. What eight? [The rest of the passage follows.]”

The stream-enterer, one practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry; the once-returner, one practicing for the realization of the fruit of once-returning; the non-returner, one practicing for the realization of the fruit of non-returning; the arahant, and one practicing for arahantship.
These, monks, are the eight persons who are worthy of gifts … [as before] … an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
And the four who are practicing.
And those established in the four fruits—
this is the Saṅgha, upright,
endowed with wisdom and virtue.
For those people who are sacrificers,
for living beings seeking merit,
performing worldly merit—
“Gifts given to the Saṅgha bring great fruit.
Thus ends the ninth [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.60

“Bhikkhus, these eight persons are worthy of offerings … they are an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
Which eight?

for those people who offer sacrifices, it is the best.

The Discourse on Wishes (Icchāsutta): “Bhikkhus,

What are the eight?
Here, monks, a bhikkhu living in seclusion, leading an independent life, conceives a desire for gain.
He exerts himself, strives, and makes an effort for the sake of gain.
Though he rises, exerts himself, and strives for gain, no gain arises for him.
Because of that lack of gain, he sorrows, languishes, and laments; he beats his breast, weeps, and falls into confusion.
This, monks, is called:
“A bhikkhu dwells desiring gain; he exerts himself, strives, and makes an effort for the sake of gain, yet he does not obtain it. He grieves and laments, and he has fallen away from the true Dhamma.
But here, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu dwells secluded and lives independently, a desire arises in him for gain.
He exerts himself, strives, and makes an effort for the sake of gain.
As he exerts himself, strives, and makes an effort for the sake of gain, gain arises for him.
He becomes intoxicated by that gain, becomes negligent, and falls into heedlessness.
This, monks, is called:
“A bhikkhu dwells desiring gain; he exerts himself, strives, and makes an effort for the sake of gain; yet he is one who gains, and is intoxicated and negligent, fallen away from the true Dhamma.
But here, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu dwells secluded, living independently, a desire arises in him for gain.
He does not exert himself, strive, or make an effort for the sake of gain.
For one who does not strive, exert himself, or make an effort for the sake of gain, gain does not arise.
Because of that lack of gain, he sorrows, languishes, laments, beats his breast, and falls into confusion.
This, monks, is called:

“A bhikkhu dwells desiring gain; he does not exert himself, strive, or make an effort for the sake of gain, and he does not obtain it. He grieves and laments, and he has fallen away from the true Dhamma.
But here, monks, when a bhikkhu dwells secluded, living independently, a desire arises in him for gain.
He does not exert himself, strive, or make an effort for the sake of gain.
Though he does not strive, exert himself, or make an effort for the sake of gain, gain arises for him.
He becomes intoxicated by that gain, becomes negligent, and falls into heedlessness.
This, monks, is called:

‘A bhikkhu dwells desiring gain; he does not exert himself, strive, or make an effort for the sake of gain; yet he gains it, becomes intoxicated by it, is negligent, and has fallen away from the true Dhamma.
But here, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu dwells secluded and lives independently, a desire arises in him for gain.
He exerts himself, strives, and makes an effort for the sake of gain.
Though he exerts himself, strives, and makes an effort for gain, no gain arises for him.
Yet, because of that lack of gain, he does not grieve, he does not waste away, he does not lament; he does not beat his breast, nor does he fall into confusion.
This, monks, is called:

“A bhikkhu dwells desiring gain; he exerts himself, strives, and makes an effort for the sake of gain, yet he does not obtain it. He neither grieves nor laments, and he has not fallen away from the true Dhamma.
Furthermore, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu dwells secluded and lives independently, a desire arises in him for gain.
He exerts himself, strives, and makes an effort for the sake of gain.
As he rises, exerts himself, and strives for gain, gain arises for him.
He does not become intoxicated by that gain, does not become negligent, and does not fall into heedlessness.
This, monks, is called:

“A bhikkhu dwells desiring gain; he exerts himself, strives, and makes an effort for the sake of gain; yet he obtains it, and he is neither intoxicated nor negligent, and he has not fallen away from the true Dhamma.
But here, bhikkhus, while a bhikkhu is dwelling in seclusion and living independently, a desire arises for gain.
He does not exert himself, strive, or make an effort for the sake of gain.
For one who does not strive, exert himself, or make an effort for the sake of gain, gain does not arise.
Because of that lack of gain, he does not grieve, does not become weary, does not lament, does not beat his breast, and does not fall into confusion.
This, monks, is called:

“A bhikkhu dwells desiring gain; he does not exert himself, strive, or make an effort for the sake of gain, yet he is not one who gains it, nor is he one who grieves or laments; he has fallen away from the true Dhamma.
But here, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is dwelling in seclusion, living independently, a desire arises in him for gain.
He does not exert himself, strive, or make an effort for the sake of gain.
For one who does not strive, exert himself, or make an effort for the sake of gain, gain nevertheless arises.
He is not intoxicated by that gain, he does not become negligent, and he does not fall into heedlessness.
This, monks, is called:

“A bhikkhu who dwells desiring gain, yet does not exert himself, strive, or struggle for the sake of gain; and though he gains it, he is neither intoxicated by it nor negligent, and he has not fallen away from the true Dhamma.
These, monks, are the eight persons found existing in the world. Thus was the first [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.62 7. Bhūmicālavagga Alaṁ Sutta “Monks, there are these eight grounds for the arousal of a great earthquake. What eight? (1) “Monks, when a Tathāgata, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One arises in the world, this is the first ground for the arousal of a great earthquake. (2) “When a Tathāgata realizes the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, this is the second ground for the arousal of a great earthquake. (3) “When a Tathāgata sets in motion the unsurpassed wheel of Dhamma, this is the third ground for the arousal of a great earthquake. (4) “When a Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma to a community of monks headed by Sāriputta and Moggallāna, this is the fourth ground for the arousal of a great earthquake. (5) “When a Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma to a community of bhikkhunīs headed by Khemā and Uppalavaṇṇā, this is the fifth ground for the arousal of a great earthquake. (6) “When a Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma to a community of laymen headed by Citta and Hatthaka, this is the sixth ground for the arousal of a great earthquake. (7) “When a Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma to a community of laywomen headed by Khujjuttarā and Veḷukaṇṭakī Nandamātā, this is the seventh ground for the arousal of a great earthquake. (8) “When a Tathāgata, having attained final Nibbāna through the total ending of the five aggregates, lies down between the twin sal trees, this is the eighth ground for the arousal of a great earthquake. These, monks, are the eight grounds for the arousal of a great earthquake.”
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with six qualities is capable for himself and capable for others. With which six? [The Buddha said: (AN 8.62, PTS AN iv 296)
In this case, monks, a bhikkhu is one who possesses quick comprehension regarding wholesome states;
he is one inclined to retain the teachings he has heard;
and he is one who investigates the meaning of the teachings he has retained.
Having understood the meaning and understood the Dhamma, he practices in accordance with the Dhamma;
he is a good speaker, possessing a beautiful voice, endowed with speech that is polished, clear, flawless, and expressive of the meaning;
and he is one who instructs, exhorts, inspires, and gladdens his fellow celibates.
“Monks, a monk endowed with these six qualities is capable for himself and capable for others.
Monks, a monk endowed with five qualities is capable for himself and capable for others.
With which five? [The Buddha continued:]”
In this case, monks, a bhikkhu is not only quick to understand wholesome states,
but he is also capable of retaining the teachings he has heard;
and having retained those teachings, he is one who investigates their meaning.
Having understood the meaning and understood the Dhamma, he practices in accordance with the Dhamma;
he is a speaker of what is beautiful … [as before] … for the purpose of making the meaning known;
and he is one who instructs, encourages, inspires, and gladdens his fellow celibates.
“Monks, a monk endowed with these five qualities is capable for himself and capable for others.
Monks, a monk endowed with four qualities is capable for himself but not capable for others.
With which four?”
Here, monks, a monk is one of quick intuition regarding wholesome states;
he is of a nature to retain the teachings he has heard;
and he is one who examines the meaning of the teachings he has retained.
Having understood the goal and having understood the Dhamma, he practices in accordance with the Dhamma;
yet he is not one who is a good speaker, possessing a fine voice, endowed with speech that is polished, clear, flawless, and expressive of the meaning;
nor does he instruct, encourage, inspire, and gladden his fellow celibates.
“Monks, a monk endowed with these four qualities is capable for himself but not for others.
Monks, a monk endowed with four other qualities is capable for others but not for himself.
With which four?”
In this case, monks, a bhikkhu is one who possesses quick comprehension regarding wholesome states;
he is one who has the capacity to retain the teachings he has heard;
yet he is not one who investigates the meaning of the teachings he has retained.
And having understood the meaning and understood the Dhamma, he practices in accordance with the Dhamma;
he is a speaker of what is good and possesses a beautiful voice... for the purpose of making the meaning known;
and he is one who instructs his fellow celibate practitioners.
“Monks, a monk endowed with these four qualities is capable of helping others, but not himself.
Monks, a monk endowed with three qualities is capable of helping himself, but not others.
Which three?”
In this case, monks, a bhikkhu is not only one who possesses quick comprehension regarding wholesome states;
he is also one who has the disposition to retain the teachings he has heard;
and he is one who investigates the meaning of the teachings he has retained.
Having understood the goal and understood the Dhamma, he practices in accordance with the Dhamma;
yet he is not one who is a good speaker, possessing a refined mode of speech that is polished, distinct, flawless, and expressive of the meaning;
nor does he instruct, encourage, inspire, or gladden his fellow celibates.
“Monks, a monk endowed with these three qualities is sufficient for himself, but not for others.
Monks, a monk endowed with three other qualities is sufficient for others, but not for himself.
Which three?”
In this case, monks, a bhikkhu is not one who possesses quick comprehension regarding wholesome states;
yet he is one who has the habit of retaining the teachings he has heard;
however, he does not investigate the meaning of the teachings he has retained.
And having understood the meaning and understood the Dhamma, he practices in accordance with the Dhamma;
he is a speaker of what is good … [as before] … for the sake of making the meaning known;
and he is one who instructs, encourages, inspires, and gladdens his fellow celibates.
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with these three qualities is sufficient for others, but not for himself.
With two qualities, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is sufficient for himself, but not for others.
Which two?”
In this case, monks, a bhikkhu is not one who possesses quick comprehension regarding wholesome states;
nor is he one who has the habit of retaining the teachings he has heard;
yet he is one who examines the meaning of the teachings he has retained.
Having understood the meaning and having understood the Dhamma, he practices in accordance with the Dhamma;
yet he is not one of beautiful speech... [as above] ...in making the meaning known;
nor is he one who instructs his fellow celibates... [as above].
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with these two qualities is sufficient for himself, but not for others.
Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with two other qualities is sufficient for others, but not for himself.
Which two?”
In this case, monks, a bhikkhu is not one who possesses quick comprehension regarding wholesome states;
nor is he one who has the disposition to retain the teachings he has heard;
nor is he one who investigates the meaning of the teachings he has retained.
And having understood the goal and understood the Dhamma, he practices in accordance with the Dhamma;
he is a good speaker, possessed of a beautiful voice, endowed with speech that is polished, clear, faultless, and expressive of the meaning;
and he is one who instructs, urges, rouses, and gladdens his fellow celibates.
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with these two qualities is capable [of helping] others, but not himself.
The second.
*Aṅguttara Nikāya* 8.63
7. Bhūmicālavagga:
The Short Discourse (Saṅkhittasutta) (AN 8.63, PTS AN iv 299)
Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One... [as before] ...and sitting to one side, that bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:
"It would be well, Bhante, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute.
"In this very way, some foolish men here entreat only me."
"And when the Dhamma is spoken, they think that they must follow me alone.
"Venerable sir, let the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma in brief; let the Sugata teach me the Dhamma in brief.
Perhaps I might understand the meaning of the Blessed One's words; perhaps I might become an heir to the Blessed One's words."
“Therefore, bhikkhu, you should train yourself thus:
‘My mind will be established within, well-composed, and evil, unwholesome states that have arisen will not persist by taking hold of the mind.
It is in this way, bhikkhu, that you should train yourself.”
When, monk, your mind is settled within, well-composed, and no arisen evil unwholesome states remain obsessing the mind, then you should train yourself thus:
"The liberation of my mind through loving-kindness will be developed, cultivated, made a vehicle, made a foundation, established, consolidated, and properly undertaken.
It is in this way, monk, that you should train yourself.
When, monk, this concentration has been thus developed and cultivated by you, then, monk, you should develop this concentration with both directed thought and evaluation;
you should develop it without directed thought and with only evaluation;
you should develop it without directed thought and without evaluation; you should develop it with rapture; and you should develop it without rapture.
You should develop it accompanied by pleasure; you should develop it accompanied by equanimity.
When, monk, this concentration has been thus developed and well-developed by you, then you should train yourself thus:
"May my mind-liberation through compassion..."
‘May my liberation of mind through sympathetic joy… may my liberation of mind through equanimity be developed by me, cultivated, made a vehicle, made a foundation, established, consolidated,
and well undertaken. In this way, bhikkhu, you should train yourself.
When, monk, this concentration has been developed by you in this way and well-developed, then, monk, you should develop this concentration both with applied thought and sustained thought;

you should develop it without applied thought and with sustained thought only; you should develop it without applied thought and without sustained thought; you should develop it with rapture; and you should develop it without rapture.
You should develop it accompanied by pleasure; you should also develop it accompanied by equanimity.
When, monk, this concentration has been thus developed and well-developed by you, then you should train yourself thus:
“I will dwell contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.”
In this way, bhikkhu, you should train yourself. When, bhikkhu,
this concentration has been thus developed and cultivated by you, then, bhikkhu,
you should develop this concentration both with applied thought and sustained thought, and you should also develop it without applied thought and with sustained thought only.
"You may develop it without applied thought and sustained thought; you may develop it with rapture; you may develop it without rapture;
you may develop it accompanied by pleasure; you may develop it accompanied by equanimity.
When, monk, this concentration has been thus developed and well-developed by you, then you should train yourself thus: "

‘I shall dwell contemplating feelings in feelings … the mind in the mind … phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.’
In this way, bhikkhu, you should train yourself.
When this concentration has been thus developed and cultivated by you, bhikkhu, then you should develop this concentration with both applied thought and sustained thought;
you should also develop it without applied thought and with sustained thought only.
You may develop it without applied thought and sustained thought; you may develop it with rapture; you may develop it without rapture;
you may develop it accompanied by pleasure; you may develop it accompanied by equanimity.
When, monk, this concentration has been developed by you in this way and well-developed, then, monk, from that...
"Wherever you go, you will go in comfort; wherever you stand, you will stand in comfort;
wherever you sit, you will sit in comfort; wherever you lie down, you will lie down in comfort."

Then that bhikkhu, having been exhorted by the Blessed One with this exhortation, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to his right, departed. Then, dwelling alone, withdrawn,
diligent, ardent, and resolute, that bhikkhu in no long time realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life,
that unsurpassed consummation of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness.
Having realized it for himself through direct higher knowledge in this very life, he entered and dwelt therein.
He directly knew: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
And that bhikkhu became one of the arahants.
The Third [Sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.64.
7. The Chapter on Earthquakes (Bhūmicālavagga).
The Gayāsīsa Sutta (AN 8.64).
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Gayā on Gayāsīsa.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“… Formerly, bhikkhus, before my enlightenment, while I was still a bodhisatta, not yet fully enlightened, I perceived light but did not see forms.
Then, bhikkhus, this occurred to me:”
‘If indeed I were to perceive light and see forms,
then this knowledge and vision of mine would become even more purified.
Then, monks, dwelling at a later time diligent, ardent, and resolute, I perceived light and saw forms.
Yet I did not stand with those deities, converse with them, or engage in discussion with them.
Then, monks, this occurred to me:
"If only I were to perceive the radiance, see forms, and stand with those deities, converse with them, and engage in discussion with them."
‘In this way, may this knowledge and vision of mine become even more purified.
Then, monks, dwelling at a later time diligent, ardent, and resolute,
I perceived light and saw forms, and I stood, spoke, and engaged in conversation with those deities.
And yet, monks, those deities did not know:
"These deities belong to such-and-such or such-and-such divine host.
Then, monks, this occurred to me:
‘If indeed I were to perceive light and see forms, and were to stand together with those deities, converse with them, and engage in discussion with them,
and if I were to know those deities thus: “These deities belong to such-and-such or such-and-such divine host,” then this knowledge and vision of mine would become even more purified.’”
Then, monks, at a later time, dwelling diligent, ardent, and resolute,
I perceived a radiance and saw forms; I stood together with those deities, conversed with them,
and engaged in discussion with them, and I knew those deities:
‘These deities belong to such-and-such or such-and-such a class of gods,’ yet I do not know of those deities:
‘By the ripening of this karma, having passed away from here, these deities have been reborn there. …pe…
And I know those deities thus:
"These deities, as the result of this karma, having passed away from here, have been reborn there";
yet I do not know those deities [in this way]:
‘These deities, as the result of this karma, have such food and experience such pleasure and pain’ … [and so on] … and I know those deities:
‘These deities, as the result of this karma, have such food and experience such pleasure and pain.’
And yet I do not know those deities:
"These deities have such a long life span and endure for such a long time"... [and so on]...
and I do know those deities:
‘These deities have such a long life-span and endure for so long’;
yet I did not know whether I had previously lived together with these deities or not.
Then, monks, this occurred to me:
‘If indeed I were to perceive light, see forms, and stand together with those deities, converse with them, and engage in discussion with them; and if I were to know those deities:
“These deities belong to such and such a divine host”; and if I were to know those deities:
“By the ripening of this karma, these deities have passed away from here and been reborn there”; and if I were to know those deities:’
“May I know these deities thus: ‘These deities have such food and experience such pleasure and pain’; may I know those deities thus:
‘These deities have such a long life-span and endure for such a long time’; and may I know whether I have previously dwelt together with these deities or not;
in this way, this knowledge and vision of mine would become even more purified.”
Then, monks, as I was dwelling at a later time— heedful, ardent, and resolute—
I perceived a radiance and saw forms; I stood together with those deities, conversed with them,
and engaged in discussion with them, and I knew those deities:
‘These deities belong to such-and-such or such-and-such a class of gods,’ and I know those deities:
‘By the ripening of this karma, these deities have passed away from here and been reborn there,’ and I know those deities:
‘These deities have such food and experience such pleasure and pain,’ and I know those deities:
‘These deities have such a long life-span and endure for such a long time,’ and I know those deities whether I had previously dwelt together with them or not.
As long as, monks, this knowledge and vision regarding the higher gods in its eightfold cycle was not thoroughly purified for me, so long, monks, did I not claim:
‘In this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins…’ [I did not claim to have attained supreme enlightenment].
“I have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment for the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, for this generation with its recluses and brahmins,” I declared.
And when, monks, this knowledge and vision regarding the eightfold turning had become thoroughly purified for me, then, monks, [I knew]:
“In this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās...”
“I declared, ‘I have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment for the generation of beings, including gods and humans’;
knowledge and vision arose within me:
my deliverance of mind is unshakable; this is the final birth, now there is no further becoming.”
The Fourth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.65.
7. The Chapter on Earthquakes (Bhūmicālavagga).
Abhibhāyatanasutta (AN 8.65, PTS AN iv 305):
“Monks, there are these eight bases of mastery.”
What are the eight?
One percipient of forms internally sees forms externally as limited, beautiful or ugly.
Having mastered them, one perceives: "I know, I see. Such is his perception.
This is the first base of mastery.
Perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are immeasurable, beautiful and ugly;
having mastered them, one perceives: "I know, I see. This is how one has such a perception.
This is the second base of mastery.
Internally perceiving no form, one sees external forms that are limited, beautiful or ugly;
having mastered them, one perceives: "I know, I see. This is how one has such a perception.
This is the third base of mastery.
Not perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are immeasurable, beautiful and ugly.
Having mastered them, one perceives: "I know, I see. Thus is one percipient.
This is the fourth base of mastery.
Not perceiving forms internally, one sees forms externally that are blue, blue-colored, blue-appearing, and blue-luminous.
Having mastered them, one perceives: "I know, I see. Such is his perception.
This is the fifth base of mastery.
Not perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are yellow, yellow in color, yellow in appearance, and yellow in luster.
Having mastered them, one perceives: "I know, I see. Thus is his perception.
This is the sixth base of mastery.
Not perceiving forms internally, one sees forms externally that are red, red in color, red in appearance, and red in luster.
Having mastered them, one perceives: "I know, I see. Such is his perception.
This is the seventh base of mastery.
Not perceiving forms internally, one sees forms externally that are white, of white color, white in appearance, and white in luster.
Having mastered them, one perceives: "I know, I see. Such is his perception.
This is the eighth base of mastery.
These, monks, are the eight bases of mastery. Thus ends the fifth [discourse].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.66 7.
Bhūmicālavagga Vimokkhasutta (The Discourse on Liberation)
“Monks, there are these eight liberations.
What are the eight?
Possessing form, one sees forms.
This is the first liberation.
Not perceiving form internally, one sees forms externally.
This is the second liberation.
He is intent upon the beautiful alone;
this is the third liberation.

With the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, and with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, thinking "space is infinite," one enters and dwells in the base of infinite space.
This is the fourth liberation.
With the complete surmounting of the base of infinite space, thinking "consciousness is infinite," one enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness.
This is the fifth liberation.
By completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, thinking "there is nothing," one enters and dwells in the base of nothingness.
This is the sixth liberation.
Having completely transcended the base of nothingness, he enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
This is the seventh liberation.
Having completely transcended the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling.
This is the eighth liberation.
These, monks, are the eight liberations. Thus ends the sixth [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.67 7.

Bhūmicālavagga Anariyavohārasutta (The Noble Discourse on Un-Aryan Modes of Speech) "Bhikkhus, there are these four un-Aryan modes of speech. What four? Speaking falsely, speaking divisively, speaking harshly, and speaking idle chatter. These, bhikkhus, are the four un-Aryan modes of speech. Bhikkhus, there are these four Aryan modes of speech. What four? Speaking truthfully, speaking harmoniously, speaking gently, and speaking meaningful words. These, bhikkhus, are the four Aryan modes of speech."
“Bhikkhus, there are these eight ignoble modes of speech. What eight? [The text continues with the list.]”

Claiming to have seen what was not seen; claiming to have heard what was not heard; claiming to have sensed what was not sensed; claiming to have cognized what was not cognized; claiming not to have seen what was seen; claiming not to have heard what was heard; claiming not to have sensed what was sensed; claiming not to have cognized what was cognized.
These, monks, are the eight ignoble modes of speech. Thus ends the seventh [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.68 7. Bhūmicālavagga Ariyavohārasutta (The Noble Modes of Speech) "Bhikkhus, there are these four noble modes of speech. What four? 'When one has seen, one says, "I have seen"; when one has heard, one says, "I have heard"; when one has sensed, one says, "I have sensed";

when one has cognized, one says, "I have cognized. These, bhikkhus, are the four noble modes of speech. Bhikkhus, for one who speaks thus, no fault arises; for one who speaks otherwise, a fault arises. Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus: "We will speak in such a way that no fault arises in us. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that you should train yourselves. Then, while this discourse was being spoken, the earth shook. At that time, the Venerable Ānanda thought: 'It is wonderful, it is marvelous! How the earth shakes even while this discourse is being spoken! Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: 'Ānanda, did you think: "It is wonderful, it is marvelous! How the earth shakes even while this discourse is being spoken"? 'It was so, Blessed One. 'Ānanda, there are eight causes, eight conditions for the shaking of the earth. What eight? This great earth, Ānanda, is established upon water; the water is established upon wind; the wind is established upon space. And at times, Ānanda, a great wind blows; when the great wind blows, it agitates the water; when the water is agitated, it shakes the earth. This, Ānanda, is the first cause, the first condition for the shaking of the earth. Furthermore, Ānanda, when a bodhisatta descends from the Tusita heaven into his mother’s womb, at that time the earth shakes and trembles and quakes violently. This, Ānanda, is the second cause... Furthermore, Ānanda, when a bodhisatta emerges from his mother’s womb, at that time the earth shakes and trembles and quakes violently. This, Ānanda, is the third cause... Furthermore, Ānanda, when a Tathāgata attains supreme enlightenment in the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, at that time the earth shakes and trembles and quakes violently. This, Ānanda, is the fourth cause... Furthermore, Ānanda, when a Tathāgata sets in motion the wheel of the Dhamma that has not been set in motion by any ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world, at that time the earth shakes and trembles and quakes violently. This, Ānanda, is the fifth cause... Furthermore, Ānanda, when a Tathāgata, through the destruction of the taints, realizes for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered it, dwells therein, at that time the earth shakes and trembles and quakes violently. This, Ānanda, is the sixth cause... Furthermore, Ānanda, when a Tathāgata, having attained final Nibbāna through the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining, passes away, at that time the earth shakes and trembles and quakes violently. This, Ānanda, is the seventh cause... Furthermore, Ānanda, when a Sangha of bhikkhus, having split, later reconciles, at that time the earth shakes and trembles and quakes violently. This, Ānanda, is the eighth cause, the eighth condition for the shaking of the earth. These, Ānanda, are the eight causes, the eight conditions for the shaking of the earth. And while this discourse was being spoken, the earth shook. "
“Bhikkhus, there are these eight noble modes of speech.
What are the eight?

“Bhikkhus, there are these eight noble modes of speech: speaking of what has not been seen as ‘not seen’; speaking of what has not been heard as ‘not heard’; speaking of what has not been sensed as ‘not sensed’; speaking of what has not been cognized as ‘not cognized’; speaking of what has been seen as ‘seen’; speaking of what has been heard as ‘heard’; speaking of what has been sensed as ‘sensed’; speaking of what has been cognized as ‘cognized.
These, bhikkhus, are the eight noble modes of speech. The eighth.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.69 7. Bhūmicālavagga Parisāsutta “Monks, there are these eight assemblies. What eight? The assembly of Khattiyas, the assembly of Brahmins, the assembly of householders, the assembly of ascetics, the assembly of Cātumahārājika devas, the assembly of Tāvatiṃsa devas, the assembly of Māras, and the assembly of Brahmās. These, monks, are the eight assemblies. When a noble disciple possesses four things, he enters upon the certainty of rightness and is no longer subject to decline. What four? He possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally realized by the wise. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. He possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones: unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, freeing, praised by the wise, ungrasped, leading to concentration. When a noble disciple possesses these four things, he enters upon the certainty of rightness and is no longer subject to decline.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these eight assemblies. Which eight? [The text continues with the enumeration of the eight assemblies.]”

The assembly of kṣatriyas, the assembly of brahmins, the assembly of householders, the assembly of ascetics, the assembly of the Four Great Kings, the assembly of the Thirty-three Gods, the assembly of Māra, and the assembly of Brahmā.
Indeed, monks, I recall having approached many hundreds of assemblies of kṣatriyas;
there too, I have previously sat together, conversed, and engaged in discussion.
In that regard, whatever their complexion was, such was my complexion; whatever their voice was, such was my voice.
I instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened them with a discourse on the Dhamma.
And while I was speaking, they did not know me:
‘Who is this speaking? Is it a god or a human?
Having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened them with a discourse on the Dhamma, I vanish.
And when I have vanished, they do not know me.
‘Who is this who has vanished—is he a deva or a human?
Furthermore, monks, I recall having addressed an assembly of many hundreds of brahmins...
[and so on] ...an assembly of householders...
the assembly of recluses … the assembly of the Four Great Kings … the assembly of the Thirty-three Gods …
I have approached the assembly of Māra... and the assembly of Brahmā.
There too, I have previously sat together, conversed, and engaged in discussion.
In that regard, whatever their complexion was, such was my complexion; whatever their voice was, such was my voice.
I instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened them with a discourse on the Dhamma.
And while I was speaking, they did not know me:
‘Who is this speaking? Is it a god or a human?
Having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened them with a discourse on the Dharma, I vanish.
And when I have vanished, they do not know me.
‘Who indeed is this who has vanished—is he a deva or a human?
These, monks, are the eight assemblies.
This is the ninth [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.70 7.
Bhūmicālavagga Bhūmicālasutta (The Earthquake Sutta)
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Gabled Hall.
Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Vesālī for alms.
Having walked for alms in Vesālī, after his meal, returning from his alms round, he addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Take your sitting mat, Ānanda;
we shall go to the Cāpāla Shrine for the day’s rest.
“Very well, Bhante,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One, and taking his sitting mat, he followed closely behind the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One went to the Cāpāla Shrine; having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Delightful, Ānanda, is Vesālī; delightful is the Udena Shrine; delightful is the Gotamaka Shrine.”
The Sattamba Cetiya is delightful, the Bahuputtaka Cetiya is delightful, the Sārandada Cetiya is delightful, and the Cāpāla Cetiya is delightful.

For anyone, Ānanda, who has developed, cultivated, mastered, established, consolidated, and properly undertaken the four bases for psychic power, if he so desires, Ānanda, he could remain for an eon or for the remainder of an eon.
“Ānanda, the four bases for spiritual power have been developed, cultivated, made a vehicle, made a foundation, established, consolidated, and properly undertaken by the Tathāgata.
If he so desired, Ānanda, the Tathāgata could remain for an eon, or for the remainder of an eon.
Yet even when the Blessed One was making such a gross sign and providing such a gross indication, the Venerable Ānanda was unable to penetrate it.
He did not entreat the Blessed One, saying:

"Venerable sir, may the Blessed One remain for an eon; may the Sugata remain for an eon for the welfare of many people, for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans," because his mind was obsessed by Māra.
A second time also, the Blessed One... [as before]...
A third time, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:

“Delightful, Ānanda, is Vesālī; delightful is the Udena Shrine, delightful is the Gotamaka Shrine, delightful is the Sattamba Shrine, delightful is the Bahuputta Shrine, and delightful is the Sārandada Shrine.”
“There is the Cāpāla Shrine, Ānanda, the delightful Cāpāla Shrine.

For anyone, Ānanda, whose four bases for psychic power have been developed, cultivated, made a vehicle, made a foundation, established, consolidated, and properly undertaken—if he so desired, Ānanda, he could remain for an eon or for the remainder of an eon.
Now, Ānanda, the Tathāgata’s four bases for psychic power have been developed … [as above] … if he so desired, Ānanda, the Tathāgata could remain for an eon or for the remainder of an eon.”
In this way, although the Blessed One gave such a gross hint and such a gross indication, the Venerable Ānanda was unable to penetrate it;
he did not entreat the Blessed One, saying:

"May the Blessed One remain, O Lord, for an eon! May the Sugata remain for an eon, for the welfare of many people, for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans," because his mind was possessed by Māra.
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Go, Ānanda, at whatever time you deem appropriate.

“Very well, Bhante,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One. Rising from his seat, he paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping him to his right, and sat down at the foot of a certain tree not far from the Blessed One.
Then, not long after the Venerable Ānanda had departed, Māra the Evil One said this to the Blessed One:
“May the Blessed One now attain final Nibbāna, may the Sugata now attain final Nibbāna. Now is the time for the Blessed One’s final Nibbāna, venerable sir.
For these words were indeed spoken by the Blessed One:”
“Evil One, I shall not attain final nibbāna as long as my bhikkhu disciples are not yet accomplished—
trained, confident, secure in the attainment of safety, learned, bearers of the Dhamma, practicing in accordance with the Dhamma, practicing with proper conduct, living in conformity with the Dhamma—
and having mastered their own teacher’s instruction, they will proclaim it, teach it, and set it forth.”
‘They will establish, reveal, analyze, and clarify it; having thoroughly refuted with reasoned argument any opposing doctrines that have arisen, they will teach the Dhamma accompanied by miracles.
Venerable sir, at present the bhikkhus who are the Blessed One’s disciples are discerning, disciplined, confident, and have attained security from bondage.
They are learned, bearers of the Dhamma, practitioners of the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma, practitioners of proper conduct, and followers of the Dhamma.
Having mastered their own teachers’ tradition, they explain, teach, describe, establish, disclose, analyze, and clarify it.
Having thoroughly refuted, by means of the Dhamma, the doctrines of others that have arisen, they teach the Dhamma accompanied by wonders.
“May the Blessed One now attain final nibbāna, venerable sir; may the Sugata now attain final nibbāna. The time for the Blessed One’s final nibbāna has now come, venerable sir.
For this word was indeed spoken by the Blessed One:
‘I shall not attain final nibbāna, O Evil One, as long as my bhikkhunīs have not become disciples... [and so on].
Until my male lay followers become disciples...
[and so on] ...until my female lay followers become female disciples— disciples who are proficient, disciplined, confident, attained to security from bondage, learned, bearers of the Dhamma,
practitioners of the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma, practitioners of the proper way, and followers of the Dhamma, each maintaining their own teacher’s tradition.
‘Having mastered them, they will declare, teach, proclaim, establish, reveal, analyze, and clarify them;
and having thoroughly refuted with reasoned argument any opposing doctrines that have arisen,
they will teach the Dhamma accompanied by its miraculous demonstration.’”
At present, Bhante, there are female lay disciples who are the Blessed One’s followers— discerning, disciplined, confident, having attained security from bondage, learned, bearers of the Dhamma,
practicing in accordance with the Dhamma, practicing with propriety, and living according to the Dhamma— who,
having mastered their own teacher’s instruction, declare it, teach it, describe it, establish it, reveal it, and analyze it.
They clarify [the teaching], and having thoroughly refuted arisen doctrines of others with reasoned arguments, they teach the Dhamma accompanied by miracles.

Then, at the Cāpāla Shrine, the Blessed One—mindful and clearly comprehending—relinquished the life-force.
When the Blessed One had relinquished the life-force, there was a great earthquake, terrifying and hair-raising, and the divine drums resounded.
Then the Blessed One, having understood this matter, on that occasion uttered this inspired utterance:
“The measurable and the immeasurable, and their arising...”
The Sage relinquished the formative force of existence;
delighting within himself and composed,
he shattered his own rebirth like a coat of mail.
Then it occurred to the Venerable Ānanda:
"This is indeed a great earthquake!
This is truly a very great earthquake, terrifying and hair-raising, and the drums of the gods have resounded."
“What, indeed, is the cause, what is the reason for the manifestation of this great earthquake?

Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
“This earthquake, Bhante, is truly great.”
“Venerable sir, this great earthquake has indeed been most terrifying, hair-raising, and the divine drums have resounded.
What, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the reason for the manifestation of such a great earthquake?
“Ānanda, there are these eight causes, these eight reasons for the manifestation of a great earthquake.”
Which eight?
This great earth, Ānanda, is established upon water; the water is established upon wind; the wind is established upon space.
There comes a time, Ānanda, when great winds blow; the great winds blowing cause the water to tremble;
Water that has been shaken causes the earth to shake.
This, Ānanda, is the first cause, the first condition for the manifestation of a great earthquake.
Furthermore, Ānanda, a recluse or a brahmin who possesses psychic power and has attained mastery over the mind, or a deity of great psychic power—
He is of great power. He has developed a limited perception of earth and an immeasurable perception of water.
He causes this earth to tremble, to shake, to quiver, and to quake.
This, Ānanda, is the second cause, the second condition for the manifestation of a great earthquake.
Furthermore, Ānanda, when the Bodhisatta, mindful and clearly comprehending, descends from the Tusita realm into his mother’s womb, then this earth shakes, trembles, and quakes violently.
This, Ānanda, is the third cause, the third condition for the manifestation of a great earthquake.
Furthermore, Ānanda, when the Bodhisatta, mindful and clearly comprehending, emerges from his mother’s womb, then this earth shakes, trembles, and quakes violently.
This, Ānanda, is the fourth cause, the fourth condition for the manifestation of a great earthquake.
Furthermore, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata awakens to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, then this earth shakes, trembles, quakes, and convulses.
This, Ānanda, is the fifth cause, the fifth condition for the manifestation of a great earthquake.
Furthermore, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata sets in motion the unsurpassed Wheel of Dhamma, then this earth shakes, trembles, quakes, and shudders.
This, Ānanda, is the sixth cause, the sixth condition for the manifestation of a great earthquake.
Furthermore, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata, mindful and clearly comprehending, relinquishes the life-force, then this earth shakes, trembles, quakes, and shudders.
This, Ānanda, is the seventh cause, the seventh condition for the manifestation of a great earthquake.
Furthermore, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata passes away into the Nibbāna-element without remainder, then this earth shakes, trembles, quakes, and convulses.
This, Ānanda, is the eighth cause, the eighth condition for the manifestation of a great earthquake.
“Ānanda, these are the eight causes and eight conditions for the manifestation of a great earthquake.

“Monks, a monk may have faith, yet he is not virtuous.
In this way, he is incomplete with respect to that factor.
Therefore, he should fulfill that factor:”
‘But how might I be both endowed with faith and possessed of virtue?
But when, monks, a monk is both endowed with faith and possessed of virtue,
he is thus complete in that factor.
"Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu may be endowed with faith and virtuous, yet not learned.
In this way, he is incomplete in that factor.
Therefore, he should fulfill that factor: [thus it should be said]."
‘But how might I be endowed with faith, virtuous, and learned?
But when, monks, a monk is indeed endowed with faith, virtuous, and learned,
he is thus fulfilled in that respect.
“Monks, a monk may be endowed with faith and virtuous, and he may be learned, yet he is not an expounder of the Dhamma...
[and so on] ...he may be an expounder of the Dhamma, yet he does not frequent assemblies...
[and so on] ...he may frequent assemblies, yet he does not teach the Dhamma confidently in an assembly... [and so on]...”

He teaches the Dhamma confidently in the assembly, yet he does not gain at will, without difficulty, and without trouble, the four jhānas that are higher mental states providing a pleasant dwelling in this very life;

... [and so on] ... he gains at will, without difficulty, and without trouble, the four jhānas that are higher mental states providing a pleasant dwelling in this very life, yet he does not, through the destruction of the taints, realize for himself in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom.
He dwells having realized it for himself through direct knowledge and attained it;
thus, he is incomplete in that factor.
Therefore, that factor must be fulfilled:
‘But what if I were to be endowed with faith, virtuous, learned, a speaker on the Dhamma, one who frequents assemblies, and confident enough to teach the Dhamma in an assembly;
and if I were to be one who gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the four jhānas that constitute higher mental states and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life;
and if, through the destruction of the taints, I were to realize for myself the taintless liberation of mind?’
‘May I, by realizing it for myself with direct knowledge, enter and dwell in liberation through wisdom in this very life.
But when, monks, a monk is endowed with faith, virtuous, learned, a speaker of the Dhamma, one who frequents assemblies,
and confidently teaches the Dhamma to an assembly, and [possesses] the four jhānas that constitute higher mental states—
He is one who obtains at will, without difficulty, and without trouble, those pleasant dwellings in this very life;
and with the destruction of the taints, having realized for himself through direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom,
he enters and dwells therein.
"In this way, he is complete in that respect.
Indeed, monks, a monk endowed with these eight qualities is one who inspires universal confidence and is complete in every aspect. Thus was the first [discourse].

(AN 8.73, PTS AN iv 316) On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Nādika in the Brick Hall.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Monks,” [he said].
“Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One spoke as follows:
“Bhikkhus, mindfulness of death, when developed and cultivated, is of great fruit and great benefit; it plunges into the Deathless and culminates in the Deathless.
Develop mindfulness of death, bhikkhus.
When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, I indeed cultivate mindfulness of death.
“But how, monk, do you cultivate mindfulness of death?
“Here, venerable sir, this occurs to me:”
“‘Oh, may I live for a day and night! May I attend to the Blessed One’s teaching; much indeed would have been accomplished by me.
It is in this way, Bhante, that I develop mindfulness of death.
Then another bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, I too cultivate mindfulness of death.
“But how, monk, do you cultivate mindfulness of death?
“Here, venerable sir, this occurs to me:”

Thus, Bhante, do I develop mindfulness of death.
Another bhikkhu also said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, I too cultivate mindfulness of death.
