“Venerable sir, I too cultivate mindfulness of death.
“But in what way, monk, do you cultivate mindfulness of death?
“Here, venerable sir, this occurs to me:”
"‘Oh, may I live for just as long as it takes to chew and swallow a single mouthful of food, so that I might attend to the Blessed One’s teaching; indeed, much would have been accomplished by me!
It is in this way, Bhante, that I develop mindfulness of death.
Then another bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, I too cultivate mindfulness of death.
“But how, monk, do you cultivate mindfulness of death?
“Here, venerable sir, this occurs to me:”

“‘Oh, may I live for just the interval between an inhalation and an exhalation, or between an exhalation and an inhalation, so that I might attend to the Blessed One’s teaching; much indeed would have been accomplished by me!
It is in this way, Bhante, that I develop mindfulness of death.
When this was said, the Blessed One addressed those bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, there is this bhikkhu who develops mindfulness of death thus:
‘O, may I live for a day and night, so that I might attend to the Blessed One’s teaching; much indeed would have been accomplished by me.
And there is this other bhikkhu, bhikkhus, who develops mindfulness of death thus:”
‘Oh, may I live for a whole day so that I might attend to the Blessed One’s teaching; much indeed would be accomplished by me!
And there is, monks, this other monk who develops mindfulness of death thus:
‘Oh, may I live for half a day so that I might attend to the Blessed One’s teaching; much indeed would be accomplished by me!’”
And as for the bhikkhu, monks, who develops mindfulness of death thus:
"O, may I live just long enough to eat a single alms-meal, to attend to the Blessed One’s teaching, and much indeed would have been accomplished by me";
and as for the bhikkhu, monks, who develops mindfulness of death thus: [further elaborations].

“O, may I live for as long as it takes to eat half an alms-meal, so that I might attend to the Blessed One’s teaching; much indeed would have been accomplished by me! And, monks, when a bhikkhu develops mindfulness of death in this way: “O, may I live for as long as it takes to chew and swallow four or five mouthfuls, so that I might attend to the Blessed One’s teaching; much indeed would have been accomplished by me!”—this is called a bhikkhu who develops mindfulness of death with a short range. This is called a bhikkhu who develops mindfulness of death with a medium range.

This is called a bhikkhu who develops mindfulness of death with a long range. Monks, when a bhikkhu develops mindfulness of death in this way: “O, may I live for as long as it takes to chew and swallow one mouthful after another, so that I might attend to the Blessed One’s teaching; much indeed would have been accomplished by me!”—this is called a bhikkhu who develops mindfulness of death with a very short range. Monks, when a bhikkhu develops mindfulness of death in this way: “O, may I live for as long as it takes to breathe out after breathing in, or to breathe in after breathing out, so that I might attend to the Blessed One’s teaching; much indeed would have been accomplished by me!”—this is called a bhikkhu who develops mindfulness of death with an extremely short range. Monks, a bhikkhu who develops mindfulness of death with an extremely short range is close to nibbāna. Why is that? Because, monks, mindfulness of death, when developed and cultivated, leads to a supreme sense of urgency, leads to supreme spiritual arousal, leads to supreme seclusion, leads to supreme non-delusion, leads to the attainment of the unattained, leads to the realization of the unrealized, leads to the final knowledge of the unknown, and leads to final nibbāna.

Therefore, monks, you should develop mindfulness of death in this way: “O, may I live for as long as it takes to breathe out after breathing in, or to breathe in after breathing out, so that I might attend to the Blessed One’s teaching; much indeed would have been accomplished by me! Thus should you train yourselves.’”
“Monks, these are called ‘monks who dwell negligently; they develop mindfulness of death sluggishly for the destruction of the taints.
But as for that monk, monks, who develops mindfulness of death thus:

‘O, may I live just the length of time it takes to chew and swallow a single mouthful of food, so that I might attend to the Blessed One’s teaching; indeed, much would have been accomplished by me’—this, monks, is called a monk who develops mindfulness of death ardently for the destruction of the taints.”
And as for the bhikkhu, monks, who develops mindfulness of death thus:
“O, may I live just the length of time it takes to breathe out after breathing in, or to breathe in after breathing out, so that I may attend to the Blessed One’s teaching;
much indeed would have been accomplished by me”—these, monks, are called bhikkhus who dwell heedfully, developing keen mindfulness of death for the sake of the destruction of the taints.
"Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus:
'We will dwell heedfully; we will develop keen mindfulness of death for the sake of the destruction of the taints.
It is in this way, bhikkhus, that you should train yourselves."
Third.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.74 8.
The Chapter on Pairs (Yamakavagga)
The Second Discourse on Mindfulness of Death (AN 8.74).
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Nādika in the Brick Hall.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“… Bhikkhus, mindfulness of death, when developed and cultivated, is of great fruit and great benefit; it plunges into the Deathless and culminates in the Deathless.
And how, bhikkhus, is mindfulness of death developed and cultivated so that it is of great fruit and great benefit, plunging into the Deathless and culminating in the Deathless?”
In this case, monks, when the day has passed and night has arrived, a monk reflects thus:
"There are many conditions for my death:
a snake might bite me, a scorpion might sting me, or a centipede might bite me."
Because of that, my death would come about; it would be an obstacle for me.

I might stumble and fall into a precipice, or the food I have eaten might cause illness, or bile might be provoked in me, or phlegm might be provoked in me, or the wind-humors might be provoked in me, or humans might attack me.
"Non-human beings might attack me;
because of that, my death would come about; that would be an obstacle for me.
Monks, that monk should reflect thus:
‘Are there, indeed, any evil unwholesome states not yet abandoned in me that might become an obstacle for me as I am passing away during the night?
Monks, if, upon reviewing, a monk knows thus:
‘There are evil unwholesome states not yet abandoned in me that might become an obstacle for me as I am passing away during the night,’ [he should strive to abandon them].”

Therefore, monks, that bhikkhu must apply intense desire, effort, exertion, perseverance, undauntedness, mindfulness, and clear comprehension for the sake of abandoning those very same evil, unwholesome states.
It is just as if one’s clothes were on fire, or one’s head were on fire; [one would act] for the sake of that very garment or that very head.
He should exercise an intense desire, effort, exertion, perseverance, indefatigability, mindfulness,
and clear comprehension for their extinguishing;
even so, monks, should that bhikkhu [deal] with those very same evil, unwholesome states.
For the sake of abandoning [them], there must be intense desire, effort, exertion, perseverance, indefatigability, mindfulness,
and clear comprehension. But if, monks, while examining himself, a monk knows thus:
‘There are no evil, unwholesome states that have not been abandoned by me which might become an obstacle for me as I am passing away during the night,’ with this,
monks, that bhikkhu should dwell in joy and gladness, training day and night in wholesome states. Furthermore, monks,
when the night has passed and the day has dawned, a bhikkhu reflects thus:
‘There are indeed many conditions for my death:
a snake might bite me, a scorpion might sting me, or a centipede might sting me;
by that I would meet my end. That would be an obstacle for me.’
"I might stumble and fall, or the food I have eaten might cause illness, or bile might be disturbed in me,
or phlegm might be disturbed in me, or the wind-humors might be disturbed in me,
or humans might attack me, or non-humans might attack me."
“Because of that, my death would come about;
that would be an obstacle for me. Monks, that monk should reflect thus:
“Are there indeed any evil, unwholesome states not yet abandoned by me that might become an obstacle for me if I were to die during the day?”
If, monks, while reflecting, a monk knows thus: "There are evil,
unwholesome states not yet abandoned by me which would be an obstacle for me were I to die during the day," then,
monks, that monk should apply himself with excessive effort for the abandoning of those very same evil, unwholesome states.
Zeal, effort, exertion, perseverance, indefatigability, mindfulness, and clear comprehension must be exercised. Just as, monks,
one whose clothes are on fire or whose head is on fire would apply excessive zeal,
effort, exertion, perseverance, indefatigability, and mindfulness solely for the purpose of extinguishing those very clothes or that very head;
And he should maintain clear comprehension.
In the same way, monks, that bhikkhu should have intense desire, effort, exertion, ardor, indefatigability, and mindfulness for the abandoning of those very same evil, unwholesome states.
And full awareness should be maintained.
But if, monks, while reflecting, a monk knows thus:
"There are no evil, unwholesome states unabandoned by me that might be an obstacle for me were I to die during the day," [he may rest assured].
"Therefore, bhikkhus, that bhikkhu should dwell with that very same rapture and gladness, training day and night in wholesome states.
Thus developed, bhikkhus, thus cultivated, mindfulness of death is of great fruit and great benefit; it has the Deathless as its ground and the Deathless as its consummation.
The fourth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.75 8.

Yamaka-vagga First Discourse on Accomplishment (Paṭhama-sampadā-sutta) "Bhikkhus, there are these eight accomplishments. What eight? Accomplishment in faith, accomplishment in virtuous behavior, accomplishment in learning, accomplishment in generosity, accomplishment in wisdom, accomplishment in loving-kindness, accomplishment in compassion, and accomplishment in sympathetic joy. These, bhikkhus, are the eight accomplishments."
“Monks, there are these eight accomplishments.
What eight?
Perfection in exertion, perfection in protection, good friendship, balanced livelihood, perfection in faith, perfection in virtue,
perfection in generosity, and perfection in wisdom— these, monks, are the eight perfections.
One who exerts himself in the fields of action...
Diligent and methodical,
he makes his livelihood balanced and guards his accumulated store.
Endowed with faith, perfected in virtue,
generous and free from stinginess,
one constantly purifies the path.
And security for the future life—
these eight qualities belong to the faithful seeker of the household life.
Proclaimed under the name of Truth,
it brings happiness in both worlds;
for the sake of welfare and benefit in this very life, it is taught.
And for the sake of happiness in the future life;
thus, for householders,
through generosity, merit increases.”
Fifth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.76 8.
Yamaka Chapter (The Book of the Pairs)
The Discourse on the Second Attainment (Dutiyasampadāsutta): “Monks,
there are these eight attainments.”
What are the eight?

Accomplishment in initiative, accomplishment in protection, good friendship, balanced livelihood, accomplishment in faith, accomplishment in virtue, accomplishment in generosity, and accomplishment in wisdom.
And what, monks, is accomplishment in initiative?
In this case, monks, a clansman maintains his life by means of a certain craft—
whether by agriculture, commerce, cattle-herding, archery, government service, or some other craft—
in which he is skillful and diligent, endowed with the necessary wisdom, capable of performing and capable of providing.
This, monks, is called accomplishment in exertion.
And what, monks, is accomplishment in protection?

Here, monks, a clansman possesses wealth acquired through exertion and energy, gathered by the strength of his arms, earned by the sweat of his brow, righteous, and righteously obtained; he brings that wealth to fulfillment through protection and guarding: [this is accomplishment in protection].
‘How may kings not take away my wealth, nor thieves take it, nor fire burn it, nor water sweep it away, nor unwelcome heirs take it?
This, monks, is called perfection in protection.
And what, monks, is good friendship?
In this case, monks, whatever village or town a clansman resides in, there he associates with, converses with,
and engages in discussion with those householders or householders’ sons— whether young but mature in character,
or old— who are endowed with faith, endowed with virtue, endowed with generosity, and endowed with wisdom.
He enters [upon this state]; he trains himself in the perfection of faith of those who are endowed with faith,
he trains himself in the perfection of virtue of those who are endowed with virtue, he trains himself in the perfection of generosity of those who are endowed with generosity,
and he trains himself in the perfection of wisdom of those who are endowed with wisdom.
This, monks, is called having virtuous friends.
And what, monks, is balanced living?
Here, monks, a clansman, having understood both the income of his wealth and the expenditure of his wealth, lives in balance.
He makes his living neither too high nor too low, [thinking]: "In this way my income will cover my expenses, and my expenses will not exceed my income.
Just as, monks, a scale-maker or a scale-maker’s apprentice, having held up the scale, knows: "By this much it has tilted down, or by this much it has tilted up."
In the same way, monks, a clansman, having understood the income of his wealth and having understood the expenditure of his wealth,
maintains a balanced livelihood— neither too extravagant nor too frugal— thinking: "In this way, my income will suffice for my expenditure, and my expenditure will not exceed my income."
“Bhikkhus, if this clansman has small income yet maintains a luxurious livelihood, there will be those who say of him: ‘This clansman eats his wealth like one eating figs.
But if this clansman has a large income yet maintains a frugal livelihood, there will be those who say of him: ‘This clansman will die an untimely death.
However, bhikkhus, when a clansman understands both the income of his wealth and the expenditure of his wealth, [he lives well].”
One maintains a livelihood that is balanced, neither excessive nor deficient, thinking: "In this way my income will suffice for my expenses, and my expenses will not exceed my income.
This, monks, is called balanced living.
And what, monks, is the accomplishment of faith?
Here, monks, a clansman is endowed with faith; he has faith in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata:
"Thus indeed is that Blessed One: ... [as above] ... the Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One."
This, monks, is called the perfection of faith.
And what, monks, is the perfection of virtue?
Here, monks, a clansman abstains from the destruction of life … [as above] … he abstains from the occasion for negligence consisting in fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants.
This, monks, is called accomplishment in virtue.
And what, monks, is accomplishment in generosity?
Here, monks, a clansman dwells at home with a mind free from the stain of stinginess, open-handed, delighting in relinquishment, devoted to charity, and fond of distributing gifts.
This, monks, is called the perfection of generosity.
And what, monks, is the perfection of wisdom?
Here, monks, a clansman is wise … [as before] … leading to the complete destruction of suffering.
This, monks, is called the perfection of wisdom.
These, monks, are the eight perfections.
One who exerts themselves in their fields of action...
Diligent and observant of the rules,
he maintains his livelihood with moderation and protects his accumulated store.
Endowed with faith, perfected in virtue,
generous and free from stinginess,
one constantly purifies the path.
And security for the life to come—
these eight qualities belong to the faithful seeker of the household life.
Proclaimed under the name of Truth,
it brings happiness in both worlds;
for the sake of welfare and benefit in this very life, it leads to the goal.
And for the sake of happiness in the future life;
thus, for householders,
through such giving, merit increases.”
The Sixth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.77 8.
The Chapter on Pairs (Yamakavagga)

In that place, the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus: “The Discourse on Wishes” (Icchāsutta). (AN 8.77, PTS AN iv 325) There, the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus: [“Friends, there are these three wishes...”]
“Friends, monks.
“Friend,” those monks replied to the Venerable Sāriputta.
The Venerable Sāriputta said this:
“Friends, these eight persons are found existing in the world.
Which eight?
Here, friends, while a bhikkhu is dwelling in seclusion and living independently, a desire arises for gain.
Thus he exerts himself, strives, and makes an effort for the sake of gain.
While he is exerting himself, striving, and making an effort for the sake of gain, no gain arises.
On account of that lack of gain, he sorrows, languishes, and laments; he weeps, beating his breast, and falls into confusion.

"Friends, this is called a bhikkhu who dwells desiring gain; he exerts himself, strives, and makes an effort for the sake of gain, yet he does not obtain it. He grieves and laments, fallen away from the true Dhamma.
But here, friends, while a bhikkhu is dwelling in seclusion and living independently, a desire arises for gain.
He exerts himself, strives, and makes an effort for the sake of gain."
As he exerts himself, strives, and makes an effort for the sake of gain, gain arises for him.
He becomes intoxicated by that gain, becomes negligent, and falls into heedlessness.

This, friends, is called a bhikkhu who dwells desiring gain, who exerts himself, strives, and makes an effort for the sake of gain, yet who, though having gained it, is intoxicated, negligent, and heedless, and has fallen away from the true Dhamma.
Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu dwells in seclusion, living independently, a desire for gain arises in him.
He does not exert himself, strive, or make an effort for the sake of gain.
Because he does not exert himself, strive, or make an effort for the sake of gain, no gain arises for him.
Thus, because of that lack of gain, he sorrows, becomes weary, and laments; he beats his breast and falls into confusion.

This, friends, is called a monk who dwells desiring gain, yet does not exert himself, strive, or make an effort for the sake of gain; he does not obtain gain, but sorrows and laments, and has fallen away from the true Dhamma.
But here, friends, when a monk dwells secluded and lives independently, a desire arises in him for gain.
Thus he does not exert himself, strive, or make an effort for the sake of gain.
While he does not exert himself, strive, or make an effort for the sake of gain, gain arises for him.
He becomes intoxicated by that gain, becomes negligent, and falls into heedlessness.

"Friends, this is called a bhikkhu who dwells desiring gain, yet does not exert himself, strive, or make an effort for the sake of gain; though he obtains gain, he is intoxicated and negligent, and has fallen away from the true Dhamma.
But here, friends, when a bhikkhu dwells in seclusion, living independently, a desire arises in him for gain.
He exerts himself, strives, and makes an effort for the sake of gain."
As he rises, strives, and exerts himself for the sake of gain, no gain arises.
Because of that lack of gain, he does not sorrow, does not languish, does not lament; he does not beat his breast and does not fall into confusion.

This, friends, is called a bhikkhu who dwells desiring gain, who rises, strives, and exerts himself for the sake of gain, yet is without gain, without sorrow, and without lamentation—one who has not fallen away from the true Dhamma.
"Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu dwells in seclusion, living independently, a desire arises in him for gain.
He exerts himself, strives, and makes an effort for the sake of gain.
As he exerts himself, strives, and makes an effort for the sake of gain, gain arises for him."
Thus, by means of that gain, he does not become intoxicated, does not become negligent, and does not fall into heedlessness.

This, friends, is called a bhikkhu who dwells desiring gain, who exerts himself, strives, and makes an effort for the sake of gain; and being one who obtains gain, he is neither intoxicated nor negligent, and he has not fallen away from the true Dhamma.
But here, friends, when a bhikkhu dwells in seclusion, living independently, a desire arises in him for gain.
Thus he does not exert himself, strive, or make an effort for the sake of gain.
Because he does not exert himself, strive, or make an effort for the sake of gain, gain does not arise for him.
On account of that lack of gain, he does not sorrow, does not become distressed, does not lament, does not beat his breast, and does not fall into confusion.

"Friends, this is called a monk who dwells desiring gain, yet he does not exert himself, strive, or make an effort for the sake of gain; he does not obtain gain, nor does he grieve or lament; and he has not fallen away from the true Dhamma.
Furthermore, friends, while a monk is dwelling in seclusion and living independently, a desire arises in him for gain.
He does not exert himself, strive, or make an effort for the sake of gain."
Though he does not strive, exert himself, or make an effort for the sake of gain, gain arises for him.
He is not intoxicated by that gain, does not become negligent, and does not fall into heedlessness.

This, friends, is called a bhikkhu who dwells with desire for gain, yet though he does not strive, exert himself, or make an effort for the sake of gain, he is nonetheless possessed of gain; he is neither intoxicated nor negligent, and he has not fallen away from the true Dhamma.
“Friends, these eight persons are found existing in the world.
The seventh [discourse]. *Aṅguttara Nikāya* 8.78.

8. Yamaka Vagga Alaṃ Sutta (Discourse on Enough) “Bhikkhus, there are these five things that are enough for a bhikkhu who has gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, to dwell at ease. What five? (1) ‘Enough for me today with the robe; let me dwell with contentment regarding the robe. (2) ‘Enough for me today with almsfood; let me dwell with contentment regarding almsfood. (3) ‘Enough for me today with lodging; let me dwell with contentment regarding lodging. (4) ‘Enough for me today with medicinal requisites for the sick; let me dwell with contentment regarding medicinal requisites. (5) ‘Enough for me today with the delight in non-affliction; let me dwell with contentment regarding the delight in non-affliction. These, bhikkhus, are the five things that are enough for a bhikkhu who has gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, to dwell at ease.”
There the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus:
“… Friends, a bhikkhu endowed with six qualities is capable of helping himself and capable of helping others.
With which six?
Here, friends, a bhikkhu is one of quick comprehension regarding wholesome states;
he is by nature capable of retaining the teachings he has heard;
and he is one who investigates the meaning of the teachings he has retained.
Having understood the meaning and understood the Dhamma, he practices in accordance with the Dhamma;
he is a good speaker, possessing a beautiful voice, endowed with speech that is polished, distinct, flawless, and expressive of the meaning;
and he is one who instructs, urges, inspires, and gladdens his fellow celibates.
"Friends, a bhikkhu endowed with these six qualities is capable of helping himself and capable of helping others.
Friends, a bhikkhu endowed with five qualities is capable of helping himself and capable of helping others.
With which five?"
Here, friends, a bhikkhu is not only quick to understand wholesome states,
but he is also capable of retaining the teachings he has heard,
and he is one who investigates the meaning of the teachings he has retained.
Having understood the goal and understood the Dhamma, he practices in accordance with the Dhamma;
he is a speaker of what is beautiful...
[and so on] ...he is one who instructs his fellow celibates.
"Friends, a bhikkhu endowed with these five qualities is capable of helping himself and capable of helping others.
Friends, a bhikkhu endowed with four qualities is capable of helping himself, but not capable of helping others.
With which four?"
Here, friends, a bhikkhu is one of quick intuition regarding wholesome states;
he is naturally disposed to retain the teachings he has heard;
and he is one who investigates the meaning of the teachings he has retained.
Having understood the meaning and understood the Dhamma, one practices in accordance with the Dhamma;
yet one is not a speaker of what is good … nor is one an instructor of one’s fellow celibates.
"Friends, a bhikkhu endowed with these four qualities is sufficient for himself, but not for others.
Friends, a bhikkhu endowed with [another] four qualities is sufficient for others, but not for himself.
Which four?"
Here, friends, a bhikkhu is quick to understand wholesome states;
he is capable of retaining the teachings he has heard;
yet he does not investigate the meaning of the teachings he has retained.
And having understood the meaning and understood the Dhamma, he practices in accordance with the Dhamma;
he is a speaker of what is beautiful …pe… and he is one who instructs his fellow celibates …pe….
"Friends, a bhikkhu endowed with these four qualities is sufficient for others, but not for himself.
Friends, a bhikkhu endowed with three qualities is sufficient for himself, but not for others.
With which three?"
In this case, friends, a bhikkhu is not only quick to understand wholesome states,
but he is also naturally inclined to retain the teachings he has heard;
and having retained those teachings, he is one who investigates their meaning.
Having understood the meaning and understood the Dhamma, one practices in accordance with the Dhamma;
yet one is not a speaker of good speech … [and so on] … nor is one an instructor of one’s fellow celibates.
"Friends, a bhikkhu endowed with these three qualities is sufficient for himself, but not for others.
Friends, a bhikkhu endowed with [another] three qualities is sufficient for others, but not for himself.
With which three?"
In this case, friends, a bhikkhu is not one who possesses quick comprehension regarding wholesome states;
yet he is one who has the habit of retaining the teachings he has heard,
though he does not investigate the meaning of those teachings he has retained.
And having understood the meaning and understood the Dhamma, he practices in accordance with the Dhamma;
he is a speaker of what is good … [as before] … for the purpose of making the meaning known;
and he is one who instructs his fellow celibates … [as before] … in the holy life.
"Friends, a bhikkhu endowed with these three qualities is capable of helping others, but not himself.
Friends, a bhikkhu endowed with two qualities is capable of helping himself, but not others.
With which two?"
In this case, friends, a bhikkhu is not one who possesses quick comprehension regarding wholesome states;
nor is he one who has the habit of retaining the teachings he has heard;
yet he is one who examines the meaning of the teachings he has retained.
Having understood the goal and having understood the Dhamma, he practices in accordance with the Dhamma;
yet he is not one of beautiful speech … [and so on] … nor is he one who instructs his fellow celibates.
"Friends, a bhikkhu endowed with these two qualities is sufficient for himself, but not for others.
Friends, a bhikkhu endowed with two other qualities is sufficient for others, but not for himself.
Which two?"
In this case, friends, a bhikkhu is not one who quickly gains confidence in wholesome states;
nor is he one who has the habit of retaining the teachings he has heard;
nor is he one who examines the meaning of the teachings he has retained.
And having understood the goal and understood the Dhamma, he practices in accordance with the Dhamma;
he is a good speaker, possessed of a beautiful voice, endowed with speech that is courteous, distinct, flawless, and expressive of the meaning;
and he is one who instructs, urges, rouses, and gladdens his fellow celibates.
“Friends, a bhikkhu who possesses these two qualities is capable of helping others, but not himself.
The eighth. *Aṅguttara Nikāya* 8.79
8. Yamaka Chapter:
Discourse on Decline (Parihānasutta) (AN 8.79, PTS AN iv 331)
“Bhikkhus, these eight things lead to the decline of a bhikkhu who is a trainee.
What eight?

Delight in work, delight in talk, delight in sleep, delight in company, lack of restraint over the sense faculties, lack of moderation in eating, delight in socializing, and delight in conceptual proliferation.”
“Monks, these eight qualities lead to the decline of a bhikkhu who is still in training.
Monks, these eight qualities lead to the non-decline of a bhikkhu who is still in training.
What are the eight?”

"Not delighting in work, not delighting in talk, not delighting in sleep, not delighting in company; guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, delighting in non-association, and delighting in the unproliferated—these, monks, are the eight qualities that lead to the non-decline of a bhikkhu in training.
Thus ends the ninth [discourse].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.80 8. Yamaka Vagga Kusītārambhavatthu Sutta:

The Foundation for Laziness and Exertion “Monks, there are these two foundations for laziness. What two? Delight in sleep and delight in company. These, monks, are the two foundations for laziness. “There are, monks, these two foundations for the arousal of energy. What two? Discontent with regard to all unwholesome states and delight in undertaking wholesome states. These, monks, are the two foundations for the arousal of energy.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these eight grounds for laziness.
What are the eight?
In this case, monks, a monk has work to be done.
It occurs to him:
“I have work that must be done. While doing the work, my body will become weary. Come now, I shall lie down.”
Thus he lies down and does not arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the reaching of the unreached, for the realization of the unrealized.
This, monks, is the first ground of laziness.
Furthermore, monks, a deed has been done by a monk.
It occurs to him:
"I have indeed performed work. While performing that work, my body is weary. Come now, I shall lie down.
He lies down; he does not arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the reaching of the unreached, for the realization of the unrealized.
This, monks, is the second ground for laziness.
Furthermore, monks, a monk must travel along a road.
It occurs to him:
‘I shall have a road to travel. While traveling on that road, my body will become weary. Come now, I shall lie down.
He lies down and does not arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the reaching of the unreached, for the realization of the unrealized.
This, monks, is the third ground of laziness.
Furthermore, monks, a monk has traveled along a road.
It occurs to him:
“I have indeed traveled along a road. While traveling along the road, my body is weary. Come now, I shall lie down.”
He lies down and does not arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the reaching of the unreached, for the realization of the unrealized.
This, monks, is the fourth ground of laziness.
Furthermore, monks, while a monk is wandering for alms in a village or town, he does not obtain sufficient and complete food, whether coarse or refined, to his heart's content.
It occurs to him:

“While wandering for alms in a village or town, I did not obtain as much coarse or refined food as I required for my full satisfaction. My body is weary and unfit for work; come now, I shall lie down.
He lies down and does not arouse energy... [as before]...
This, monks, is the fifth ground for laziness.
Furthermore, monks, while a monk is wandering for alms in a village or town, he obtains as much as he needs and a full measure of food, whether coarse or refined.
It occurs to him:
‘While wandering for alms in a village or town, I received as much coarse or refined food as I required for my full satisfaction.
My body is heavy and unwieldy, as if covered with fat. Come now, I shall lie down.
He lies down and does not arouse energy... [as before] ...”
This, monks, is the sixth ground for laziness.
Furthermore, monks, a slight illness arises in a monk.
It occurs to him:
‘This slight ailment has arisen in me; it would be fitting for me to lie down. Come now, I shall lie down.
He lies down and does not arouse energy...
This, monks, is the seventh ground of laziness.
Furthermore, monks, a monk has recovered from an illness and has not long been free from that sickness.
It occurs to him:
‘I have indeed recovered from an illness and have not long been free from that sickness; my body is weak and unworkable. Come now, I shall lie down.’
Thus he lies down and does not arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the reaching of the unreached, for the realization of the unrealized.
This, monks, is the eighth ground of laziness.
These, monks, are the eight grounds of laziness.
“Monks, there are these eight grounds for undertaking action. What eight?
Here, monks, a task is to be performed by a monk.”
It occurs to him:
"I have work that must be done. While performing this work, it will not be easy for me to attend to the teaching of the Buddhas.
Come now, I shall exert energy in advance for the attainment of what has not been attained and for the realization of what has not been realized."

‘For the attainment of what has not been attained, for the realization of what has not been realized, for the direct experience of what has not been directly experienced. He arouses energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the realization of the unrealized, for the direct experience of the unexperienced.
This, monks, is the first ground for exertion.
Furthermore, monks, a monk has performed an action.
It occurs to him:
‘I have indeed performed an action; while performing that action, however, I was unable to attend to the teaching of the Buddhas.’
‘Let me arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the achievement of the unachieved, for the realization of the unrealized.

It occurs to him:

This, monks, is the third ground for exertion.

and it occurs to him:
“I indeed set out on a journey. While traveling on that journey, I was unable to attend to the teaching of the Buddhas.
Come now, let me arouse energy…” … “This, monks, is the fourth basis for exertion.

9. Sativagga Satisampajaññasutta (AN 8.81, PTS AN iv 336) “Monks, when mindfulness and clear comprehension are developed and cultivated, they lead to a great result and great benefit. And how, monks, are mindfulness and clear comprehension developed and cultivated so as to lead to a great result and great benefit? Here, monks, a monk is mindful of the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating the nature of arising in the body, he dwells contemplating the nature of passing away in the body, he dwells contemplating the nature of both arising and passing away in the body; further, his mindfulness that ‘there is a body’ is established to the extent necessary for bare knowledge and mindfulness. And he dwells independent, not clinging to anything in the world. He is mindful of feelings in feelings... He is mindful of the mind in the mind... He is mindful of phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating the nature of arising in phenomena, he dwells contemplating the nature of passing away in phenomena, he dwells contemplating the nature of both arising and passing away in phenomena; further, his mindfulness that ‘there are phenomena’ is established to the extent necessary for bare knowledge and mindfulness. And he dwells independent, not clinging to anything in the world. It is in this way, monks, that mindfulness and clear comprehension are developed and cultivated so as to lead to a great result and great benefit.”
“Bhikkhus, when mindfulness and clear comprehension are absent, for one deficient in mindfulness and clear comprehension, moral shame and moral dread lack their proximate cause.
When moral shame and moral dread are absent, for one deficient in moral shame and moral dread, restraint of the sense faculties lacks its proximate cause.
When restraint of the sense faculties is absent, for one deficient in restraint of the sense faculties, virtuous conduct lacks its proximate cause.”
When virtue is absent, for one deficient in virtue, right concentration lacks its proximate cause.
When right concentration is absent, for one deficient in right concentration, the knowledge and vision of things as they truly are lacks its proximate cause.

When the knowledge and vision of things as they truly are is absent, for one deficient in the knowledge and vision of things as they truly are, disenchantment and dispassion lack their proximate cause.
When disenchantment and dispassion are absent, for one devoid of disenchantment and dispassion, the knowledge and vision of liberation lacks its proximate cause. Just as, monks,
a tree that is deprived of branches and foliage does not reach full development in its shoots, nor in its bark, nor in its sapwood, nor in its heartwood— so too, monks,
when mindfulness and clear comprehension are absent, for one devoid of mindfulness and clear comprehension, moral shame and moral dread lack their proximate cause.
When moral shame and moral dread are absent, for one deficient in moral shame and moral dread, the proximate cause is destroyed...
[and so on] ...up to the knowledge and vision of liberation.
When mindfulness and clear comprehension are present, bhikkhus, for one endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension, moral shame and moral dread possess their proximate cause.
When there is moral shame and dread of wrongdoing, for one endowed with moral shame and dread of wrongdoing, restraint of the sense faculties is endowed with its proximate cause.
When there is restraint of the sense faculties, for one endowed with restraint of the sense faculties, virtuous conduct is endowed with its proximate cause.
When there is virtuous conduct, for one endowed with virtuous conduct, right concentration is endowed with its proximate cause.
When right concentration exists, for one endowed with right concentration, the knowledge and vision of things as they really are is possessed of its proximate cause.

When the knowledge and vision of things as they really are exists, for one endowed with the knowledge and vision of things as they really are, disenchantment and dispassion are possessed of their proximate cause.
When disenchantment and dispassion exist, for one endowed with disenchantment and dispassion, the knowledge and vision of liberation is possessed of its proximate cause.

“Just as, monks, a tree endowed with branches and foliage reaches fullness in its outer bark, its inner bark, its softwood, and its heartwood—just so, monks, when there is mindfulness and clear comprehension, for one endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension, moral shame and moral dread reach their supporting conditions;
when there is moral shame and moral dread, for one endowed with moral shame and moral dread, [the other qualities] reach their supporting conditions... [and so on].”
“...the knowledge and vision of liberation.

Then the Venerable Puṇṇiya approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. “It is not easy, Puṇṇiya, for one who has not seen for himself the nature of things to teach the Dhamma in brief. But since you have requested it, listen and attend closely; I will speak. “Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Puṇṇiya replied. The Blessed One said this: “Puṇṇiya, when a bhikkhu is mindful and clearly comprehending, he dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. When he dwells thus, Puṇṇiya, a bhikkhu is called ‘one who dwells in the presence of mindfulness. When this was said, the Venerable Puṇṇiya said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how does a bhikkhu dwell mindful and clearly comprehending? “Here, Puṇṇiya, a bhikkhu, having gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down. Having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness in front of him, ever mindful he breathes in, mindful he breathes out. Breathing in long, he understands: ‘I breathe in long’; or breathing out long, he understands: ‘I breathe out long. Breathing in short, he understands: ‘I breathe in short’; or breathing out short, he understands: ‘I breathe out short. He trains thus: ‘Experiencing the whole body, I shall breathe in’; he trains thus: ‘Experiencing the whole body, I shall breathe out. He trains thus: ‘Tranquillizing the bodily formation, I shall breathe in’; he trains thus: ‘Tranquillizing the bodily formation, I shall breathe out. Just as a skilled turner or his apprentice, when making a long turn, understands: ‘I make a long turn,’ or when making a short turn, understands: ‘I make a short turn’—so too, Puṇṇiya, a bhikkhu, breathing in long, understands: ‘I breathe in long’... [as above] ...he trains thus: ‘Tranquillizing the bodily formation, I shall breathe out. He feels the rapture that arises within the body and understands: ‘I feel rapture. He feels the pleasure that arises within the body and understands: ‘I feel pleasure. He feels the mental formations that arise within the body and understands: ‘I feel mental formations. He trains thus: ‘Tranquillizing the mental formations, I shall breathe in’; he trains thus: ‘Tranquillizing the mental formations, I shall breathe out. [as above] ...he trains thus: ‘Tranquillizing the mental formations, I shall breathe out. He feels the mind and understands: ‘I feel the mind. He gladdens the mind and understands: ‘I gladden the mind. He concentrates the mind and understands: ‘I concentrate the mind. He liberates the mind and understands: ‘I liberate the mind. Then the Venerable Puṇṇiya approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Puṇṇiya said this to the Blessed One:
“What, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the reason why sometimes the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dhamma occurs to him, and sometimes it does not?
“Puṇṇiya, a bhikkhu may have faith, yet he does not approach [the Teacher].”
The Tathāgata does not feel inclined to teach the Dhamma.
But when, Puṇṇiya, a bhikkhu is endowed with faith and approaches [the Teacher],
then the Tathāgata feels inclined to teach the Dhamma.
“Puṇṇiya, a bhikkhu may be endowed with faith, yet he does not approach [the teacher]; or he approaches, but he does not attend upon him;
or he attends upon him, but he does not inquire;
or he inquires, but he does not listen to the Dhamma with an attentive ear.”
One listens to the Dhamma with an attentive ear, yet having heard it, one does not retain the Dhamma;
or one retains the Dhamma after hearing it, yet one does not examine the meaning of the teachings retained;
or one examines the meaning of the teachings retained, yet having understood the meaning and understood the Dhamma, one does not practice in accordance with the Dhamma.
The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dhamma does not yet manifest itself to me.
But when, Puṇṇiya, a bhikkhu is endowed with faith, approaches [the teacher], pays respect, inquires,

listens to the Dhamma with attentive ears, and having heard it, retains the Dhamma in mind, and understands the meaning of the teachings he has retained— then the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dhamma manifests itself to him.
He investigates thoroughly, having understood the meaning and understood the Dhamma, and he practices in accordance with the Dhamma.
It is in this way that the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dhamma becomes manifest.
Puṇṇiya, when endowed with these eight qualities, the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dhamma is invariably manifest.”

Thus, bhikkhus, being asked by those wanderers of other sects, you should answer them in this way.”
The Third [Discourse].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.84 9. The Chapter on Mindfulness (Sativagga)
The Robbers Sutta (AN 8.84): “Bhikkhus,
a great robber endowed with eight factors quickly comes to ruin and does not last long.”

Which eight? He strikes back at one who does not strike him; he takes everything without leaving anything behind; he kills a woman; he violates a maiden; he plunders one who has gone forth; he plunders the royal treasury; he performs his work too close [to the king]; and he is not skilled in hoarding.
Possessing these eight factors, monks, a great thief quickly comes to ruin and does not last long.
“Monks, a great thief endowed with eight factors does not quickly come to ruin; he remains for a long time. With which eight?
He does not strike back at one who has not struck him; he does not take anything without leaving a remainder; he does not kill a woman; he does not defile a young girl.”
“He does not plunder those who have gone forth; he does not plunder the royal treasury; he does not carry out his work too close [to the city];
and he is skilled in hiding his hoard. Possessing these eight factors, monks, a great thief does not quickly come to ruin and remains for a long time.
This is the fourth.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.85 9. Sativagga Samaṇasutta (The Recluse) “Monks, there are these four kinds of recluses. What four? The recluse who is like a washed and cleaned cloth that is ready to take dye; the recluse who is like a bronze vessel that has been well polished and is ready to receive an image; the recluse who is like a dry, hollow gourd that is empty, open, and ready to receive water; and the recluse who is like a man who has lost his way and is wandering about in confusion. And how, monks, is a recluse like a washed and cleaned cloth that is ready to take dye? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... mind in the mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. This, monks, is called a recluse who is like a washed and cleaned cloth that is ready to take dye. And how, monks, is a recluse like a bronze vessel that has been well polished and is ready to receive an image? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body... feelings in feelings... mind in the mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. This, monks, is called a recluse who is like a bronze vessel that has been well polished and is ready to receive an image. And how, monks, is a recluse like a dry, hollow gourd that is empty, open, and ready to receive water? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body... feelings in feelings... mind in the mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. This, monks, is called a recluse who is like a dry, hollow gourd that is empty, open, and ready to receive water. And how, monks, is a recluse like a man who has lost his way and is wandering about in confusion? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, but his mind is distracted externally and not settled internally. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... mind in the mind... phenomena in phenomena, but his mind is distracted externally and not settled internally. This, monks, is called a recluse who is like a man who has lost his way and is wandering about in confusion. These, monks, are the four kinds of recluses.”
“‘Ascetic,’ monks,
is a designation for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
‘Brahmin,’ monks, is a designation for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.”
‘Master of the Vedas,’ monks, is a designation for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
‘Physician,’ monks, is a designation for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
‘Stainless,’ monks, is a designation for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
‘Vimala,’ monks, is a designation for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
‘Ñāṇī,’ monks, is a designation for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
‘Vimutta,’ monks, is a designation for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
That which is to be attained by a recluse,
by a brahmin who is established in virtue,
and that which is to be attained by one who has mastered the Vedas—
That which is to be attained by one who is stainless, pure, and virtuous— the unsurpassed state by means of the supreme physician.
That supreme state which is to be attained by the wise one who is liberated—
having conquered the battle, I am that one.
“Freed, I release from bondage;
I am no longer a nāga, but one supremely tamed,
an adept, fully extinguished.”
Fifth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.86 9.
Sativagga (The Chapter on Mindfulness)
The Yaśas Sutta.
On one occasion the Blessed One, while wandering on tour among the Kosalans with a large community of monks, arrived at a brahmin village of the Kosalans named Icchānaṅgala.
There the Blessed One stayed at Icchānaṅgala, in the grove of Icchānaṅgala.
The brahmin householders of Icchānaṅgala heard:
"The ascetic Gotama, the son of the Sakyans who went forth from the Sakyan clan, has arrived at Icchānaṅgala and is staying at Icchānaṅgala in the grove of Icchānaṅgala."
Furthermore, this excellent report of the venerable Gotama has spread abroad:
“Such indeed is that Blessed One— worthy and perfectly enlightened … it is truly good to see such worthy ones.”

Then, when that night had passed, the brahmin householders of Icchānaṅgala took a great quantity of hard and soft food and approached the Icchānaṅgala forest grove; having arrived, they stood outside the gatehouse,
making a loud noise and a great clamor.
Now at that time, the Venerable Nāgita was the Blessed One’s attendant.
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Nāgita:
“Nāgita, what is this loud noise, this great clamor? One would think it were fishermen over a haul of fish.”

“Venerable sir, these brahmin householders of Icchānaṅgala have brought abundant food, both hard and soft, and are standing outside the gate, intending it specifically for the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
“Nāgita, let there be no meeting with fame, and let there be no fame from me.
For whoever, Nāgita, does not [cling] to this happiness of renunciation, this happiness of seclusion, this happiness of peace, this happiness of enlightenment—”

"May he be one who obtains at will, without difficulty, and without trouble. For if I am one who obtains at will, without difficulty, and without trouble that bliss of renunciation, that bliss of seclusion, that bliss of peace,
and that bliss of awakening, then he might accept that filthy pleasure, that drowsy pleasure, that pleasure of gain, honor, and fame."
“May the Blessed One now consent, venerable sir; may the Sugata now consent.
Now is the time for the Blessed One’s consent, venerable sir.
Whichever way the Blessed One goes now, venerable sir, the brahmins and householders, both those of the towns and the countryside, will incline in that very direction.”
"Just as, venerable sir, when it rains in thick drops, the waters flow along according to the slope of the land;
even so, venerable sir, wherever the Blessed One now goes, the brahmins, householders, townspeople, and countryfolk will incline in that very direction. And why is that?"
"For it is thus, Bhante, with the Blessed One’s virtue and wisdom.
"Nāgita, let there be no meeting of me with fame, and let there be no fame for me.
For whoever, Nāgita, does not [cling] to this happiness of renunciation, this happiness of seclusion, this happiness of peace, this happiness of awakening—"

May he be one who obtains at will, without difficulty, and without trouble. If I am one who obtains at will, without difficulty, and without trouble that bliss of renunciation, that bliss of seclusion, that bliss of peace,
and that bliss of enlightenment, then he might accept that dregs of pleasure, that slothful pleasure, that pleasure of gain, honor, and fame.
Furthermore, Nāgita, there are some deities who do not obtain at will,
without difficulty, and without hardship, this happiness of renunciation,
this happiness of seclusion, this happiness of peace, this happiness of awakening, which I obtain at will, without difficulty, and without hardship.
“Nāgita, when you too live gathered together, assembled, and devoted to dwelling in social company, this thought occurs to you:

‘Surely these venerable ones must not be obtaining at will, without difficulty, and without hardship, this happiness of renunciation, this happiness of seclusion, this happiness of peace, this happiness of awakening—of which I [have spoken]. [And so on regarding the happiness of renunciation...]
"One who gains at will, without difficulty or trouble, the bliss of seclusion, the bliss of peace,
and the bliss of enlightenment— yet these venerable ones, having gathered and come together, dwell devoted to living in company. Here, Nāgita,
I see monks laughing and playing with one another, poking each other with their fingers.
Then, Nāgita, this occurred to me:

"Surely these venerable ones must be those who obtain at will, without difficulty, and without hardship, this happiness of renunciation, this happiness of seclusion, this happiness of peace, and this happiness of awakening— this happiness of renunciation for which I [strive]."
"One who is a companion in the bliss of seclusion, the bliss of tranquility, and the bliss of enlightenment obtains these at will, without difficulty, and without hardship.
Yet, venerable sirs, you instead joke and play with one another by poking each other with your fingers!

But here, Nāgita, I see monks who, having eaten as much as they desire until their bellies are full, dwell devoted to the pleasure of lying down, the pleasure of reclining, and the pleasure of sloth."
Then, Nāgita, this occurred to me:
‘Surely these venerable ones must be obtainers of this happiness of renunciation, this happiness of seclusion, this happiness of peace,
this happiness of awakening, at will, without difficulty, and without hardship— this happiness of renunciation of which I [am speaking].’”
"One who gains at will, without difficulty, and without hardship, the bliss of seclusion, the bliss of peace, and the bliss of enlightenment.
Yet these venerable ones, having eaten as much as they desire until their bellies are full, dwell devoted to the pleasure of reclining, the pleasure of lying down, and the pleasure of drowsiness.
Here, Nāgita, I see a bhikkhu living in a village dwelling who is seated in concentration."
Then, Nāgita, this thought occurred to me:
"Now either a monastery attendant or a novice will attend upon this venerable one, and he will cause him to fall away from that concentration.
Therefore, Nāgita, I was not pleased with that bhikkhu’s dwelling in the vicinity of a village.
Furthermore, Nāgita, I see a forest-dwelling bhikkhu sitting nodding in the forest.
Then, Nāgita, it occurs to me:
‘Now this venerable one, having dispelled this fatigue of drowsiness, will attend to the very perception of the forest as a single unity.’
Therefore, Nāgita, I am pleased with that bhikkhu’s dwelling in the forest.
However, Nāgita, here I see a forest-dwelling bhikkhu sitting in the forest who is not concentrated.
Then, Nāgita, this occurs to me:
‘Now this venerable one will concentrate his unconcentrated mind, or he will protect his concentrated mind.
For that reason, Nāgita, I am pleased with that bhikkhu’s dwelling in the forest.
But here, Nāgita, I see a bhikkhu who is a forest-dweller sitting in the forest with a concentrated mind.
It occurs to me, Nāgita:
‘Now this venerable one will either liberate an unliberated mind, or he will protect a liberated mind.
Therefore, Nāgita, I am pleased with that bhikkhu’s dwelling in the forest.
Furthermore, Nāgita, here I see a bhikkhu living in a village who receives robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
Craving that gain, honor, and fame, he neglects seclusion and neglects remote lodgings in forests and jungle groves;
having descended to the village, town, or capital, he makes his dwelling there.
Therefore, Nāgita, I am not pleased with that bhikkhu’s dwelling in the vicinity of a village.
But here, Nāgita, I see a forest-dwelling bhikkhu who receives robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick;
yet, having set aside those gains, honors, and fame, he does not neglect seclusion, nor does he neglect remote lodgings in forests and jungle groves.
"Therefore, Nāgita, I am pleased with that bhikkhu’s dwelling in the forest.

Because, Nāgita, when I am traveling along a highway at a time when I see no one ahead or behind me, on that occasion, Nāgita, I have comfort even for the purpose of attending to defecation and urination.
The sixth [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.87 9. Sativagga Pattanikujjanasutta – The Discourse on Bending the Alms Bowl "Bhikkhus, there are these eight qualities of one who bends his alms bowl down. What eight? (1) Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is endowed with faith; he places faith in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata thus: 'The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. This is the first quality of one who bends his alms bowl down. (2) Again, a bhikkhu is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of good conduct and resort, seeing danger in minute faults. Having undertaken the training rules, he trains in them. This is the second quality of one who bends his alms bowl down. (3) Again, a bhikkhu has learned much, remembers what he has learned, and accumulates what he has learned. Those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the perfectly complete and pure spiritual life—such teachings as these he has learned much of, retained in mind, recited verbally, investigated mentally, and penetrated well through view. This is the third quality of one who bends his alms bowl down. (4) Again, a bhikkhu is one who gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the four jhānas that constitute the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life. This is the fourth quality of one who bends his alms bowl down. (5) Again, a bhikkhu possesses the wisdom that arises from seclusion, which is noble and penetrative and leads to the complete destruction of suffering. This is the fifth quality of one who bends his alms bowl down. (6) Again, a bhikkhu is one who gains the noble eye of Dhamma; he sees that 'This is suffering'... 'This is the origin of suffering'... 'This is the cessation of suffering'... 'This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. This is the sixth quality of one who bends his alms bowl down. (7) Again, a bhikkhu is one who gains the noble knowledge; he knows that 'Birth is destroyed, the spiritual life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being. This is the seventh quality of one who bends his alms bowl down. (8) Again, a bhikkhu is one who gains the noble liberation; he is liberated by non-clinging through the destruction of craving. This is the eighth quality of one who bends his alms bowl down. These, bhikkhus, are the eight qualities of one who bends his alms bowl down."
“Bhikkhus, when a lay follower is possessed of eight qualities, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may overturn his bowl. Which eight? [The text continues with the eight qualities.]”
He strives for the non-acquisition of gains for the bhikkhus; he strives for the harm of the bhikkhus;
he strives for the displacement of the bhikkhus; he reviles and abuses the bhikkhus; he causes dissension among the bhikkhus;
he speaks dispraise of the Buddha; he speaks dispraise of the Dhamma; he speaks dispraise of the Saṅgha.
“Monks, when a lay follower is endowed with these eight qualities, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may overturn his bowl.
Monks, when a lay follower is endowed with eight qualities, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may turn his bowl upright.
What are the eight?”
He does not strive for the monks' lack of gain; he does not strive for the monks' harm;
he does not strive for the monks' displacement from their dwellings; he does not revile or abuse the monks; he does not cause dissension among the monks;
he speaks in praise of the Buddha, he speaks in praise of the Dhamma, and he speaks in praise of the Saṅgha.
“Monks, when a lay follower is possessed of these eight qualities, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may overturn his bowl.
Thus was the seventh [sutta]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.88

9. Sativagga Appasādapavedanīyasutta (AN 8.88, PTS AN iv 345) “Monks, there are these five things that should be experienced with a lack of confidence. What five? One experiences with a lack of confidence: ‘I am subject to aging; I have not transcended aging. One experiences with a lack of confidence: ‘I am subject to illness; I have not transcended illness. One experiences with a lack of confidence: ‘I am subject to death; I have not transcended death. One experiences with a lack of confidence: ‘I will grow different, become another, and pass away; I will cease to be what I am. One experiences with a lack of confidence: ‘Whatever in this world is acquired through clinging and cherished, all that is subject to change, to vanishing, to dissolution, to dispassion, and to cessation. These, monks, are the five things that should be experienced with a lack of confidence.”
“Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu possesses eight qualities, lay followers who so desire may proclaim their lack of confidence in him.
What are the eight?
He strives for the loss of householders; he strives for the harm of householders; he reviles and insults householders.”
He causes a layperson to fall away from other laypersons; he speaks dispraise of the Buddha; he speaks dispraise of the Dhamma;
he speaks dispraise of the Saṅgha; and they see him in improper resort.
It is when a bhikkhu possesses these eight qualities, bhikkhus, that lay followers who so desire might announce their lack of confidence in him.
“Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu possesses eight qualities, lay followers who desire it may express their confidence in him.
What are the eight?
He does not strive for the loss of householders; he does not strive for the harm of householders; he does not revile householders.”

“He reviles [the laity], yet he does not cause a householder to be divided from other householders; he speaks in praise of the Buddha, he speaks in praise of the Dhamma, he speaks in praise of the Saṅgha, and they see him in his proper sphere of activity.
Possessed of these eight qualities, monks, lay followers who so desire would proclaim their confidence in a bhikkhu.”
The Eighth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.89 9.

The Discourse on the Act of Reconciliation (Paṭisāraṇīyasutta).
“Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu possesses eight qualities, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out an act of reconciliation against him.”
Which eight? He strives for the loss of householders; he strives for the harm of householders; he reviles and abuses householders;
he causes dissension among householders; he speaks dispraise of the Buddha; he speaks dispraise of the Dhamma; he [speaks dispraise] of the Saṅgha...
He speaks dispraise of [a fellow monk], and he does not fulfill his lawful promise to laypeople.
Monks, when a monk possesses these eight qualities, the Saṅgha may, if it so desires, carry out a procedure of reconciliation against him.
Monks, when a monk possesses eight qualities, the Saṅgha may, if it so desires, suspend a procedure of reconciliation against him.
Which eight? He does not strive for the loss of householders; he does not strive for the harm of householders; he does not revile or abuse householders;
he does not cause division between householders; he speaks in praise of the Buddha; he speaks in praise of the Dhamma.
“He speaks in praise of the Saṅgha and fulfills his lawful promise to laypeople.
Monks, when a monk possesses these eight qualities, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may revoke the act of reconciliation.
Thus ends the ninth [section].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.90 9. Sativagga Sammāvattanā Sutta: Right Conduct “Monks, there are these eight qualities of one who conducts themselves rightly. What eight? (1) Here, monks, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus:

‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. (2) He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally realized by the wise. (3) He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. (4) He possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones—unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, freeing, praised by the wise, ungrasped, leading to concentration. (5) He has heard much, retained what he has heard, stored what he has heard. Whatever teachings are admirable in the beginning, admirable in the middle, and admirable in the end, which proclaim the holy life both in its particulars and in its essence, entirely complete, surpassingly pure: such teachings he has heard much of, retained, and stored. (6) He is content with any kind of robe, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites. (7) He is easy to correct and possesses qualities that make him easy to correct; he is patient and receives instruction respectfully. (8) He is endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension regarding his bodily postures and activities. These, monks, are the eight qualities of one who conducts themselves rightly.”
“Monks, a monk who has had a *tassapāpiyasika-kamma* performed against him should conduct himself rightly in eight matters: he should not confer full ordination;
he should not give formal support (*nissaya*); he should not have a novice attend upon him; he should not be appointed as an instructor of bhikkhunīs...”
He must not accept [any formal act]; even though he has been authorized, he must not exhort the bhikkhunīs; he must not accept any authorization from the Saṅgha;
he must not be appointed to any individual position; nor must he be rehabilitated on the basis of that root offense.
"Monks, a monk who has had a *tassapāpiyasika* legal procedure performed against him should conduct himself properly in these eight matters."
The tenth.
The fourth chapter on Mindfulness.
Its summary verse:
The fifth [was attained] by the monk Cora through the root of the merit of the *Satipaṭṭhāna*; Yaśas,
through faith in the Tathāgata.
And the procedure of reconciliation.

The Series on Passion (Rāgapeyyāla).

What eight?”

11. The Series on Lust (Rāgapeyyāla).
“Bhikkhus, for the direct knowledge of lust, eight things are to be developed.”
Which eight?
Perceiving forms internally, one sees forms externally that are limited, beautiful or ugly;
having mastered them, one has the perception: "I know, I see."
Perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are immeasurable, beautiful or ugly; having mastered them, one has the perception: “I know, I see.
Not perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are limited, beautiful or ugly; having mastered them, one has the perception: “I know, I see.
Not perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are immeasurable, beautiful or ugly; having mastered them, one has the perception: “I know, I see.”
Not perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are blue, blue-colored, blue in appearance, and blue in luster;
or yellow, yellow-colored...
[and so on] ...or red, red-colored... [and so on].
“White things, white in color... with a white radiance;
having mastered these, one perceives thus: ‘I know, I see.
For the direct knowledge of lust, monks, these eight things are to be developed.”
Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.11.

Rāgapeyyāla (AN 8.120, PTS AN iv 349) [The Section on Lust] “Bhikkhus, there are these eight persons worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. What eight? The one liberated-in-both-ways, the one liberated-by-wisdom, the body-witness, the one attained-to-view, the one liberated-by-faith, the Dhamma-follower, the faith-follower, and the person who is a stream-enterer. These, bhikkhus, are the eight persons worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. [And so on with the remaining suttas of the Rāgapeyyāla section.]
“Monks, for the direct knowledge of lust, eight things are to be developed.
What eight?
Possessing form, one sees forms; not perceiving form internally, one sees forms externally; being intent upon the beautiful...”

By completely transcending perceptions of form, by the disappearance of perceptions of sensory resistance, and by non-attention to perceptions of diversity, thinking "space is infinite," he enters and dwells in the base of infinite space; by completely transcending the base of infinite space, thinking "consciousness is infinite," he enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness;
by completely transcending the base of infinite space... [he enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness].
Having completely transcended the base of infinite consciousness, thinking "there is nothing," he enters and dwells in the base of nothingness;
having completely transcended the base of nothingness, he enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
having completely transcended the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling.
“Bhikkhus, for direct knowledge of lust, these eight things are to be developed.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.11.

these eight things are to be developed.
